My dog, Reggie, has Cherry eye. If left untreated, can it have a negative effect on his vision? Money is an matter for me right now.â.

Cherry eye happens when the gland of the third eyelid, which helps produce tears, slips out of its normal position and becomes visible as a pink or red cherry-looking bulge in the corner of your dog's eye. I understand that veterinary expenses can be difficult to manage, and it is notable to know what needs attention right away and what can safely wait a bit longer.

Industry observers note that cherry eye does not usually cause blindness directly, but leaving it untreated can put Reggie's eye health at risk. The exposed gland can become irritated, inflamed, or damaged, and its tear production may be reduced over time. Because this gland contributes to keeping the eye moist and protected, reduced tear production can increase the risk of dry eye, a condition that can lead to corneal damage, scarring, and impaired vision if it becomes severe. Think of the gland as part of the eye's built-in lubrication system. Even if the eye looks comfortable today, problems can develop gradually.

If surgery is not financially possible right now, please arrange a veterinary examination to confirm the diagnosis, assess tear production, and check the cornea.

Industry observers note that talk to your vet about a payment blueprint, or you might be able to find a veterinary teaching hospital or nonprofit clinic that may offer lower-cost care. Your veterinarian may recommend a suitable lubricating eye product while you work toward surgery, but lubrication will not reposition the gland. Please make sure you avoid human eye drops, leftover medications, or steroid eye drops unless specifically prescribed, as some of these can worsen an undiagnosed corneal ulcer. The gland should generally be repositioned and preserved rather than removed. If the gland is removed, you would need to use eye drops to supplement Reggieâs tear production for the rest of his life.

Please seek same-day veterinary care if you see Reggie squinting, holding the eye closed, rubbing it persistently, developing a cloudy or bluish cornea, or producing thick yellow or green discharge. These can be signs of a painful or more serious eye problem. If the eye is comfortable and clear, it may not be an immediate emergency, but I would not leave cherry eye unassessed for weeks or months. The most crucial first step is protecting the eye while finding an affordable treatment option.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that did you know that your compost pile keeps working over winter? While the decomposition process might slow, microorganisms are still active in compost as long as it doesn’t freeze. Ignoring your compost over winter is a missed opportunity to keep making and using the garden's black gold.

In a recent development, during winter composting, microorganisms slow down their activities, and freezing temperatures can temporarily stop them, but they won’t necessarily die. A sufficiently large and well-managed compost pile can stay warm enough in the center to keep the little critters working and breaking down waste materials.

According to recent reports, tackle these six tasks now to keep composting at home this winter. Even if decomposition slows in the cold, these steps will help you get more usable compost earlier next spring. Our tips work for all main types of composting, including open heaps, compost bins, and enclosed tumblers.

Now is a good time to remove any finished compost to use as winter mulch in your garden beds. Then, it’s time for one last turn for the season. Turning compost helps aerate the pile, introducing oxygen to the microorganisms that need it to decompose materials. It also distributes moisture and materials more evenly.

A sturdy garden fork will do the job, but a compost aerator tool, like this Squeeze Master one from Amazon, makes it much easier to get air deep into the pile without having to dig everything out and turn it by hand.

This should be your final turn before freezing conditions begin. You don’t want to keep turning compost over the winter, as this will release heat and slow the decomposition process. As you make the final turn, look for and break up any wet clumps or large pieces of material that haven’t broken down much. If you note a sour or rotten smell, add more dry, brown materials.

Industry observers note that larger compost piles retain heat better than smaller piles because they have a greater volume of material relative to their surface area, which is exposed to the cold. The more you can add to your pile now, the more likely it is that the center will remain warm and active throughout winter. A long-probe compost thermometer, like the Vivosun Compost, is a handy way to check what's happening deep inside the pile without disturbing it.

Sources indicate that for a compost pile, aim for three feet (0.9 m) wide, deep, and high. Bulk up your pile during your final turn, adding a good mix of green and brown materials. Be sure to add enough dry, coarse material to absorb moisture. A large pile won’t be any good if it becomes waterlogged and so compacted that there is no airflow.

Sources indicate that while you don’t want to turn your compost again this winter, you can still add layers of waste to it as the season progresses. Green materials, like kitchen scraps, keep coming all winter, but brown materials tend to be harder to come by. Browns include dry leaves and twigs as well as cardboard, untreated paper, and straw.

Good compost should have layers of each type of material, so stockpile your harder-to-find browns now. As you add kitchen scraps over the winter, layer in some of these stockpiled brown materials to maintain a good balance. A countertop compost caddy, like the Oxo Good Grips Easy-Clean Compost Bin, makes it easy to collect kitchen waste indoors until you're ready to take it outside. Keep a bin or pile of leaves and twigs from fall yard waste, as well as shredded paper and cardboard.

A large pile with extra waste material will help insulate the active center of your compost pile, but you can also take extra steps to insulate and protect it from cold winter temperatures. This will slow heat loss. It’s notable that you take insulating steps before the compost pile freezes.

One easy way to insulate the pile is to surround it on all sides with straw bales or bags of leaves. If you don't have straw on hand, you can pick up full-sized straw bales from Tractor Supply to create a protective barrier around your compost pile. You can also add a layer of straw or leaves on top. Wood chips and finished compost are also efficient insulators.

Sources indicate that if you have a bin or tumbler, another option is to surround it with insulating materials. Just be sure you still have easy access to add materials throughout winter.

Sources indicate that winter precipitation can saturate a compost pile, causing it to become compacted and reducing airflow. Moisture can also wash away the valuable nutrients you’re trying to collect. If you have an open compost pile, cover it with a tarp that will allow precipitation to run off and away from the compost. A heavy-duty Everbilt tarp from Home Depot is a durable option that you can secure in place to keep winter rain and snow out. If you have a bin, keep a lid on it.

According to recent reports, while keeping moisture out is vital, compost still needs airflow in winter. Don’t completely seal your pile with protective coverings. If you have a bin with a cover, there should be drainage and air holes. Make sure these don’t get clogged.

Industry observers note that moisture balance is always important in compost. It’s important to check and adjust this balance before your compost freezes this winter. To optimize microorganism activity, the composting material should feel damp when you squeeze it in your hand without excess moisture running out of it.

If your compost feels too wet, incorporate more dry, brown material. If the pile is too dry, you can add a little water before there is a real danger of it freezing. Throughout winter, as long as temperatures allow it, continue to check the pile for moisture balance and adjust as needed.

Sources indicate that many gardeners might wonder: are these efforts worthwhile, or does compost just shut down for winter? Compost does continue to break down in winter, sometimes with temporary stops during freezing conditions.

Sources indicate that however, it’s important to have realistic expectations. While microorganisms continue to break down compostable materials in winter, their processes do slow down significantly. Larger, insulated piles are more likely to stay active and break down faster than smaller piles or compost in uninsulated bins. Taking these steps to keep your pile warmer in winter is worth the effort if you can keep microorganisms active and working.

It’s important to note that if you practice vermicomposting, you should provide extra protection for the worms over winter. To keep it active over winter, keep your vermicompost bin indoors where you can control the temperature.

Sources indicate that winter doesn't have to put composting on hold. A little preparation in autumn can protect valuable organic material, reduce household waste, and give you a head start on producing nutrient-rich compost for the next growing season.

Sock Thieves, Bathtub Sleepers, and Other Household Oddballs.

Furry weirdos have interesting, different habits; Embark's examples include a dog who sleeps upside down in the bathtub, one who carries a sock around without chewing it, and a canine who spins exactly three times before lying down. Not two. Not four. Three.

Then there's the dog who refuses to walk past one particular house, or the dinner diva who won't touch a meal until someone has given it the full restaurant treatment.

According to recent reports, A sock might be a very treasured object, a source of comfort, a reminder of their favorite personâs scent, or simply something fun to carry. It has been revealed that of course, some dogs are just little weirdos, and that's part of their charm. But there's a difference between a pup who has always slept with their legs in the air and one who suddenly starts acting strangely. If your pup begins staring at walls, repeating the same movements, or turning down food when that's not normal for them, don't automatically label it as a new amusing personality trait. Pain, illness, and anxiety can all show up as changes in behavior. If something feels off, put the camera down and call the vet.

Sources indicate that genes can influence behavioral tendencies, but they don't write a complete script for an individual dog's life. Learning and environment play a substantial role, too, sometimes in ways pet parents never intended.

Take the sock thief. A dog grabs a sock, their pet parents react with dramatic excitement, and suddenly the household is involved in a thrilling chase. From our perspective, it's a laundry crime. From the pup's perspective, it may be an excellent fresh game.

Sources indicate that behaviors that lead to positive or rewarding outcomes are more likely to happen again. Attention, play, food, and access to preferred activities can all reinforce behavior, even when nobody is training anything on purpose.

It has been revealed that genetics can contribute, too. Inherited tendencies may influence a dog's motivation to chase, retrieve, explore, or seek food. But a predisposition doesn't guarantee a particular behavior, nor does it explain every individual habit. A dog's behavior comes from a combination of biology and learned experience, which is often less convenient than blaming everything on their breed, but it is much closer to reality.

A 2022 study published in Science looked at the behavior and DNA of thousands of dogs. Researchers found that a dog's breed explained only about 9% of the differences in behavior between individual dogs. In other words, dogs of the same breed can have very different personalities and behaviors. Genetics plays a role, but it doesn't tell the whole story.

That doesn't mean genetics is irrelevant. The researchers found evidence that many behavioral traits do have a heritable component. Rather, the findings show why breed alone is a poor crystal ball for predicting how an individual dog will behave.

Some dogs may be especially motivated to retrieve, chase, or investigate, reflecting tendencies shaped partly by their ancestry and breeding history. But individual dogs still vary, and experience helps shape how those tendencies appear. However, with more data, we may learn new things; science is ever evolving along with our technologies.

Embark's Behavior Insights & Training feature connects genetic information with behavioral insights and training guidance. Genetic results can be useful, but they are one piece of the puzzle and not a personality prediction.

Behavior is best understood in context. Has the habit been present for years, or did it start last week? What happens before the behavior? Could pain, fear, stress, or another medical problem be contributing?

According to recent reports, if a pup is safe and comfortable, there's often no reason to stop a peculiar routine unless itâs a problem. A dog who carries a favorite toy around the house doesn't need a corrective training plan. When a behavior does create a problem, redirection and positive reinforcement can help teach an alternative response without relying on intimidation or punishment. This is the science of behavioral modification.

The goal isn't to turn every pup into a perfectly polished obedience champion, but to help us understand what each dog needs and help them become great family members.

It has been revealed that catster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission at no cost to you. Learn more.

Humans have a rather complex and contradictory relationship with their hair. Many of us willingly put ourselves through torturous procedures to remove it from our legs, armpits, and just about anywhere else, while, at the same time, the quest to keep a full and lustrous head of hair fuels a billion-dollar hair growth industry. Since the 1980s, a chemical called Minoxidil has become increasingly popular as both a topical and oral treatment for baldness, but what few people realize is that the very product promising hair growth poses a serious risk to their pets. The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) is warning consumers about minoxidil toxicity in cats and dogs, highlighting a danger that deserves considerably more attention.

It has been revealed that anyone who shares a home with a cat knows that personal space is more of a suggestion than a household rule. Cats rub against our heads, groom our hair, curl up on our pillows, and somehow manage to investigate just about everything we touch. These perfectly normal feline behaviors can turn deadly when minoxidil enters the picture.

The history of minoxidil shares similarities with another well-known human drug: Viagra, which essentially took a common side effect of the heart medication, sildenafil, and turned it into its primary purpose. In the 1970s, researchers developing a newly introduced blood pressure medication found that a common side effect of the drug, minoxidil, was hypertrichosis, aka excessive hair growth. Like the story of sildenafil, the makers of minoxidil leaned into this side effect, repurposing the drug as a treatment for hair loss.1.

In 1988, the FDA officially approved minoxidil, and it quickly gained popularity in products like Rogaine. Minoxidil works by widening blood vessels, a process called vasodilation, and altering the hair growth cycle to stimulate hair growth. But what helps us fight hair loss can be dangerous for our feline roommates.

Industry observers note that A 2021 study published in the Journal of the American Animal Hospital Association examined 211 reported cases of topical minoxidil exposure in dogs and cats. Of the 87 animals that developed signs of poisoning, 62 were cats, and 25 were dogs. Eight cats died. A 2025 review in the Journal of the American Academy of Dermatology identified another 94 reported cases, including 68 cats, ten of which died. Notably, 55 of 57 cases involving accidental exposure to a person's minoxidil treatment involved cats.

How does this happen? Topical minoxidil is applied directly to the scalp, either as a liquid using a dropper or as a foam spread with the fingers. Medication can remain on the hands, hair, or nearby surfaces. Cats don't need to break into the medicine cabinet; a little grooming, an affectionate head rub, or a snooze on a contaminated pillow may be enough to expose them. Some were even exposed through everyday contact with their follicle-challenged cat parents.

Minoxidil works by relaxing blood vessels and improving blood flow. In cats, however, the effects can become dangerously disruptive.

When absorbed, it can cause blood pressure to drop dramatically, a condition called hypotension. To compensate, the heart beats faster, but this doesn't necessarily solve the problem. Serious complications can follow, including fluid accumulation in the lungs (pulmonary edema) or in the space surrounding them (pleural effusion). Breathing becomes increasingly difficult, and severe poisoning can progress to cardiovascular and respiratory failure.

Now, what should you look out for? You might notice unusual tiredness, weakness, vomiting, or a sudden loss of appetite. More concerningly, your kitty may start breathing faster than usual or appear to struggle for air. And here's the tricky part: some cats may initially seem perfectly fine.

That's why a suspected exposure should never be brushed off simply because your cat appears normal. Waiting for visible signs of poisoning can waste valuable time.

Now that we are beginning to appreciate the risks this product poses to our pets, we have to wonder how many unexplained cat and dog deaths could be attributed to unknown minoxidil exposure.

Rapunzel may have had a tower to keep her hair safe, but cat owners need a different strategy: keeping minoxidil well away from curious paws.

It has been revealed that if you use topical minoxidil, make sure you apply it in a room your cat cannot access. Wash your hands thoroughly with soap and water immediately afterward, and clean up any spills promptly. Used tissues, cotton pads, applicators, and empty containers should go straight into a secure bin. That tissue you casually leave on the bathroom counter? To your cat, it might look like just another interesting thing to investigate.

It has been revealed that and what about bedtime? If you apply minoxidil in your bedroom, make closing the door part of your nighttime routine. Your cat may protest being left out of the bedroom, especially if your pillow is their favorite sleeping spot, but keeping them away from treated hair, skin, pillows, and bedding can help prevent accidental contact with medication residue. Remember, allowing the product to dry does not guarantee that every surface is free from contamination.

You might be wondering whether switching to oral minoxidil would solve the problem. Unfortunately, not entirely. Oral minoxidil is also toxic to cats if they accidentally ingest a tablet. Whichever formulation you use, keep the medication securely stored and well out of paws' reach. Or better yet, look into options that donât put your pet at risk.

It has been revealed that discuss your household's furry residents with the prescribing dermatologist and establish a routine that prevents accidental exposure. Cats are wonderfully persistent creatures. They may not appreciate a closed door or understand why their favorite pillow is suddenly off-limits, but a little inconvenience is a small price to pay for keeping them safe.

If your cat licks minoxidil, contacts a spill, or may have groomed contaminated fur, contact your veterinarian or an animal poison control service immediately, even if your kitty seems perfectly fine.

According to recent reports, treatment depends on the exposure and your cat's condition. It may involve hospitalization, cardiovascular monitoring, oxygen therapy, intravenous support, and medications to manage complications such as low blood pressure or fluid accumulation.

Recent findings suggest that never attempt to induce vomiting or administer home remedies unless specifically instructed by a veterinary professional. If medication is still on your cat's coat or skin, ask your veterinarian how to handle decontamination safely rather than delaying emergency care.

Unfortunately, not every cat survives minoxidil poisoning, making every accidental exposure a veterinary emergency.

According to recent reports, hair loss can affect confidence, and wanting to treat it is perfectly understandable. Minoxidil can be a valuable treatment for people experiencing certain types of hair loss, but sharing a home with a cat adds an notable responsibility.

It has been revealed that preventing accidental poisoning starts with awareness. As pet parents, we need to be mindful of the products we bring into our homes, even those that seem perfectly harmless to us. From seemingly innocent houseplants and everyday foods to cleaning products, medications, and personal care treatments, many things we use routinely can pose risks to our feline companions. Before introducing something newly introduced into your home, take a moment to consider whether it is safe for your cat. A little research and a few precautions can make a world of difference.

Cats will continue doing what cats do best: following their humans, investigating everything, claiming the pillows, and showing affection on their own terms. We cannot expect them to understand why a particular patch of skin or a freshly treated pillow is suddenly off-limits. That responsibility belongs to us.

In a recent development, thinning hair can be frustrating, even damaging to self-esteem, but itâs not a life-threatening condition. Losing a beloved pet to an avoidable medication exposure is a tragedy no one should have to experience.

Better bald than catless. Every single time.

The bed itself can be exciting, particularly because it smells like a favorite person and offers a chance for interaction. In other cases, a dog may simply have energy left to burn. Understanding the possible reasons can help explain why bedtime sometimes turns into playtime.

Industry observers note that dogs spend much of their time looking up at people from the floor. Climbing onto a bed changes that perspective, bringing a dog much closer to its owner's face and making interaction easier.

Sources indicate that that alone can be enough to spark a playful mood. A dog may drop into a play bow, bark for attention, or bounce around in an attempt to encourage its person to join in.

Industry observers note that being face to face can make play feel more inviting, particularly for dogs that enjoy close interaction with their owners. What looks like a sudden burst of energy may simply be a dog making the most of the opportunity to engage on a different level.

A bed carries the scent of the person who sleeps in it, making it an especially interesting place for a dog to explore. Dogs rely heavily on their noses to understand their surroundings, and familiar smells can be particularly appealing.

Recent findings suggest that for a dog that enjoys spending time with its owner, the bed may be one of the most comforting and interesting places in the home. Rolling around on the sheets or sniffing the blankets lets a dog investigate those familiar scents while enjoying a spot associated with its favorite person.

That combination of comfort, familiarity, and excitement can help explain why some dogs become especially playful once they climb onto the mattress.

Industry observers note that for dogs that love burrowing, a bed covered in sheets and blankets can feel like an invitation to play. Digging, wriggling underneath the covers, and pushing through folds of fabric can all become part of the fun.

Some breeds are particularly inclined toward this kind of behavior. Dachshunds, for example, were bred to pursue animals such as badgers and weasels into their burrows. Meanwhile, Chihuahuas seem to be particularly fond of burrowing into the warmth and security of their humanâs bed.

A dog that discovers the pleasure of diving between the sheets may swiftly turn it into a regular bedtime activity.

Dogs are often quick to learn which behaviors get a reaction from their owners. Climbing onto the bed puts them right where they're difficult to ignore, particularly if they start bouncing around or nudging someone for attention.

Bedtime can also signal that the day is winding down and an opportunity for cuddling is approaching. A dog that enjoys being close to its owner may become excited at the prospect of spending that time together.

It has been revealed that if playful behavior consistently earns attention, a dog may be encouraged to repeat it. What begins as a burst of excitement can become a familiar part of the nightly routine. Even if this nightly ritual isnât one you welcome, waving arms and raised voices often count as a positive interaction for a dog, so if youâre trying to get your dog off the bed, be careful your methods align with your message.

Sources indicate that sometimes, a dog becomes especially energetic at bedtime simply because theyâre not ready to settle down. If it hasn't had enough exercise or stimulation during the day, the bed may become an outlet for that leftover energy.

According to recent reports, A dog that is still eager to run, jump, and play may need more activity before the household turns in for the night. An evening walk or a game of tug-of-war can help provide an opportunity to burn off some energy before bedtime.

A dog that's had enough exercise and stimulation is more likely to be ready to relax, rather than treating the mattress as a playground.

Many owners enjoy sleeping alongside their dogs, while others prefer to keep their beds pet-free. Sharing a bed can feel cozy and comforting, and having a dog nearby may also be soothing for people who experience anxiety or other mental health challenges.

There are practical considerations, too. Dogs can carry dirt, bacteria, and parasites into the bed, and some owners would rather not have fur on their sheets or pillows.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, whether a dog is allowed to sleep on the bed comes down to what works for the household. If itâs not a problem, then itâs not a problem. There's no single right choice, and a dog can still enjoy plenty of affection and companionship without sharing the mattress.

In a recent development, if you do want your bed to be a dog-free zone, the simplest solution is to keep the bedroom door closed. But if youâre simply looking for a way to get them off the bed without it turning into a party, a calm and quiet approach is best. A single command or using a slip-lead to silently guide them off the bed will be far more effective than shouting and pointing.

According to recent reports, A dog getting frisky on the bed is often responding to a combination of familiar scents, opportunities for attention, and the chance to play somewhere comfortable. Blankets can add to the appeal, especially for dogs that enjoy burrowing.

Industry observers note that if the behavior seems excessive, however, it may be worth looking at how much exercise and stimulation the dog gets during the day. Adding a walk or play session before bed can help make the transition to sleep easier.

For many dogs, the bed is simply an exciting place to be close to their favorite person. With a little preparation, bedtime can still end in a peaceful night's sleep rather than an impromptu wrestling match.

According to recent reports, cats are famously persistent beggars, and a holiday table full of tempting smells gives them plenty of motivation. Although there are a handful of Thanksgiving dishes that are fine in small amounts, several can make a cat seriously ill, so it pays to know which is which before anything gets shared.

The following foods are generally harmless for cats, provided the portions stay small and there are no pre-existing health complications. Of course, safe doesnât always mean healthy, and moderation is key. Just like people, cats also differ in what they like, and many will show no interest in some of these at all.

It has been revealed that plain turkey is the best choice, since cats are obligate carnivores and tend to love it. It needs to be free of skin, fat, bones, gravy, and spices, and a small piece is plenty. The best thing to do is set aside a small amount to cook without all the frills, rather than cleaning it later.

Plain, cooked pumpkin is non-toxic and good for a catâs digestion, and it may even soothe an upset stomach. A puree or mash works well. Pumpkin pie is a different matter, because the sugar and possible dairy arenât good for cats.

Apples are safe and offer vitamins C and K, calcium, and fiber. The seeds, leaves, and stems contain cyanide and must be removed, and the fruit should be chopped into small cubes.

Recent findings suggest that plain green beans, minus butter, spices, herbs, onion, or garlic, are a good source of fiber and can even stand in for regular treats. Broccoli is also safe if it is unseasoned and boiled or steamed. Itâs unlikely a cat will want it, but it provides antioxidants and supports digestion. As with any newly introduced food, itâs best to introduce it carefully. Cranberry sauce isnât toxic, but its sugar content makes it unhealthy, so only an incredibly small taste is appropriate.

Some Thanksgiving staples should never be shared, because they can make a cat quite ill.

Industry observers note that garlic, onions, leeks, scallions, and similar vegetables can be deadly even in small amounts, and garlic powder is particularly problematic. They damage a catâs red blood cells and lead to anemia, with signs such as weakness, a high heart rate, diarrhea, vomiting, and collapse. Cats are more sensitive to them than dogs, and symptoms have reportedly appeared after less than a teaspoon of cooked onion.

Many stuffings contain onions or garlic. Even without them, stuffing is usually rich with ingredients like turkey grease that can upset a catâs stomach. It wonât be deadly without those ingredients, but it has no nutritional value and can wreak havoc on digestion.

Industry observers note that bones should stay well out of reach. Cooked bones in particular can splinter or crack and could tear the mouth, break teeth, cause choking, or block the digestive system, and bacteria are a concern too. Keep them well out of reach.

Industry observers note that chocolate is incredibly toxic to cats, and the darker it is, the worse it gets. The theobromine and caffeine it contains can cause vomiting, muscle tremors, diarrhea, an abnormal heart rate, and seizures, and it can even lead to death. Anything else with caffeine, including coffee, is off limits as well.

Grapes and raisins can lead to kidney failure, and even a tiny amount of either, or related dried fruits like craisins, can cause illness. Signs include continuous vomiting, stomach distress, and hyperactivity. Some cats show no symptoms after eating them, but that isnât a reason to take the chance.

Gravy isnât toxic, but it is salty and fatty, which cats donât need much of. Those levels could cause further problems for a cat with heart trouble. A sneaky lick is nothing to worry about, but gravy shouldnât be mixed into a catâs food.

A bowl of milk may seem harmless, but many cats are lactose intolerant. Dairy can give them a stomach ache, gas, or diarrhea, so itâs better to offer something from the safe list instead if theyâre sniffing around the kitchen.

Raw meat and fish can carry pathogens such as E. coli and Salmonella that make cats ill, so avoid the temptation to drop some scraps as youâre preparing meals.

A cat can share in the holiday with a nibble of plain turkey or a spoonful of pumpkin, but a few ordinary ingredients you may have around the table can cause illness and even death. With a little care over what goes into the bowl, both cat and family can enjoy a safe and happy Thanksgiving.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I need to remove 12 courses of blind-nailed 5-1/4-in.-wide fiber-cement lap siding with a 4-in. exposure to repair a 5-ft. by 5-ft. section of wall behind it. I’d like to reinstall the old siding without it looking like a repair. What’s the best way to remove fiber-cement lap siding without damaging the planks? How can I make removal and reinstallation less noticeable?

It’s challenging to remove blind-nailed fiber-cement lap siding, but patience and an extra set of hands make removing and reinstalling the planks easier.

First, mark out the damaged area with painter’s tape. You’ll have to remove full pieces of siding for the repair, so look for the nearest butt joints between individual planks to the left and right of the taped area. Mark the joints in every course of the taped repair area. Plank joints are generally staggered by two studs in successive courses—32 in. or 48 in., depending on the stud spacing. If you’re lucky, the repair area will fit within one 12-ft. plank, so you’ll need to remove just one plank per course between the nearest joints. More likely, you’ll need to remove two. This takes more time, but the removal process is the same.

In a recent development, the first plank is the hardest to remove. Start with the uppermost course in the area you marked out and gently pry up the overlying plank far enough to locate the nails. Then mark the nail locations with small pieces of tape on the overlying course. The butt joints to the left and right of the plank may have been caulked. If so, carefully cut through the sealant with a utility knife.

When fiber-cement planks are 8 in. or wider, you can lift the bottom edge far enough to pry out the nails from the plank below by slipping a thin flat bar under that plank and up to the shank of the nail. Gently pry the plank up slightly and then remove the flat bar. Press down on the top edge of the plank so the nail head stands proud of the surface, then set the flat bar under the nail head and pry it out.

Industry observers note that prying up narrower planks to pull 2-in. or longer nails often breaks the plank, so in these situations I use a thin cutting tool to cut the nails holding the plank—the Malco Hidden Nail Cutter is made for this job, though you can also use a reciprocating saw with a long metal-cutting blade. Set a 1-ft.-sq. piece of PVC or coil stock under the flat bar to avoid scratching the finish, gently lift the plank up about ¼ in. at each blind nail location, and use the Malco tool or recip saw to cut the nails. Don’t pry too much or you’ll break the top edge of the overlying plank. As you cut the nails, have a helper hold one end of the plank so you can control its removal and be careful sliding the plank downward so the cut-off nails don’t scratch the plank beneath.

With the first plank out of the way, most of the nails holding the next plank down are exposed. Pull the exposed nails using the flat bar method: insert the flat bar between the plank and the wall sheathing at the nail location and pry against the wall; once the nail is broken free and raised 1/4 in., push the top of the plank back against the wall so the nail head is proud, and finish pulling the nail with the flat bar. Cut any blind nails that remain before removing the plank.

Continue working down, removing planks left and right as close to the taped-out area as possible. Remove the cut nails from the planks so they don’t scratch the siding during handling, and label the planks so you can reinstall them in the same locations.

According to recent reports, after you make your wall repair, install a upcoming piece of water-resistive barrier (WRB) taped along its perimeter to the existing WRB and tuck its top under the existing WRB to shed water. Then reinstall the planks in reverse sequence. I install new nails in the old holes, using ring-shank nails with a slightly larger diameter than the originals for a secure grip. At the ends of planks where they slide beneath an overlying course, you’ll have to face-nail. Make sure the nail penetrates through the overlap at the underlying and overlying planks near where the blind nail used to be.

Work your way up the wall until you reach the last plank that will slip beneath the existing plank at the top of the repaired area, then face-nail the last reinstalled plank. Face nails can be left exposed and touched up with color-matching paint, but they will be noticeable compared to the blind-nailed siding on the rest of the wall. You can somewhat hide the heads by countersinking them: Make recesses with a drill-mounted countersink and then putty and paint the heads so they’re less obvious. Don’t try hammering the nail heads below the siding surface because you’ll break the fiber cement and the nails won’t hold well.

5 Festive Houseplants That Outlast Christmas Trees – Enjoy These Holiday Favorites for Years to Come

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1024 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A Christmas tree might be the star of the living room in December, but once the holidays are over, it usually gets packed away or recycled.
  • Whether you're looking to make your Christmas décor a little more lasting, or simply a self-confessed crazy plant lady in need of more houseplants (I'm right there with you!), then you should absolutely consider choosing a living plant this year.
  • From spectacular seasonal blooms to fragrant herbs and miniature trees, these five festive favorites offer plenty of reasons to keep growing long after the last present has been unwrapped.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A Christmas tree might be the star of the living room in December, but once the holidays are over, it usually gets packed away or recycled. Festive houseplants, on the other hand? Well, they can stick around for years – and some might become so beloved that you can't imagine your home without them.

Whether you're looking to make your Christmas décor a little more lasting, or simply a self-confessed crazy plant lady in need of more houseplants (I'm right there with you!), then you should absolutely consider choosing a living plant this year.

From spectacular seasonal blooms to fragrant herbs and miniature trees, these five festive favorites offer plenty of reasons to keep growing long after the last present has been unwrapped.

Sources indicate that I'm a huge fan of Christmas cactus, having inherited one that lived for an incredible 27 years before recently dying. (RIP, Noel; we barely knew ye!) It was a reminder of just how long these festive houseplants can last, and how attached we can become to them over time.

It has been revealed that christmas cactus (Schlumbergera) produces beautiful flowers in shades of pink, red, purple and white, usually just in time for the holidays. Even when it's not in bloom, though, its arching stems make an attractive display, particularly in a hanging pot.

Give it bright indirect light, keep it away from harsh sunshine and don't let its roots sit in soggy compost (mine loved life on our bathroom windowsill), and remember: a cooler spell and shorter days in fall help encourage flowering.

Few festive houseplants make quite as dramatic a statement as amaryllis (Hippeastrum). Its tall stems and oversized trumpet-shaped flowers bring a splash of color indoors when much of the garden is dormant, making it a favorite for Christmas displays.

Recent findings suggest that somehow, I have managed to keep my own diva alive for several years now (it's sitting on my desk as I type this, in fact), so I urge you not to discard the bulb once flowering finishes. Instead, remove the faded flowers, keep the leaves growing, give it light, water and occasional feeding as it grows, then follow a suitable resting period to encourage another round of blooms. With a little patience, the same bulb can reward you with flowers for many seasons.

You can pick up a bag of Amaryllis bulbs easily enough from the Garden State Bulb Store, if you fancy giving it a go; they'd make excellent holiday presents once you've gotten them started!

If you'd prefer something compact and relatively easy to care for, Flaming Katy (Kalanchoe blossfeldiana) is a solid choice. This succulent produces clusters of bright flowers in red, pink, orange, yellow or white, and it's widely available during the festive season.

In a recent development, its fleshy leaves store water, so it doesn't need constant watering (making it ideal for even the most forgetful plant parents everywhere). All you have to do is place it somewhere bright, allow the compost to dry a little between drinks, and avoid leaving it sitting in water.

Blooming in the fall and winter, what could be prettier than this Flaming Katy at Christmas?

Flaming Katy can be encouraged to flower again by providing a steady stint of uninterrupted nights in autumn, making it a holiday plant that's well worth keeping after its first colorful display.

Recent findings suggest that rosemary is a lovely way to bring fragrance into the home over the holidays, especially when sold clipped into a miniature living Christmas tree shape. Its evergreen needles look festive, while its scent adds a little something extra to the season – and you can snip sprigs for cooking, too.

Industry observers note that I have actually kept my own rosemary going for a long time, bringing it in and out of the house with the seasons until it grew so large that it eventually had to move permanently into the garden. It just goes to show that a small festive plant can have quite a future ahead of it!

Rosemary (even one like this Rosemary Christmas Tree from the Three Company Store) needs plenty of light and well-drained compost. Don't overwater it, and remember that it generally prefers cooler and brighter conditions than a hot room right next to a radiator.

Industry observers note that for something a little different, why not choose a small tree? Fig, olive and citrus trees can all make beautiful container plants, bringing Mediterranean charm to a bright home.

A fig tree offers attractive foliage and the possibility of homegrown fruit, while an olive tree has silvery-green leaves and a timeless look. And there's no denying that a calamondin or miniature orange tree is particularly festive, with glossy foliage, fragrant flowers and colorful fruit that can linger on the branches.

It has been revealed that naturally, these trees need the brightest spot you can offer, and citrus in particular appreciates warmth and consistent care. Indoor conditions aren't always ideal year-round, so check each tree's needs and consider moving it outdoors during suitable warmer months.

Sources indicate that A living Christmas plant is a gift that doesn't have to end when the festivities do. Choose yourself, then, a festive houseplant that suits your space, give it the care it needs, and you could be enjoying your festive favorite for many Christmases to come.

Sources indicate that or, you know, you could ask Santa to bring you one. Either or...

    Industry observers note that nearly 30 dogs have arrived in New York after being rescued from a dog-meat farm in South Korea. Their journey toward adoption is beginning, but with the country's ban still months away from taking full effect, the work is far from over.

    A plane ride to Fresh York probably wasn't on these dogs' bingo cards. Neither, for that matter, was a soft bed, a full bowl of food, or the chance to be someone's beloved family member. After spending their lives confined to cages, even the simplest things may seem exciting and new.

    According to recent reports, on October 1, nearly 30 dogs were rescued from a dog-meat farm in Gangjin, South Korea, that once bred and slaughtered as many as 1,000 dogs each year. This was part of a larger rescue operation by Humane World for Animals that saved more than 70 dogs from the property.

    In a recent development, for the organization, the operation marks its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea ahead of the country's ban, which takes full effect on February 7, 2027. Humane World for Animals has rescued nearly 3,000 dogs from farms since 2015, making this a significant milestone.

    And yes, it's a reason to celebrate. But before we get too comfortable patting ourselves on the back, there's a much bigger picture to consider. Getting these dogs out was a huge victory, but there are still thousands at risk.

    When the rescue team arrived at the farm in Gangjin, in South Korea's South Jeolla Province, they were met with disturbing scenes. Rows of rusting cages, abandoned collars scattered on the ground, and skeletal remains served as a gruesome reminder of the dogs that hadn't been so lucky.

    It's a hard reality to come to terms with, especially if your own dog is currently hogging the sofa, demanding snacks, or staring at you as though you've ruined their life by being five minutes late with dinner. The minor dramas faced by our beloved pets are a world away from what these poor dogs endured.

    Humane World for Animals has reported finding mixed breeds and dogs of different sizes during its rescue work. The survivors included Jindos, a breed native to South Korea, a husky mix, and smaller dogs, including a spitz mix. In other words, any dog could end up on the menu.

    In this most recent rescue, a concerned citizen alerted a local animal protection group, which contacted Humane World for Animals and the authorities. Officials found that the farm had broken South Korea's Animal Protection Act. The farmer, a man in his 80s, agreed to hand over the dogs and promised not to take part in the dog-meat trade again.

    More than 70 dogs were rescued. Nearly 30 travelled to New York, another 12 went to a rehabilitation center in Montreal, and some mothers and their puppies remained in South Korea because they were too young to fly safely.

    Rescuing dogs from situations like this isn't as simple as just opening a cage and booking the next available flight. International transport requires veterinary checks, vaccinations, documentation, and careful consideration about which animals are fit to travel. The priority is getting them out safely, not rushing them onto a plane for the sake of a happy headline.

    South Korea passed its Special Act on the Termination of Breeding, Slaughter, and Distribution of Dogs for Consumption in January 2024. Its key prohibitions will finally take full effect on February 7, 2027, making it illegal to breed, slaughter, or sell dogs or dog meat for human consumption. But the transition is already underway.

    Recent findings suggest that in May 2026, South Korea's Ministry of Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs reported that about 82% of the country's 1,537 registered dog-meat farms had closed. Over a thousand farms closed is something worth celebrating, but it means 272 farms are still operating.

    Another consideration is that closing a farm doesn't automatically save the dogs living there. A business can shut down, the gates can close, and the paperwork can be signed, but where do all those dogs go?

    According to Humane World for Animals, government figures indicate that of approximately 393,857 dogs counted on farms that had been closed, only 1,121 were adopted or transferred to public shelters. That's about 0.3%.

    Itâs understood that most of these dogs were sent for slaughter or moved to other farms. So, while the closure of dog meat farms is good news, itâs not a true victory if these dogs are simply moved on to face the same fate. The ban is a huge step forward, but a law is only as good as its enforcement.

    The real goal isn't just to close the farms. It's making sure the dogs are actually safe.

    Getting out of the farm is the first substantial hurdle for these dogs. Now comes veterinary care, recovery, and the not-so-small task of learning how to live in a completely different world.

    In a recent development, humane World for Animalsâ rescue protocols include veterinary exams, vaccinations, respiratory screening when needed, and the health documents required for international travel. Each dog has their own needs. Some may need treatment for skin problems, wounds, dental disease, or nutritional deficiencies.

    The second, and perhaps most challenging, hurdle for these dogs is adapting to a whole newly introduced way of life. Just because a dog has been saved doesn't automatically mean a dog feels safe.

    Imagine never having lived in a home, then suddenly finding yourself surrounded by doors, stairs, strange noises, slippery floors, and humans who keep trying to show you how much they love you. Even a well-meaning hug could be overwhelming. And the vacuum cleaner? Let's just say it probably won't be winning any popularity contests.

    Recent findings suggest that these dogs may need to learn things many pets take for granted: how to explore a room, relax around people, or understand that a hand reaching toward them isn't something to fear. Some will be curious from the start. Others may prefer to watch from a safe distance. Neither response is wrong, and patience plus a little common sense go a long way.

    A quiet place to rest, a predictable routine, and the freedom to explore without being pushed can help a dog settle in. Rewarding small steps with positive reinforcement builds confidence without turning every upcoming experience into a test.

    In a recent development, adjusting to a new life takes time, and there's no need to rush it. A dog who hides under the table on day one isn't a failed adoption. A dog who isn't ready for cuddles isn't being ungrateful. Theyâre figuring things out, and they need time to decide that this strange new place might actually be safe. Building trust and confidence can be a slow process.

    Those familiar with the process of adopting or fostering dogs, particularly those who may not have had the best start to life, may have heard of the 3-3-3 Rule for Dogs: 3 days, 3 weeks, 3 months. Itâs a simplified interpretation of the timeline many dogs tend to follow when adjusting to a new home environment.

    The first 3 days are about decompression and resetting the nervous system. It might look like a dog that is timid, constantly moving, hiding, or even showing signs of aggression. Some dogs adjust swiftly, while others may take a little longer than 3 days. The key thing to know is that this version of the dog is not usually a good representation of their true selves.

    Over the first 3 weeks, dogs will start to gain confidence and explore their fresh world. They are often testing boundaries, becoming familiar with patterns, and learning how to trust. Being consistent and providing predictable routines is paramount to this process.

    Industry observers note that by the time 3 months have passed, most dogs will be feeling more settled. It may still take some time for their full personality to appear, but with every passing month, they become more confident, more trusting, and less anxious.

    Sometimes progress looks like taking a treat from someone's hand. Sometimes it's finally falling asleep without startling at every sound. Those moments might not make a flashy before-and-after video, but for that dog, they're a substantial deal.

    One more thing: fear and behavioural changes shouldn't automatically be dismissed as consequences of a dog's past. Pain, illness, and other medical problems can affect behaviour, too. If a dog seems persistently distressed or suddenly starts acting differently, a veterinary check is notable. We don't want to assume it's trauma when there may be pain due to a treatable medical issue behind it.

    In a recent development, A second chance isn't just getting a dog out of a cage. It's giving them the medical care, space, and time to discover that life can be safe, and maybe even pretty wonderful.

    Humane World for Animals calls the Gangjin operation its final large-scale dog-meat-farm rescue in South Korea. But that doesn't mean the work is over. The organization plans to continue monitoring the ban and supporting efforts to enforce it.

    Closing farms is a huge win. Full stop. But making sure dogs aren't left behind, moved elsewhere, or subjected to illegal practices is part of making that win count. With the ban taking full effect in February 2027, the coming months will be crucial.

    For the dogs already rescued, a fresh life is finally within reach. Veterinary care. Rehabilitation. A chance to find a home where the biggest worry is whether they get the good spot on the sofa. That's quite the upgrade.

    In a recent development, now, we turn our attention to the dogs still waiting in South Koreaâs remaining farms. Stopping the dog meat trade is a huge victory, but in many ways, itâs just the beginning. Saving these dogs is more than just stopping the slaughter. Itâs making sure they all get the happy ending they deserve.

    Air Barrier for an Elevated Home

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C.
    • According to recent reports, it’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston.
    • In a recent development, there are a few ways to prevent this.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I’m about to build a house on the coast in Charleston, S.C. (Climate Zone 3A). It’s elevated on wood pilings and the space under the house is open to the outdoors, enclosed only with louvered panels between the pilings. I have most of the enclosure details nailed down, but I haven’t determined the best way to air-seal and insulate the open floor trusses above the pilings. My biggest concern is hot, humid air from below reaching the underside of the air-conditioned subfloor and condensing on the surface. What’s the best strategy to insulate and air-seal the underside of an elevated coastal home?

    According to recent reports, it’s wise to consider inward vapor drive in humid climates like Charleston. When the outdoor dew point is higher than the air-conditioned indoor temperature, there’s going to be a strong moisture drive from the outside toward the home’s interior, which allows water to accumulate in the materials below the flooring. Prolonged wetting can lead to rotted framing, mold problems, and damaged flooring, along with damage to other materials in contact with the floor.

    In a recent development, there are a few ways to prevent this. One option is to place a vapor-retarding insulation layer—spray foam—right below the subfloor. The outside (bottom) of the foam will be close enough to the outdoor temperature that water won’t condense on the surface, and the foam will substantially block moisture from moving through it. Provided no ductwork is run in the floor, it’s a way to get decent air-sealing, and the cost is reasonable as well.

    According to recent reports, that mentioned, I don’t like to use spray foam across an entire floor—it’s risky to install and full of questionable chemicals. Another option is to create a conditioned space within the floor system. The challenge is air-sealing around the posts, beams, and structural hardware that hold up the house and the plumbing and electrical lines in this area. Plus, you’ll have to condition the space, which requires additional HVAC work. This can be simple (like adding a supply register and a path back to the house) or pretty involved (running ductwork down walls to reach the underfloor space).

    According to recent reports, my third and preferred option is to create an airtight, vapor-retarding layer across the bottom of the floor trusses. A layer of XPS or foil-faced polyiso (don’t use EPS, it’s too vapor-open) across the bottom of the whole floor will help slow vapor drive into the floor system and bring practical benefits like easier air-sealing and a little additional insulation. In Climate Zone 3A, turn to the International Residential Code (IRC) Table 806.5 in the section on roof ventilation for guidance on the R-value needed, since the floor system will have insulation levels comparable to roofs. The table calls for 1/2 in. of rigid insulation. Using the calculation procedure in the table footnotes indicates a higher level (in the 11/2-in. range) might be less risky, assuming you are completely filling a 12-in. to 16-in. floor-truss cavity with blown-in cellulose or fiberglass, which will be more than the code-required R-38 when the table was developed. Cover the foam board with fiberglass-faced drywall sheathing or plywood. Air-­sealing will still be complex given the elevated construction, and attention will need to be paid to the rim joist/perimeter (spray foam works in this area, as shown in the drawing). But, this system would really slow vapor movement throughout the floor system.

    Dogs have been a fixture of family life for thousands of years, and many people who grew up with one say they canât picture their childhood without them. Beyond the obvious benefits of companionship and fun, growing up with a dog has been shown to have positive effects on physical and emotional well-being; advantages that show up in how children handle friendships, feelings, and everyday challenges.

    Recent findings suggest that of course, this doesnât mean that having a dog is right for everyone. Bringing a dog into your home is a big decision that affects budgets and daily routines for years to come, and the best outcomes tend to come from families who go in with open eyes.

    For anyone considering life with a dog, here are a few ways they can improve a childâs life, and things to consider before adopting one.

    Growing up around animals can lower the chance of developing allergies later on. Dogs, and all the things that come with living with them, expose children to a range of allergens, which helps build a more robust immune system. The key seems to be early exposure, which means the sooner a dog becomes part of a childâs world, the better.

    It has been revealed that children who are close to their dogs tend to be more securely attached to their parents, and theyâre more likely to form strong friendships, too. Strong relationships in one part of a childâs life seem to go hand in hand with strong relationships in others. Kids who share more physical contact with their dogs, from cuddles to roughhousing, tend to get along better with their moms, dads, and friends.

    Industry observers note that kids who grow up with a family dog tend to have lower rates of anxiety. The benefits reach well beyond childhood, too. Dogs can ease feelings of depression and anxiety in adults who went through childhood trauma, and they can reduce signs of post-traumatic stress, which is part of the reason theyâre so often brought into therapy.

    According to recent reports, A dog is a living, breathing creature with needs, and children who help care for one learn responsibility and dependability. A five-year-old canât take on every chore, but age-appropriate tasks are a great place to start. Young children spend much of their lives at the mercy of parents and teachers, so having a dog to look after can give them a real sense of empowerment and build self-esteem.

    Recent findings suggest that caring for an animal from an early age also builds empathy, which supports emotional intelligence and helps a child grow into a more compassionate person. The lessons go on from there. Dogs model loyalty; training and bonding teach patience, and learning to read a dogâs body language and respect their boundaries teaches respect. When a family pet eventually passes away, children also learn about death and grieving.

    Recent findings suggest that children with pets tend to have better self-esteem than children without them. The effect appears to be strongest as kids approach adolescence; an age when the emotional support of a companion animal may matter most.

    Families with dogs tend to be more physically active than their peers, getting about 11 extra minutes of exercise a day. That may not sound like much, but it adds up to roughly 5.5 hours a month in a society that is growing more sedentary all the time.

    For some children, the effect is far larger. Girls in particular gained around 52 minutes of light physical activity a day after a dog joined the family. The flip side was striking too, since girls who lost their pet saw their daily activity drop by 62 minutes.

    Recent findings suggest that children tend to handle stressful moments better with a dog nearby. They feel happier and more at ease, and being able to touch the dog calms them even further. Simply having a furry companion close by seems to help kids feel steadier inside.

    For all the upsides, adopting a dog isnât a decision to take lightly, and there are a few things every family needs to consider before racing out to get a four-legged friend.

    Budget: Dogs depend on their owners for food, veterinary care, and emergencies, and a household budget that canât cover those costs is a reason to rethink the plan.

    According to recent reports, age: Although many childhood benefits increase the earlier they start living with a dog, sometimes waiting until children are older is a good idea. St. Bernards make fantastic family pets, for example, but they can weigh as much as 180 pounds and can hurt a child accidentally. Small breeds have their own risks, since they can be fragile and prone to injury until kids learn boundaries and how to respect animals.

    It has been revealed that lifestyle: A family that works long hours and spends every evening shuttling children to activities needs a strategy for what the dog will be doing. Not every schedule has room for a pet, and that is perfectly fine, but a dog shouldnât be adopted without free time to spend with it.

    Motivation: Children often beg for a dog, promising to walk, feed, and pick up after them.

    Then, the novelty fades, and the adults end up with the bulk of the care. Although itâs a good idea to encourage children to take on some of the responsibility of looking after a dog, you should assume that youâll be the one doing most of the work â hope for the best, plan for the worst!

    Industry observers note that growing up alongside a dog can bring real benefits, from fewer allergies and lower anxiety to stronger relationships and more time spent moving. But to enjoy the benefits of living with a dog, families need to have the time, money, and genuine desire to take care of one.

    Growing up with a dog might not guarantee health and happiness, but itâs a pretty good place to start!

    #147562. How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1033 w)

    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finegardening ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Design a Garden That Solves Problems and Invites You In

    📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1033 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finegardening

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a strategy.
    • According to recent reports, I like to create purpose-driven designs.
    • Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that people often ask how I approach the garden design process and what information I gather before developing a strategy. While every client and garden is different, I usually start with the same basic questions.

    According to recent reports, I like to create purpose-driven designs. For example, I’m often called on to solve a problem, even if it is simply “I have a new house and a blank slate.” It may be just a section of the garden, the front yard, or something specific like repairing a garden after a new septic system installation or after a new house is built next door.

    Design is all about solving problems and connecting clients to their gardens, usually beginning with a questionnaire to bring all those unspoken needs to light. Questions help people consider things they would not normally think about. As a result, these conversations define their needs and desires, helping me combine different elements into a cohesive design.

    The same approach applies to projects in my own garden. I don’t give myself a questionnaire, but I do ask myself the same questions. First, I assess the challenges, the location of the area in relation to the rest of the property, and the environmental conditions that will influence the planting.

    In a latest garden, the major goal is often screening. Most people want privacy to live their lives outside without having to see a neighboring house, road, commercial area, or vacant lot.

    Privacy was one of the major considerations when planning my grass garden. There was no privacy between my property and the neighboring property. I could see my neighbors eat their dinner, watch them play with their grandchildren, and even see them argue. Their house was also too close to the property line, and in fact, their sidewalk was on my property. That was a problem.

    Because the sidewalk was already there when I moved in, I had to incorporate it into my design, but I could still make it disappear visually.

    I started out with some tall elements at the back of the bed to start the screening process. I positioned these plants so I could maintain them from my property without having branches extend over the property line. Keeping their mature size in mind also helped avoid potential conflicts with the neighboring property. Soft screens made of trees and tall shrubs (both evergreen and deciduous) offer privacy without creating a harsh, artificial boundary line.

    Read More: 20 Unique Hedging Plant Options.

    It has been revealed that looking at the space, I could see a definite focal point within my property. With the neighbor behind me, the view naturally led the eye toward the water. Therefore, I designed a one-sided border rather than an island bed meant to be viewed from multiple directions. Making the border as deep as 20 feet in places gave me enough room to continue screening the neighboring property while also providing some sound buffering.

    Understanding the environmental conditions was the next step. The back edge is on the north side of my property. The large trees and shrubs would not shade the rest of the bed. This meant the bed would be in full sun all day, all season long.

    Recent findings suggest that what a challenge for this PNW native who grew up mostly in the forest (or woods, as we called it). I had to learn about plants that liked full sun, drying winds, and dry soil so they could thrive. Rather than trying to re-create the shaded woodland conditions I knew best, I needed to work with what the site naturally offered.

    Read More: Summer-Dry Gardening: A Visit to Beth Chatto’s Gravel Garden.

    Growing up in the forest, I longed for wide-open sky and long views. Above all, I wanted to immerse myself in the garden. A long row of hedging plants that I could only look at wasn’t what I had in mind. I wanted to become part of the blowing, rustling movement of the grasses. While experiencing the plants, I also wanted to connect with insects, pollinators, birds, frogs, and even a few rabbits.

    Recent findings suggest that I consider the challenge met. The amount of wildlife activity surrounding me in the garden never ceases to amaze me. I feel as if I’m in a different world while surrounded by all the action and movement of the grasses and perennials, far away from massive cedar trees, moss, and ferns. Sun, wind, fragrant flowers, and the smell of warm earth are all-encompassing there.

    Sources indicate that even during the winter, this garden pulls me out, bundled up and coffee in hand, to see what is happening. Early spring bulbs push through the soil, mice shelter under the evergreen sedges, and birds search for a breakfast of grass seeds and gather bits and pieces to build new nests.

    The ultimate goal of any designer is finding the right outdoor elements to pull people outside and connect them with nature. Those elements are individual to each client. They could be an eating area, outdoor kitchen, hot tub, play area, pond, fountain, or hidden sitting area. Maybe the goal is plant-driven, with a vegetable garden, cutting garden, or collection of conifers.

    When these features are thoughtfully integrated with immersive, naturalistic plantings, the result is an outdoor space that invites people to experience their gardens throughout the year.

    #147561. This Christmas Lights Trick Could Save Your Potted Plants From Frost – Here's How to Get It Right

    📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1219 w)

    This Christmas Lights Trick Could Save Your Potted Plants From Frost – Here's How to Get It Right

    📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1219 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that every November, boxes of holiday lights come down from the attic, and a few gardeners start eyeing those tangled strands for a second job.
    • Recent findings suggest that there's some truth to it.
    • The catch is that only certain bulbs produce enough heat to help, and most modern porch strands won't help at all.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that every November, boxes of holiday lights come down from the attic, and a few gardeners start eyeing those tangled strands for a second job. On paper, Christmas lights frost protection sounds like a neighbor's tip over coffee – string up a potted lemon tree, plug it in, and hope it makes it to morning.

    Recent findings suggest that there's some truth to it. Gardeners have relied on heat from old-style bulbs for years, and it can work alongside the usual steps for winterizing container plants, like covering pots or moving them under shelter. When used safely with a suitable cover or enclosure, that heat can nudge the temperature around a plant up a few degrees.

    The catch is that only certain bulbs produce enough heat to help, and most modern porch strands won't help at all. But using the right bulbs comes with its own risks. Mix hot bulbs, fabric covers, and unprotected electrical connections outdoors carelessly, and you have a fire and shock hazard.

    Christmas lights keep plants warm only if the bulbs run hot. Old-fashioned incandescent bulbs, like these C7 Christmas lights from Amazon, give off a fair amount of heat along with their light, so running a strand beneath a properly supported frost cover or inside a cold frame can warm the small area around a plant. University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources advises home citrus growers to use traditional non-LED lights to provide extra warmth, with or without a frost blanket.

    According to recent reports, colorado State University Extension measured the effect in cold frame trials in Fort Collins. One string of 25 mid-size C7 bulbs hung inside a covered cold frame, with a space blanket over the frame, kept each frame noticeably warmer than the night outside. A string also beat a single large bulb at warming the cold corners.

    If you want to recreate an enclosed space like that, use a cold frame or mini greenhouse, but only if the structure allows the lights to be safely suspended away from the plants and covering.

    Sources indicate that pick up a string of Christmas lights in a store today, and you'll likely find they're LEDs. They convert far more of their electricity into light, leaving little heat behind – fine for decoration but useless for shielding a citrus tree on a 28°F (-2°C) night. When it comes to LED lights, frost protection just isn't on the table – they don't generate enough warmth.

    Industry observers note that university frost guidelines specifically recommend incandescent bulbs when you need real heat. Traditional incandescent mini lights can provide some warmth, while larger C7 and C9 bulbs, like these from Novelty Lights Store, produce more heat per bulb.

    Any set used should carry an outdoor rating and be suitable for the intended setup. With incandescent Christmas lights, plants under a properly supported cover can gain extra heat, but the same heat makes the bulbs a hazard if they touch foliage or covering materials.

    According to recent reports, several vulnerable container plants could benefit, but growers most often protect potted citrus this way. Cold damage can begin around 30°F (-1°C), depending on the variety and duration of exposure, with limes generally more sensitive than mandarins. A potted lemon on the patio faces a specific risk that an in-ground tree doesn't. Its roots are far less cold-hardy than its branches, and the small amount of potting mix around them can cool and freeze much faster than the soil around an in-ground tree.

    Sources indicate that that means the lights can help through brief cold spells – just a few nights with light frost. They're not enough to protect tropical plants during weeks of hard freezes. A larger container holds more potting mix and can provide some extra insulation for the roots, so a pot like the ModernNest fiberstone planter from Walmart, designed to withstand freezing conditions, gives a citrus tree a sturdier home but won't prevent its roots from freezing.

    Hot incandescent bulbs can cause damage if they come into contact with foliage or covering materials. Incandescent bulbs can burn leaves if they touch them directly. Frost cloth, sheets, plastic wrap, and space blankets should never be pressed against the lights, where they can scorch, melt, or become a fire risk. Hang the strand so each bulb has enough clearance from surrounding materials, and use a separate frame, stakes, or supports to keep covers up and away from the bulbs. Make sure the lights are securely positioned so they cannot shift into contact with the covering.

    It has been revealed that water and electricity can create hazards on cold nights. Use only outdoor-rated lights and cords outside, and plug them into a GFCI-protected outlet. Throw out any strand with cracked sockets or frayed wire instead of hanging it. Keep indoor strands and household power strips indoors, and don't rely on tape to waterproof electrical connections. Follow the manufacturer's limits on how many strings can be connected end to end, and follow the safety instructions packed with the product.

    In a recent development, start by moving the pot. An unheated garage, shed, or closed-in porch that stays above freezing can carry a citrus tree through a cold snap with no wiring. Pots that stay outside belong together, up against a house wall or in a corner out of the wind. Water them well before the cold comes, since moist potting mix freezes more slowly than dry.

    In a recent development, covers and wraps add another layer. Lowe's sells a 2-ounce frost blanket that can go over the plant on cold nights and come off during the day. Around the container, slip on an Eonox drawstring pot insulation cover to keep cold wind off the root zone.

    For plants that need steady heat for weeks, a thermostatically controlled heater inside a greenhouse built to house one is the safer setup – the Dr Infrared greenhouse heater has an adjustable thermostat.

    Under a cover or in a cold frame, old incandescent holiday lights can add a few degrees, maybe enough to see potted citrus through a short, light frost. You can't count on them, though, and the method needs careful setup, even though it's recommended by several university extension services. An LED strand won't give a cold plant any real protection.

    Using hot bulbs with fabric and outdoor power for improvised heating carries risks that are easy to underestimate. Proper shelter, insulation, and a good frost blanket are generally safer options, although they won't always provide as much warmth as a safely heated enclosure.

    Sources indicate that for most gardeners, the simplest solution is to keep the twinkling lights on the porch this year and move your lemon tree into a frost-free garage when cold weather hits. It'll still be green when the holiday decorations go back in the attic.

    Tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success demonstrates that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

    War Dogs of History: Sergeant Stubby and the Birth of the American War Dog Legend

    💡 Key Takeaways
