    • According to recent reports, long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat.
    • According to recent reports, stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in Newly introduced Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    According to recent reports, long before the United States military established an official war dog program, one small stray taught the Army what a dog could do in combat. His name was Stubby, and by the time the First World War ended, he had become the most decorated dog in American military history.

    According to recent reports, stubbyâs story began in the summer of 1917 at Yale Field in Newly introduced Haven, Connecticut, where the 102nd Infantry Regiment of the 26th âYankeeâ Division was training before deployment to France. A short-tailed, brindle-colored dog of uncertain breeding, likely part Boston terrier and part American bull terrier, wandered into camp and was adopted by Private J. Robert Conroy. Soldiers were not permitted to keep pets, but Stubby won over the men, and eventually the officers, by learning to mimic military customs. He reportedly marched in step with the troops and raised a paw to his brow in a passable salute.

    Industry observers note that when the 102nd Infantry shipped out for France, the transport ships barred dogs. Conroy smuggled Stubby aboard the SS Minnesota hidden beneath his overcoat. Conroyâs commanding officer discovered Stubby during the crossing, but his salute reportedly charmed the officer into letting him stay.

    Once in France, Stubbyâs role shifted from morale booster to something closer to that of a working soldier. He entered combat on February 5, 1918, at Chemin des Dames, enduring shelling for over a month, and went on to serve through 17 battles over 18 months on the Western Front.

    Industry observers note that after surviving a mustard gas attack, Stubby developed a heightened sensitivity to the smell of gas. Historians and contemporary newspaper accounts credit him with warning his regiment of subsequent gas attacks before the men could detect it themselves. This allowed soldiers time to don their masks. He was also credited with locating wounded soldiers in no manâs land and comforting them until stretcher bearers arrived.

    Stubbyâs most famous exploit occurred when he discovered a German soldier mapping the layout of Allied trenches. According to accounts preserved by military historians, Stubby seized the man until American soldiers arrived to take him prisoner. For this act, Stubby was informally promoted to the rank of sergeant, making him, according to most accounts, the first dog to receive a rank in the United States Armed Forces. This was, of course, an honorary and unofficial designation rather than a formal commission, since the military does not commission dogs.

    During the April 1918 German offensive on the town of Seicheprey, France, Stubby was wounded in the chest and leg by grenade shrapnel while accompanying the 102nd Infantry in combat. After recovering, he returned to visiting wounded soldiers in the hospital, walking the wards to lift the spirits of recovering men.

    Stubby returned home a celebrity. He led parades, attended war bond rallies, and met three sitting or future presidents: Woodrow Wilson, Warren G. Harding, and Calvin Coolidge. General John J. Pershing personally honored him at a 1921 ceremony for the 102nd Infantry Regiment, presenting him with a gold medal from the Humane Education Society, an award that, while not an official military commendation, cemented his reputation as the greatest war dog of his era.

    Industry observers note that conroy went on to attend Georgetown University Law Center, and Stubby went with him, becoming the unofficial mascot of the Georgetown Hoyas football team. At halftime, he would nudge a football around the field to the delight of the crowd.

    It has been revealed that stubby died in 1929, reportedly in Conroyâs arms. His remains were preserved and are held today by the Smithsonianâs National Museum of American History, where he wears the medals and blanket he wore during his years of service. In 2018, an animated film called Sgt. Stubby: An American Hero introduced his story to a latest generation. That same year, the descendants of Conroy dedicated a life-sized bronze statue of him at the Connecticut Trees of Honor Memorial in Middletown, Connecticut.

    Sources indicate that stubby served nearly a quarter century before the United States Army established a formal War Dog Program in 1942. He had no training pipeline, no breeding program, and no structure to recognize what he did. He was, in the truest sense, an amateur who became indispensable through instinct, loyalty, and repeated exposure to danger alongside the men who fed and sheltered him. Later advocates of formal military working dog programs often cite his legacy as early proof of concept: a dogâs senses, courage, and bond with a handler could save human lives on a modern battlefield.

    Industry observers note that every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

    In a recent development, support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

    Learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

    Keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

    Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

    These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

    If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

    #147559. Finding the Right Clients

    📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2356 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Finehomebuilding ↗ Open Full Page

    Finding the Right Clients

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2356 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Finehomebuilding

    ⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing.
    • My first response is usually that this is a good thing.
    • Recent findings suggest that but I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    I spend a lot of time talking with builders who tell me they don’t really do marketing. Usually they say it with pride: “We’ve never had to. All of our work comes from word of mouth.”.

    My first response is usually that this is a good thing. If you’ve spent years building a company where past clients, architects, and trade partners keep sending work your way, you’ve built something valuable. In construction, reputation matters, and that kind of trust is earned over time. I would never tell a builder to replace that with advertising.

    Recent findings suggest that but I have also seen construction companies reach a point where the business landscape has changed, and reputation alone is not leading to the right clients. Good builders often struggle because the right people don’t know they exist.

    The phone may still be ringing, but the work coming in doesn’t always match where the tech giant wants to go next. The business has evolved, but what people know about it hasn’t necessarily evolved with it.

    It has been revealed that those are the moments when someone usually says, often a little reluctantly, “I guess we need to do some marketing.” That may indeed be the case. But I think there is a simpler and more useful way to frame the problem: Are you known for the work you actually want to do? That is where I would start.

    I’ve spent more than 20 years helping businesses and organizations grow, evolve, and connect with the people they want to reach, from owning and running a design and marketing agency to leading a destination marketing organization and working across marketing, branding, organizational leadership, consulting, and coaching. Today, as director of marketing and a business consultant with HELM Construction Solutions, I bring those experiences together in my work with builders, helping them think about where their business is going, the work they want more of, and what makes them different.

    Sources indicate that sit across the table with an experienced builder and you promptly understand what makes them different. But if you haven’t had that conversation, how would you know? I see this all the time: Some of the most valuable things about a construction tech giant live almost entirely in the owner’s head. The challenge is making more of that knowledge visible.

    Before I talk with a builder about websites, social media, advertising, or anything else that might get labeled “marketing,” I want to understand the business they are trying to build. What kind of work would they happily do again? Which projects are profitable? Which projects make the crew proud? Which clients trust the process? Where do they want to work? Who do they want to work alongside? What do they want the manufacturer to look like in five years? And—just as notable—what do they want less of?

    That last question can be surprisingly provocative. Construction companies are often encouraged to think about growth only in terms of more: more projects, more employees, more revenue, more leads. But growth doesn’t always mean more projects. Sometimes it means being more intentional about the work you take on.

    I’ll ask why a builder does something a certain way, and suddenly we’re deep into a story about a detail, a process, or a hard-earned lesson that changed how they work. Those stories are usually where the good stuff is, and where what makes a tech giant different becomes clear.

    At this point, a lot of decisions get easier. You don’t need to reach everybody. You just need to become more visible to the people who value that kind of work.

    Industry observers note that if you aren’t sure how to identify the right types of projects for your business, I often suggest looking backward before looking forward. Choose three to five projects from the last few years that you would happily do again. Think about the jobs where the fit was right—the client trusted you, the work suited the strengths of your crew, the project was financially healthy, and the architect or designer was collaborative. Problems came up, as they always do, but the team solved them together rather than turning on one another. When the project ended, you were proud not only of what you built but of how you built it.

    Sources indicate that then ask a simple question: How did that project find us? You may discover that the same architect appears several times. Maybe a handful of past clients have been quietly sending people your way for years. Perhaps one designer, Realtor, supplier, or fellow builder keeps connecting you to projects that are an unusually good fit. Those patterns matter. They show you where to focus your time and attention. And when you’re trying to become known somewhere newly introduced, that kind of focus becomes even more notable.

    Recent findings suggest that for example, Sycamore Builders in western North Carolina has strong experience with architect-led custom homes in mountain communities. But as the company looks to expand into nearby markets, it faces a familiar challenge: Reputation is local.

    Sources indicate that in some of those communities, builders have been around for generations. Their trucks are familiar. Realtors and architects know them. Their projects are part of the landscape. That familiarity has been built over years. You cannot advertise your way into a 25-year relationship.

    So Sycamore is taking a patient approach by building relationships with architects and Realtors, sharing more of the stories behind its work, and showing up consistently in a few specific communities. The goal isn’t a flood of calls. One or two well-aligned latest builds a year can make a ­meaningful difference.

    If the word marketing makes you want to stop reading, forget about marketing for a minute. Take an hour with your business partner, project manager, or someone who knows your company well and work through these questions. Let your answers guide you in pinpointing the type of work you want to find. Once you do, you won’t need to network every week, post every day, or constantly update your website. Pick a few actions that fit your business, and keep doing them.

    What work do people call you for—and what work do you wish people called you for?

    Sources indicate that be honest with yourself. Is the work you’re doing now the work you want to be doing? If not, that’s your starting point.

    What are five projects you’d do again tomorrow?

    What made those projects good for the client, the crew, and the business? Writing the answers down can help you determine the type of work you want to do more of.

    How did each of those projects find you?

    Maybe it was a past client, an architect, a builder, a Realtor, a jobsite sign, a Google search, or something else. Don’t guess—find out. Then you can use those same methods to find similar projects in the future.

    Who is connected to the work you want?

    Make a list of the Realtors, architects, designers, and trade partners who are connected to the kinds of projects and clients you want more of, using your favorite projects as a guide. Who do you already know? Who consistently connects you to good-fit work? Who would you like to build a stronger relationship with?

    How can you stay connected to those people?

    Could you invite someone to a jobsite, meet for coffee, share an interesting project over email, attend an industry event, or simply check in occasionally? Staying in touch helps potential partners remember you and your business when the right project comes along.

    When someone looks you up, can they see what you want to be known for?

    Do your website and social media show the types of projects you want to do? Are you telling the stories behind that work and making your expertise visible? The clearer you are about the work you want, the easier it is for the right clients and partners to recognize that you’re the right fit.

    According to recent reports, this is usually the point where someone says, “Carrie, I have houses to build. I can’t spend all my time updating a website, posting on social media, meeting architects for coffee, and telling project stories.”.

    That’s fair, and I don’t want you to. Go back to what you learned about your best projects, and choose two or three things you can realistically keep doing to continue getting this sort of work. For example, maybe that means staying connected to a small group of architects and adding a strong project story to your website every few months.

    According to recent reports, then pay attention to what happens. Ask every new caller how they heard about you, notice which relationships lead to good-fit projects, and see whether the work coming through the door starts to look more like the work you want.

    For example, longtime high-performance builder Steve DeMetrick of DeMetrick Housewrights has spent more than two decades developing a reputation for building homes that demonstrate thoughtful craftsmanship, durability, and energy-efficiency. Most of his work has come through referrals. He has deep expertise, strong relationships, and plenty of experience. He is not trying to make the phone ring more.

    In fact, when we started talking about where he wants the organization to go next, his answer was almost the opposite of what we typically associate with growth. He wants to slow down. He wants fewer projects at a time, larger scope, deeper involvement with each client, earlier collaboration with architects, and more opportunity to use the knowledge he has accumulated over decades.

    Industry observers note that the more we talked, the clearer it became that high-performance construction is only part of what makes his organization valuable. What really stands out is how he approaches the whole process—bringing design, budget, and scope together early and getting everyone working together sooner. That can lead to better decisions, fewer surprises, and a better experience for everyone involved. But that type of value is a lot harder to advertise on the side of a truck.

    Sources indicate that the goal isn’t simply to tell more people that DeMetrick Housewrights builds high-performance homes. It is to make more of Steve’s thinking visible, to tell the stories behind projects, to explain why he approaches preconstruction the way he does, and to give potential clients and collaborators a better sense of what it is actually like to work with him. The point isn’t to create content for the sake of content. It is to help people see expertise that is already there.

    I’ve seen the same thing with Bell Street Builders in Maine, an employee-owned cooperative that does thoughtful restoration and renovation work around Portland and Casco Bay, including historic homes, architect-driven projects, and coastal and island construction. Those projects come with the kinds of challenges experienced builders know well: older structures that reveal surprises, coastal exposure, difficult logistics, complicated sequencing, and the need to make decisions carefully when clients may be living elsewhere.

    When I worked on Bell Street’s strategic direction, one theme kept reappearing: Bell Street knows old buildings. This is much more useful than generically saying the organization does “quality construction.”.

    Recent findings suggest that if you own a 100-year-old house in Portland and are about to open walls that may be hiding decades of complications, you want a builder who understands what they’re looking at and can respond without turning every surprise into a crisis. If you’re an architect working on that house, you want a builder who can solve problems collaboratively and respect the building while still moving the project forward.

    Bell Street did not need to become known to every homeowner in southern Maine. The better opportunity was to become more recognizable for the work the company does best and in the places where it wants to do more of it. That meant making sure its website and social channels highlighted more of its historic work and the stories behind complex projects, staying connected with architects and designers who work on those kinds of homes, and building relationships in priority communities such as Portland’s West End, Foreside communities, and the Casco Bay islands.

    Becoming recognizable doesn’t have to mean constantly creating something new. One good project can go a long way. Document the challenges during construction, photograph the finished work, explain what the team had to solve, and share that story on a website, social media, or directly with architects and past clients who may know someone planning a similar project.

    I genuinely appreciate builders’ resistance to marketing. It usually stems from a belief that the work should matter most. I think so too.

    A clever website cannot make up for poor craftsmanship. Advertising cannot replace trust, and social media cannot substitute for treating clients well, running a good jobsite, respecting trade partners, or standing behind what you build. Your reputation still has to be earned.

    It has been revealed that once you’ve earned it, however, there is nothing wrong with helping it travel. That doesn’t require becoming a marketer. It simply means being a little more intentional about making the work, knowledge, and people behind your tech giant visible.

    And there is a benefit beyond finding the kinds of projects you want. The same things that help clients, architects, designers, and trade partners understand your tech giant also help potential employees understand it. Most builder websites show houses, but far fewer show the people behind them. A good carpenter who is considering their next move may want to know what kinds of projects they would work on, who they would work alongside, whether people stay, and whether there is room to grow.

    It has been revealed that make it easier for future employees and clients alike to understand who you are, what you do well, and where you’re headed. Because good work will lead to more good work, but only if people know about it.

    — Carrie Simmons is director of marketing and a business consultant at HELM Construction Solutions. Photo courtesy of HELM Construction Solutions.

    According to recent reports, I have a question about my dog, Jethro. Sometimes when he alerts, the hackles between his shoulders rise. Other times they are prominent along his lower back. What does each appearance indicate about how he is responding?â.

    That is a great observation! When a dogâs hackles rise, it is an involuntary response controlled by the autonomic nervous system called piloerection, and it tells us that his arousal level has increased. However, the location of the raised hair does not reliably tell us which emotion a dog is experiencing.

    In a recent development, when the hackles rise between his shoulders, it can accompany alertness, excitement, uncertainty, or concern. When they appear along his lower back, the same range of emotional responses is possible. Neither pattern automatically indicates aggression, fear, or a particular level of threat. Think of hackles as a little emotional alarm bell; they tell us Jethro is experiencing heightened arousal, but not exactly why.

    Sources indicate that different dogs will respond to different stimuli in different ways, so thereâs no âone size fits allâ explanation for why different areas are triggered. I would pay close attention to what is happening around him when this occurs. Is he alerting to a stranger approaching the house, another dog walking past, an unfamiliar noise, or something unexpected in the environment? You might want to start keeping a record of what is going on before and after Jethroâs hackles are raised, and whether itâs his shoulders or lower back that is involved.

    Combine that context with his facial expression, ear position, tail carriage, posture, muscle tension, and ability to disengage. Looking at the whole picture helps us understand whether Jethro is curious, excited, uncertain, or uncomfortable, and, most importantly, how we can best support him. These details, together with what triggered the alert, give us a much clearer picture of how Jethro is feeling.

    Sources indicate that one of Arianne’s fabulous container combinations features Tropicanna Gold canna (Canna ‘Mactro’, Zones 8–11), purple shield (Strobilanthes dyerianus, annual), begonias (Begonia cvs., annual), flowering kale (Brassica oleracea, annual), and parrot’s beak (Lotus berthelotii, annual).     Sources indicate that just around the corner from the photo above. Another gorgeous tropical container, and ‘Blue Shadow’ fothergilla (Fothergilla × intermedia ‘Blue Shadow’, Zones 5–8) grows on the left in this view.

    According to recent reports, surfing isnât an activity for every dog, and thatâs okay. Waiting on the beach for their pet parents is a perfectly wonderful way to spend the day, too. As long as everyone is happy and the beach is left clean, that's a win for dogs and people alike.

    Of course, the fun of watching dogs surf is only part of what made this event special. It also brought together two things that are so much a part of Sayulita: its surf culture and its affection for dogs.

    It has been revealed that the 2026 dog-surfing event added something genuinely newly introduced to the International DÃ­a de Muertos Surf Tournament. While the main competition celebrated its third year, the dogs were making their own history and adding to the unique charm of the event.

    In a recent development, one of the nicest parts of returning to town was seeing how naturally dogs fit into both everyday life and local traditions. From the pups waiting patiently on the beach as their owners enjoy the waves, to the little altars honoring those who had passed away, there were reminders everywhere of the special place dogs hold in this community. Watching these dogs enjoy the waves alongside their pet parents was a lovely addition to a weekend already filled with celebration, music, and remembrance. Seeing just how much dogs are woven into Sayulita's culture, thereâs surely no better place for a doggy surfing competition.

    In a recent development, after years as a building-performance consultant, Margo Valdes grew frustrated of seeing the problems that arise when contractors ignore fundamental building science. Three years ago, she founded Athena Building Performance, a weatherization company built on the premise that getting the details right starts with understanding why a building behaves the way it does.

    Margo graduated from college with degrees in economics and physics, but her favorite course was “Castles,” taken during a semester abroad in England. The class explored how to determine the age of a castle, identify the type of stone used to build it, and understand the reasoning behind its design. Margo loved it.

    Sources indicate that after working an unfulfilling office job, Margo saw an ad for a HERS rater at Conservation Services Group (now CLEAResult). The job sounded like a good fit, so she applied, and her career in building performance began.

    Margo spent about six years at CSG and credits the manufacturer with giving her a strong foundation in building science. Though her work as a HERS rater focused on testing and evaluating, she received hands-on training in air-sealing and choosing and installing insulation. After leaving CSG, Margo’s focus shifted from new construction to existing buildings. She joined a consulting firm, where she spent seven years as director of the Existing Buildings team.

    Industry observers note that over the years, Margo became increasingly aware of how much the quality of weatherization work depends on understanding the building as a system—adding insulation affects moisture, and sealing air leaks changes ventilation. She decided the best way to improve the work was to get closer to it. That led her to the contractor side of the business, and to founding Athena.

    Industry observers note that today, Athena operates as a specialized weatherization contractor, tackling residential air-sealing and insulation upgrades. While Margo spends most of her time managing the business, knowledgeable practice remains at its heart: Every latest hire spends weeks doing hands-on field training and diagnostic walk-throughs to understand not just how the work is done, but why.

    Margo envisions eventually expanding Athena into a full-service building-enclosure firm. For now, she’s focused on centering the company around what started it all: thoughtful, educated work.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Hingham, Massachusetts, for some beautiful fall color from Nancy. Nancy sent in photos of the trees and shrubs winding down the season in her garden, along with one of the last flowers still hanging on.

    This is our sugar maple (Acer saccharum, Zones 3–8) showing off its fall foliage before it drops its leaves to keep my gardens warm this winter.

    My ‘Forest Pansy’ eastern redbud (Cercis canadensis ‘Forest Pansy’, Zones 5–9) is maroon most of the year until fall, when it turns a lovely yellow.

    My paperbark maple (Acer griseum, Zones 4–8) has had a hard time coping with our summer droughts and water restrictions, but it looked a lovely red this fall.

    Recent findings suggest that this is another native tree that many people are not familiar with, fringe tree (Chionanthus virginicus, Zones 4–9), which has fragrant white flowers hanging from its branches in late spring to early summer. As you can see, it also looks beautiful in its yellow fall foliage.

    Recent findings suggest that in the front of this picture is a young sweetgum (Liquidambar styraciflua, Zones 5–9), which has spectacular red color in the fall and develops spiky seed balls as it matures. In the distance is a blackhaw viburnum (Viburnum prunifolium, Zones 3–9) showing its orange fall color.

    Recent findings suggest that ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla (Fothergilla ‘Mount Airy’, Zones 5–8) glows red and orange in front of fragrant abelia (Abelia mosanensis, Zones 4–8), whose fall color is beginning to fade. The abelia will charm us all again in spring with its fragrant blooms.

    According to recent reports, sweetshrub (Calycanthus floridus, Zones 5–9) on the right has turned a lovely yellow. Amazingly, all three sweetshrubs shown here had the bark eaten off around every trunk by rabbits last winter, killing every one. They all grew back from the roots, showing just how resilient they are. On the left, ‘Mount Airy’ fothergilla is showing off its red fall foliage, and in back is ‘Alice’ oakleaf hydrangea (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Alice’, Zones 5–9) with maroon fall foliage.

    One of the only flowers left blooming is ‘Sheffield Pink’ chrysanthemum (Chrysanthemum ‘Sheffield Pink’, Zones 5–9), which complements the dark foliage of Diabolo ninebark (Physocarpus opulifolius ‘Monlo’, Zones 3–7) behind it.

    Thanks for sharing your fall garden with us, Nancy! Nancy claims she’s ready to wander the garden, make her list of what needs dividing in spring, and figure out what upcoming plants need to be bought. Sounds like a good way to spend the off-season to me!

    Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    It has been revealed that puppyhood is a huge learning curve â for both owner and dog â and managing a puppyâs energy can be one of the hardest parts of it. Hyperactivity is common, and the good news is that knowing what causes it makes it much easier to help a puppy calm down. The reasons range from ordinary puppy exuberance to, on rare occasions, a health problem.

    Puppies burn energy by exploring and playing, but they can run out of things to do. A mix of toys, activities, and walks helps manage their energy. Without it, boredom and frustration can lead to destructive behavior or aggression, or to zooming around the house. A puppy with no good outlet, such as a sturdy chew toy, will release that pent-up energy by barking, running around, or jumping on people.

    The opposite problem is just as real. Just like toddlers who throw tantrums when theyâre overtired, puppies that have too much going on can become hyperactive because they donât understand that they need a nap, and the discomfort frustrates them. Finding the balance gets easier as an owner learns a puppyâs energy levels. Plenty of activities and training sessions help, as do regular quiet times for cooling off and a quick nap to recharge.

    Puppies learn swiftly, and that includes behaviors that owners donât mean to encourage. If a puppy gets attention every time it becomes overexcited during play, even when the owner is trying to say stop, the puppy sees it as a reward, and the next time it feels neglected, hyper behavior may seem like a good way to get noticed. The fix is to interact when the puppy is gentle or relaxed, and to become less interesting when it gets overexcited, by dropping the tug toy and stepping away.

    According to recent reports, all puppies have energy, but the amount varies by breed, and a breedâs original purpose matters as much as its size. Border Collies, bred to herd sheep all day, require lots of physical and mental stimulation to keep up with their boundless energy. A more sedate breed, like the French Bulldog or King Charles Spaniel, tends to have far less energy to burn. A Border Collie puppy has less stamina than an adult, but it still has plenty of energy to manage.

    In a recent development, food affects everything from digestion to brain development, and it can influence sleep cycles, energy levels, and skin health. The wrong diet may contain too much of certain ingredients, often protein, which can lead to hyperactivity. Researching a puppyâs nutritional needs and checking the ingredients with a vet is worthwhile.

    It has been revealed that obedience training teaches a dog how to manage its behavior, and socialization helps it get used to people, other pets, and new situations. Without them, a puppy doesnât know how to react, and a quick play session can end with an overexcited puppy that canât calm down. A tiny puppy climbing on people or nipping fingers may seem cute, but puppies donât always stay small, and an adult dog that bites or jumps can be dangerous, especially around a child or a stranger.

    Recent findings suggest that most of the time, hyperactivity is easily corrected and comes down to diet, breed, or limited exercise. Health problems are a rare cause. If a puppy is still hyper after changes to diet, activity, and training, a vet check to rule out any health concerns is always a good idea. The earlier a problem is diagnosed, the easier it is to treat.

    Puppies are still learning what their bodies are telling them. One of the most common signs is becoming hyper or restless when they need to go. An older puppy getting used to house training may be asking to go out, while a younger one may not understand the signal and burst into a case of the zoomies until it figures it out.

    Industry observers note that most hyperactivity simply comes from being a puppy. Younger dogs are more excitable, and they need lots of energy to explore the world without yet knowing how to manage it. Puppies steadily grow out of it. They may still get the zoomies later on, but they settle and learn better control. Rewarding calm behavior, working on obedience, and giving a working breed a job to do all help.

    It has been revealed that researching a breed before bringing a puppy home matters, since a high-energy herding breed can be too much for some households. Time matters too, because a long workday followed by evening chores may leave little room for the exercise a puppy needs.

    It has been revealed that activity is the best way to manage energy, and it shouldnât be only physical. Puzzles and other mental activities keep a brain busy as well. Calm behavior deserves rewards with treats and attention, and disengaging when a puppy gets overexcited teaches that playing nicely keeps the game going longer. Training helps too, because some hyper behavior is really bad manners learned along the way, such as jumping up or racing around when the leash comes out.

    In a recent development, most puppies grow out of their boundless energy as they reach adulthood and learn self-control, which can take between one and two years depending on breed. Some breeds are naturally quieter and happier to laze around, while more active breeds never lose their energy. A routine tailored to a dogâs needs is essential, along with choosing a puppy that suits the family.

    According to recent reports, A puppyâs energy can come from exuberance, overstimulation, tiredness, boredom, diet, or, on rare occasions, health concerns. Working out which one applies, and adjusting the daily schedule to match, is the key to keeping it manageable.

    #147550. Tech Report: Christmas Cactus Not Blooming? 5 Common Mistakes That Stop the Holiday Flower Show

    📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1257 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Christmas Cactus Not Blooming? 5 Common Mistakes That Stop the Holiday Flower Show

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Industry observers note that A Christmas cactus not blooming is a common holiday letdown, and it stings more when the plant seems perfectly healthy with plump green stems.
    • A healthy Christmas cactus doesn't automatically mean you have a holiday houseplant that's ready to flower.
    • There are five common mistakes that lead to zero holiday flowers.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Industry observers note that A Christmas cactus not blooming is a common holiday letdown, and it stings more when the plant seems perfectly healthy with plump green stems. And you ask yourself, why won't my Christmas cactus flower when the plant looks just fine? A Christmas cactus not showing buds by the end of November is usually reacting to light, warmth, water or a move at the wrong moment. And, once you've worked out what the cause is, there's still time to fix some mistakes so you can enjoy the holiday flower show.

    A healthy Christmas cactus doesn't automatically mean you have a holiday houseplant that's ready to flower. Buds form in response to fall conditions – long dark nights and cooler temperatures – and many folk create the exact environment to make sure a Christmas cactus blooms right on time for the holidays. So, unless it gets those triggers to start forming buds, the plant won't flower even if you give your Christmas cactus all the care it needs in November to keep it healthy. Another common problem with a Christmas cactus not flowering is that it does form buds, but drops them before they open.

    There are five common mistakes that lead to zero holiday flowers. Which of these issues is the reason why your Christmas cactus doesn't have buds yet?

    In a recent development, holiday cacti set flower buds when nights grow long. They need about 13 to 14 hours of uninterrupted darkness each night for six weeks or more, and that dark period must be truly dark. Even a table lamp switched on in the evening, a street light shining through the window or a hallway light left on overnight can interrupt the cycle, causing the plant to keep making stems instead of buds. This mistake shows up as no buds at all.

    Sources indicate that if you suspect this is the reason your Schlumbergera doesn't have buds yet, place your plant in complete darkness after dinner then bring it back to bright, indirect light in the morning. A dark room that isn't used is perfect, and you can block any artificial light coming through the window with blackout curtains like Sun Zero Curtain Panels, available from Walmart. Another option is simply to cover the plant in an upturned cardboard box overnight.

    Once buds have set, night length stops mattering as much, so evening light isn't a problem.

    According to recent reports, cool nights are the other half of the trigger to get a Christmas cactus to flower. Holiday cacti need nights between 50°F and 59°F (10–15°C) to set buds, so keep a living room warm all evening with the furnace running and that signal disappears.

    Move your Christmas cactus to a cooler spot at night, not a cold one. An unheated bedroom or a sunroom that cools down after dark often works, as long as temperature doesn't dip below 50°F (10°C). It's hard to guess how cool a room gets at three o'clock in the morning so a cheap indoor thermometer that records the maximum and minimum temperatures, like the TempPro digital indoor thermometer on Amazon, is handy to check the overnight number.

    Once your plant has formed buds, it'' still very sensitive to environmental conditions, so be sure to avoid the common spots that cause a Christmas cactus to lose its buds.

    Industry observers note that holiday cacti aren't desert cacti. They grow on rainforest trees in Brazil so don't like to bake dry the way a barrel cactus loves. Let the potting mix dry out hard while buds are forming and the plant may make fewer of them, or wilt and drop the ones it has. Keep the mix soggy and the roots can rot, which ends the same way – limp stems and buds on the floor.

    Industry observers note that once buds appear, keep the potting mix evenly moist but never wet. An easy way to check if your Christmas cactus needs watering is to push a long wooden skewer like these bamboo skewers from Walmart to the bottom of the pot and pull it out: if damp soil clings to the wood, wait a few days before watering again. An indoor watering can with a long goose-neck spout like this houseplant can from Walmart makes it much easier to be precise about how much water you're giving your plant. Empty the saucer after every watering too.

    It has been revealed that once buds have formed, moving your plant is one of the easiest ways to lose them. Any sudden shift in light, temperature or humidity can trigger bud loss. Christmas cacti are so sensitive to their environment, it's not just moving the plant from a cool back bedroom to a warm, dim spot beside the tree that causes bud drop. Even moving your holiday houseplant to a different spot in the same room or rotating the pot can be enough to lose those precious buds.

    Choose the spot where your plant will stay through the holidays as soon as buds appear, then leave it there. Check that spot for heat and drafts first. Buds also drop on plants near heating vents, a gas fireplace or a bowl of ripening fruit which gives off ethylene gas. The same care applies if you buy a plant with buds already set, such as this pack of 2 Holiday Christmas Cactus from Costa Farms, via The Home Depot. Ask for the plant to be wrapped against the cold for the trip home and put it in its final spot as soon as it arrives. A few buds will fall while it settles in but most will stay put as long as you don't move the plant again.

    Holiday cacti should only be fed during active growth from spring through late summer, so don't fertilize after September. That break from fertilizer helps plants set more flower buds in fall. November feeding won't help a plant that already lacks buds and, on a stressed plant, extra salts in the pot do more harm than good.

    Wait until the flowers finish and new growth starts in spring, then use a balanced food for indoor flowering plants such as Espoma Organic Violet! plant food, available on Amazon, once a month at half strength through summer.

    If you don't see any signs of buds on your holiday houseplant by late November, it's worth trying the banana bag trick to trigger Christmas cactus blooms. However, flowers will likely open in early January rather than on Christmas morning.

    Next year, start the dark nights in late September or early October so the timing lines up. Buds usually show up three to four weeks after long nights begin, and the flowers open after roughly six to eight weeks of short days.

    A plant that already has small buds at its stem tips in mid-November has done the hard part, however, so as long as you keep your Christmas cactus in one spot that's not too warm at night, and evenly moist, those flowers should open on schedule.

    In a recent development, tyler’s passion began with indoor gardening and deepened as he studied plant-fungi interactions in controlled settings. With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    If Sergeant Stubby proved what an untrained stray could do in the First World War, Chips proved what a dog could do once the United States built an actual program around him. Chips became the most decorated American dog of World War II. His story also marks the moment the Army decided it should never again give such awards to an animal.

    Chips was a mix of German Shepherd, Collie, and Husky, born around 1940 and raised as a family pet by Edward Wren and his family in Pleasantville, New York. In 1942, the Wrens donated Chips to the newly formed Dogs for Defense program, part of the Armyâs larger War Dog Program, formally authorized on March 13, 1942. Chips trained at the War Dog Training Center in Front Royal, Virginia, and was partnered with Private John P. Rowell. The two served in the 3rd Military Police Platoon, 30th Infantry Regiment, 3rd Infantry Division, under General George S. Patton.

    Chips and Rowell landed in North Africa during Operation Torch in November 1942 and served through campaigns in Sicily, Italy, southern France, and the Rhineland and central European theaters. He was also present as a sentry dog at the 1943 Casablanca Conference, guarding the meeting between Winteon Churchill and Franklin D. Roosevelt.

    Chips earned his fame during the Allied invasion of Sicily, Operation Husky, on the morning of July 10, 1943. As Rowell and Chips came ashore, a hidden machine gun nest opened fire and pinned down their platoon. Chips tore free of his handler and charged the position alone, seizing the gunner by the throat and forcing the crew to surrender. As a result, four Italian soldiers surrendered. That same night, Chips alerted the platoon to ten additional enemy soldiers attempting to slip through the lines under cover of darkness, leading to their capture as well.

    According to recent reports, chips did not escape the encounter unscathed. He suffered burns around his mouth and eye and a wound to his scalp. His actions, however, quickly became national news. Captain Edward G. Parr, the manufacturer commander, recommended Chips for the Distinguished Service Cross, citing his âcourageous action in single-handedly eliminating a dangerous machine gun nest and causing surrender of its crewâ. On November 19, 1943, Major General Lucian K. Truscott Jr. awarded Chips the Silver Star, and accounts differ slightly on whether the Distinguished Service Cross was also formally conferred or only recommended. What is well documented is that Chips also received a Purple Heart for his wounds.

    In 1945, Chips met General Dwight (Ike) D. Eisenhower, who bent down to pet the famous dog. Chips, true to his sentry training, nipped the generalâs hand. The incident became one of the more good-humored footnotes in his legend.

    Industry observers note that washington reacted less good-humoredly to the idea of a dog receiving human military honors. After public objection to the precedent of awarding animals medals intended for soldiers, the War Department revoked Chipsâs Silver Star, Distinguished Service Cross, and Purple Heart in early 1944. His platoon nonetheless unofficially awarded him a Theater Ribbon with Arrowhead, an honor reserved for assault landings, along with eight battle stars, one for each campaign in which he served. Chips was honorably discharged on December 10, 1945, and returned to the Wren family in Pleasantville. He died a few months after returning home, from complications related to his wartime wounds.

    In January 2018, more than seven decades after his service, the United Kingdomâs PDSA posthumously awarded Chips its Dickin Medal, the animal equivalent of the Victoria Cross, in a ceremony at the Churchill War Rooms in London on the 75th anniversary of the Casablanca Conference. John Wren, then 76, traveled from the United States to accept the medal on Chipsâs behalf. PDSA Director General Jan McLoughlin remarked that the honor finally allowed Chips to âtake his place in the history books as one of the most heroic dogs to serve with the US Armyâ.

    Recent findings suggest that chips is estimated to have been one of more than 10,000 dogs who served in the American military during World War II. His story, and the controversy his medals caused, shaped military policy for decades: no American war dog would again receive an official human combat decoration, a policy that held until working dogs began receiving other forms of formal recognition much later in the twentieth century.

    In a recent development, every military working dog story, whether it unfolded in the trenches of World War I or on a patrol in Afghanistan, is also the story of a partnership. Learning that history is one of the simplest ways to honor the generations of dogs and handlers who served side by side. If these stories have moved you, there are meaningful ways to help carry them forward.

    Support retired dogs. Not every military working dog can retire to a family couch. The Ddamien Project provides lifelong homes for retired military, contract, and law enforcement dogs whose medical or behavioral needs make typical adoption difficult.

    Industry observers note that learn more. The Military Working Dog Heritage Museum, founded by former K9 handlers, is gathering the photographs, documents, and firsthand accounts of the dogs and people who served. Its newsletter, The Paw Print, shares many of these stories with the public.

    It has been revealed that keep today's working dogs strong. Canine Advancement Group, led by veterinarian Dr. Brian Farr, advocates for treating working dogs as the athletes they are, offering evidence-based guidance on fitness, welfare, and handler education.

    Follow the national tribute. The National Service Animals Monument, planned for Washington, DC, will honor service animals and their handlers across military, law enforcement, and assistance roles, including generations of military working dogs.

    These dogs are part of our history. By preserving their stories, honoring their service, and caring for the dogs still serving and those who have come home, we help make sure their legacy endures.

    It has been revealed that among the dogs of the 26th Infantry Scout Dog Platoon, one German Shepherd stood out for the length and success of its combat record. Scout Dog York is credited with taking part in 148 combat missions without a single man in his patrol being killed, a record that made him one of the war's most celebrated scout dogs.

    I’m in love with these ‘Annabelle’ smooth hydrangeas (Hydrangea arborescens ‘Annabelle’, Zones 3–9). They are all over my yard.

    Another hydrangea vignette with viburnum, boxwood, and Japanese forest grass (Hakonechloa macra, Zones 5–9) in front.

    I love the beautiful colors of this barberry.

    Around the other side of our yard, the dwarf smokebush shines among the evergreens and the orange leaves of the mountain ash and honey locust (Gleditsia triacanthos, Zones 3–8) trees.

    Looking toward the front yard, the dwarf smokebush steals the show!

    Another view from the front yard.

    A weeping Norway spruce (Picea abies, Zones 3–7) and barberry make a beautiful combination.

    In a recent development, thanks for sharing your beautiful fall garden with us, Bonnie! The trees are gorgeous, but I agree that the shrubs really stole the show this year.

    Turn a Cheap Christmas Tree Into a Showstopper – 6 Easy Steps to Make It Lush and Luxurious

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • When you take the kids out to choose a Christmas tree, everyone has in mind a lush, deep green, perfectly shaped evergreen that is featured in holiday advertisements.
    • But don’t worry, an inexpensive grocery store Christmas tree can be “spruced up” nicely with a few simple tricks.
    • According to recent reports, in this guide, I'm going to walk you through the easy steps you can take to improve your tree dramatically, from a sparse Christmas tree to a festive showstopper.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When you take the kids out to choose a Christmas tree, everyone has in mind a lush, deep green, perfectly shaped evergreen that is featured in holiday advertisements. But not every evergreen in the lot has that kind of sex appeal, especially budget trees for sale in grocery stores, supermarkets, and big-box retailers. These affordable trees can look thin, sparse, and like they didn’t get any sleep last night.

    But don’t worry, an inexpensive grocery store Christmas tree can be “spruced up” nicely with a few simple tricks. Yes, you can turn ugly ducklings into beautiful centerpieces by taking steps to make a Christmas tree look fuller, well-structured, and fresh. I’ll explain how to make a real Christmas tree look better with Christmas tree care tips that boost your tree's wow-power.

    According to recent reports, in this guide, I'm going to walk you through the easy steps you can take to improve your tree dramatically, from a sparse Christmas tree to a festive showstopper. And I promise it won’t cost you a fortune.

    Industry observers note that there are many reasons that a freshly cut Christmas tree can look droopy and sparse in the store. These include transport stress and dehydration. One of the quickest fixes with a big punch is to make a fresh cut on the bottom of the trunk, taking off around ½ inch. A good folding saw, such as the Rexberi 11-Inch Folding Saw from Amazon, will make light work of this, and it's handy for pruning jobs around the garden, too.

    Immediately after cutting, pop the tree into a sturdy stand with water. The Krinner Genie Christmas Tree Stand has a foot-pedal mechanism that makes it easy to secure the tree, plus a built-in water reservoir. But it's not cheap, and if you're buying a budget tree, chances are you'll want a budget-friendly stand to go with it. The Leejec Christmas Tree Stand is a good, affordable alternative, with a generous water reservoir and a handy water level indicator.

    Don't leave the tree sitting around after making the cut. The cut surface can dry out, reducing moisture uptake, so getting it into water promptly gives it the best chance of staying fresh.

    Sources indicate that that sorrowful evergreen you brought home needs time to relax. Once you prune off the very bottom of the trunk, set the tree in a bucket of water and give it time to rehydrate. Leave it wrapped in its netting overnight, which will also make it easier to maneuver into its stand the next day.

    In a recent development, once the tree is securely in place, remove the wrapping and let the branches gradually drop and spread into their natural shape for a few hours. You might be surprised how much fuller it looks after a little time to settle.

    Now it's time to give your tree a little makeover. Walk around it and look carefully at its shape. There will likely be a few stray or uneven branches that need tidying up, particularly if you've bought a cheaper tree that hasn't been professionally shaped.

    To prune your Christmas tree, take a sharp pair of bypass pruners – Fiskars Bypass Pruning Shears from Amazon are a good, affordable option – and start by removing any broken, damaged, or awkwardly protruding branches. Trim back overly long branches to a side shoot where possible, rather than cutting bluntly through the tips.

    Recent findings suggest that pay particular attention to the lower branches. Remove any that drag on the floor or interfere with the stand, making clean cuts close to the trunk without damaging the bark. This will give the tree a neater silhouette and make it easier to reach the water reservoir.

    Industry observers note that step back regularly to check your progress, working toward a balanced cone shape without making the tree look unnaturally perfect. Go easy, though – you can always take more off, but you can't put a branch back.

    Industry observers note that starting at the bottom of the tree, gently separate any branches that have become compressed during transport. Work your way upward, easing crowded branches apart and encouraging them to spread into their natural positions. Take care not to force stiff branches, as they can snap.

    In a recent development, once you've worked your way around the tree, step back and look for any obvious gaps. You may be able to gently reposition flexible branches to make the tree look fuller, but avoid bending or twisting them into unnatural shapes.

    Pay particular attention to the lower branches, spreading them outward where possible to help disguise the trunk and tree stand. Near the top, gently separate crowded branches to create a more balanced, tapered shape. Don't worry about making everything perfectly symmetrical – a little natural irregularity is part of the charm of a real Christmas tree.

    According to recent reports, have you ever used hair extensions? Or had a friend who used hair weaving to change the volume of their hair? You can use this same technique to fill in the canopy of your Christmas tree by tucking extra evergreen branches into bare spots. It’s a quick way to give a sparse Christmas tree a fuller figure.

    According to recent reports, what to use for this type of branch extension? Start with any healthy branches you removed when pruning your tree earlier. You can also use evergreen clippings from your own yard or ask for spare branches from the Christmas tree lot. Choose branches that closely match your tree for the most natural finish, or mix two or three types of evergreen to add depth and texture.

    According to recent reports, for larger bare patches, try tucking in realistic faux evergreen sprays, like these Hananona pine branches. Cedar and pine sprays work particularly well, blending into the natural foliage while adding extra volume.

    According to recent reports, tuck the cut ends in toward the trunk, positioning the foliage to disguise any obvious gaps. Use green floral wire, like this Pauleen wire from Amazon, to secure the stems discreetly to existing branches, making sure they're firmly attached. Step back occasionally to check the overall effect, adding a few more sprigs wherever the tree still looks sparse.

    Recent findings suggest that we all have good sides and bad sides, and your Christmas tree might too. If one side is lopsided or less impressive, simply turn it toward the wall. Of course, this trick works less well if you have a revolving tree stand.

    According to recent reports, some gaps may still be visible after fluffing up the branches and adding extras, but that's where clever decorating comes to the rescue. Tuck large ornaments deep inside the tree, closer to the trunk, to disguise bare spots and create a sense of depth.

    Sources indicate that another great trick is to cluster smaller ornaments in groups of three to make sparse areas look fuller. If one part of the tree is overloaded with decorations, move a few into the gaps to create a more balanced look. You can also use pinecones, artificial flowers, or decorative picks to add texture and interest.

    Recent findings suggest that finally, try weaving wide ribbons or garlands through the branches to disguise any remaining gaps. Rather than wrapping them tightly around the outside, tuck sections deeper into the tree and let them billow outward. This creates the illusion of a much fuller, more luxurious Christmas tree without spending a fortune.

    Keeping your tree looking good until Christmas requires a little effort. Here are some top tips:.

    This Beautiful Festive Tradition Lets You Grow Your Own Centerpiece In Time For Christmas

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Traditions connect generations, carrying the cultural and moral values of ancestors to new generations, giving them a sense of identity and belonging.
    • It has been revealed that the sowing of Christmas wheat is a tradition across Europe from France to Ukraine and the Balkans.
    • In a recent development, you don’t have to live in the South of France or other parts of Europe to practice this lovely tradition.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Traditions connect generations, carrying the cultural and moral values of ancestors to new generations, giving them a sense of identity and belonging. Some of these traditions are so lovely that they are adopted more widely. The beautiful old Christmas tradition of Christmas wheat is one of them.

    It has been revealed that the sowing of Christmas wheat is a tradition across Europe from France to Ukraine and the Balkans. Early in December, people “plant” wheatgrass seeds in bowls indoors early in December and let the shoots grow until Christmas. Initially the growing wheat seeds were considered a blessing for the coming harvest. But beyond that, the green shoots have come to symbolize fertility, new life, and eternal renewal.

    In a recent development, you don’t have to live in the South of France or other parts of Europe to practice this lovely tradition. We’ll tell you all about the custom of growing wheatgrass indoors and how you can make it your own this Christmas.

    All around the globe, cultural heritage shapes how people celebrate, and also how they express beauty. The lovely tradition of planting Christmas wheat is still very much a part of Christmas festivities in Europe, thought to have been inherited from the Romans.

    Sources indicate that it is practiced in the Province area of France, as well as Croatia, Ukraine, and parts of Italy and Portugal, each region claiming it as their own. In Province, it is called Saint-Barbe wheat (le blé de la Sainte-Barbe) because the day of planting, December 4, is the feast day of Saint Barbara. By Christmas day, the seeds have grown fresh green shoots that become decorations on the Christmas table.

    In a recent development, in Province, this age-old tradition involves sprouting grains of wheat in three separate bowls. The ritual is noted to ensure prosperity and happiness for the coming year, a promise memorialized in the old Provençal adage, “when wheat goes well, everything goes well.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in Croatia, the origins of this tradition are still related to religion, but they are different. Growing wheatgrass is related to the story of the holy family fleeing Herod’s soldiers. It is said that the family found a farmer sowing wheat. The family requested that the farmer tell the Herod’s soldiers that the family had already passed through.

    Industry observers note that the wheat grew remarkably fast that year so by the time the soldiers came, there was a fine crop. Then, the farmer told them that the family passed through while he was sowing his crop. Because the wheat was so tall, the soldiers assumed that the family had passed by long ago and abandoned their quest. As such, wheat seeds are sown in December to represent light found amid the winter's darkness.

    So, how to grow your own wheat?

    Well, if you would like to incorporate this ancient tradition into your own holiday celebrations, we’ll walk you through the steps. There are three: gather what you need, “plant” the seeds, then arrange the centerpiece.

    The most vital "ingredient" you will require to grow your own Christmas wheat are the wheat grains themselves. Traditionally, you use hard red winter wheat berries (sold as "wheatgrass seeds”) although it is possible to use alternatives like lentils or chickpeas instead.

    Industry observers note that the presentation also varies from region to region. In Province, for Saint Barbe’s wheat, they use three small bowls or saucers and damp cotton wool. The three containers have religious significance, representing the Holy Trinity. In Croatia, you can use any container, but you still need to line it with either cotton wool or soil as a growing medium. A more practical alternative is to use a growing tray filled with potting soil with a solid tray beneath it to catch water.

    Soak the grains overnight in water. After that, place them evenly on the growing medium - like the bed of damp cotton wool or the potting soil. If you are using three bowls, spread it evenly between them. If you are using a tray, spread the seeds there.

    Industry observers note that place the seeded container near a bright window at a mild temperature. Spray it with water and cover with plastic paper or a plastic bag. Remove this plastic when the seeds begin to germinate.

    Sources indicate that mist the cotton with water daily to keep it moist. This allows the shoots to germinate and grow straight and green.

    In a recent development, how you choose to arrange the centerpiece depends entirely on your own preferences and traditions. By Christmas Eve, the little shoots are green and straight,.

    Industry observers note that in Croatia, the wheat sprouts are often decorated with the Croatian tricolour – a red-white-blue ribbon. This adds patriotic symbolism. The Croatians sometimes add a red candle or even a red apple in the centre of the container to add more holiday cheer.

    It has been revealed that in Province, the French often toe up the sprouted wheat with red and yellow or red and green ribbons. The wheat display becomes the centerpiece for their traditional Christmas Eve feast. After Christmas, the French place the pots in or near the family crèche (aka the nativity scene) alongside handmade clay saint images. Finally, the wheat can be planted in open ground or burned in the fireplace for protection.

    In a recent development, remember, this is a lovely tradition, but while wheatgrass might look like a microgreen it should not be used as one. Yes, it has many incredible health properties (it is remarked to prevent some types of cancer, fight infection and improve cognitive function), but it is not edible.

    Sources indicate that that being said, you can juice it and drink its juice, which is full of vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants. Sounds like a great tipple after a big holiday feast, eh?

    Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler right now splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, this home was designed with two main goals in mind. The first was for it to integrate into its forest setting, making it feel at home among the trees. The second was to capture forest views from a light-filled yet intimate interior. By focusing on these goals, the architects designed a home that feels less like an object in the forest than a place quietly woven into it.

    Outside, three irregular, offset buildings—the main house, a sauna, and a garden shed—mimic the tree-filled landscape, while Nakamoto Forestry’s Gendai yakisugi charred-wood siding provides a darkened exterior reminiscent of the texture of tree bark.

    Inside, the dark, textured exterior gives way to bright, airy interiors filled with natural light, lighter wood finishes, and carefully framed views. Because the living spaces are stacked to fill the irregular form of the main house, each room provides a unique view of the landscape, with windows that vary in scale.

    Large windows in the living room and a sliding glass door in the dining area allow in sunlight and views from different directions, the primary bedroom on the top floor includes a small north-facing window, and a large window next to the bathtub frames the view of an eastern hilltop.

    The design team used the height of the ceilings to guide the function of each space, with cathedral ceilings creating a spacious effect in the main living spaces, cozier sloped ceilings in the primary bedroom and bathroom, and a welcoming reading nook in the second-floor bedroom where the roof slope drops to a low kneewall.

    Industry observers note that for families who have just lost a beloved pet, arranging cremation is often one of the last acts of love they can offer. They choose a service, pay for the arrangements, and believe that their companion will be treated with dignity and respect. They may never see what happens behind the crematorium doors, but they trust that their furry family member is in caring hands.

    Sadly, for hundreds of families in the Philippines, that trust has been destroyed.

    Industry observers note that what began as a neighborhood concern over a foul smell rapidly turned into a disturbing discovery. On October 29, 2026, residents of Barangay Minuyan in San Jose del Monte, Bulacan, were disturbed by a strong, suffocating, and foul odor coming from a nearby vacant lot. The terrible stink prompted a report and closer inspection, leading to the nightmare-worthy discovery of seven large sacks containing the remains of 26 dogs and three cats; each one wrapped in plastic bags bearing identification labels with their names and weights.

    The investigation eventually led to Ahjay Paws Aftercare Pet Crematorium in Bacoor, Cavite, where many families had entrusted their deceased pets for cremation.

    Sources indicate that by November 4, authorities had recovered 29 animal carcasses, while 20 containers of ashes surrendered by families were undergoing forensic examination. The National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) is investigating possible fraud and other violations, and at least 250 pet owners have reportedly filed complaints against the organization.

    According to recent reports, the questions are heartbreaking. Were these families given the ashes of their own pets? Were some animals never cremated at all? How did companions entrusted to a professional aftercare service end up in plastic bags beside a road?

    For grieving pet owners, discovering that their furry family member's final arrangements may have been mishandled is an especially cruel betrayal.

    Sadly, this is not the only case, or the only country, where fraud and deception have pervaded what should be a sacred service. In 2025, the Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Quintana Roo, Mexico, exposed a similarly disturbing situation. Authorities investigating a Chetumal pet crematorium found that families had paid to have their beloved companions cremated, only to receive urns containing soil instead of their pets' ashes. Even worse, more than 180 animal carcasses were reportedly discovered during searches connected with the investigation. The case involved allegations of fraud and improper disposal of animal remains, with legal proceedings continuing into 2026.

    According to recent reports, different countries, different businesses, but an eerily similar betrayal. And in both cases, the damage potentially reaches far beyond the families who were deceived.

    It has been revealed that another disturbing side of these horrific stories is the environmental impact. Improperly discarded animal remains can create environmental hazards, particularly when several carcasses accumulate in unmanaged locations.

    As tissues decompose, bodily fluids and organic material are released. These substances can contribute to leachate, a liquid that may move through soil with rainfall and drainage. Depending on soil conditions, groundwater depth, and proximity to wells or waterways, this can create pathways for environmental contamination.

    According to recent reports, biohazardous runoff, odors, and potential groundwater pollution are among the concerns associated with improperly managed animal carcasses. If investigators discover that remains were repeatedly discarded at multiple locations, removing the visible carcasses may not be enough. Surrounding soil, drainage systems, and nearby water sources may also need assessment.

    The deceived pet owners deserve justice, but residents also need answers about the conditions around their homes.

    Sources indicate that exposed animal remains can attract scavengers, including free-roaming dogs, cats, and wildlife. Insects may also come into contact with decomposing material and potentially spread infectious agents between locations.

    According to recent reports, not every deceased animal carries an infectious disease, and finding carcasses does not automatically mean disease will spread. However, when the cause of death is unknown, there may be no way to determine whether the remains contain infectious agents that could expose other animals.

    There is another potential hazard that pet owners may not immediately consider: euthanasia medications.

    It has been revealed that pentobarbital, commonly used for humane euthanasia in veterinary medicine, can remain in an animal's tissues after death. Wildlife that consumes the remains of an animal euthanized with this drug can suffer secondary poisoning, with scavenging birds being particularly vulnerable.

    In a recent development, and this is where the consequences can extend much further. Scavengers play an essential role in maintaining healthy ecosystems by removing animal carcasses before they become sources of environmental contamination and disease transmission. Vultures, for example, can consume remains that might otherwise attract other scavengers or allow infectious agents to persist in the environment. When scavenger populations decline, carcasses can remain accessible for longer, potentially increasing opportunities for pathogen transmission and disease spread.

    In a recent development, A carcass that should have been cremated could therefore become a source of danger to another animal. The irony is that the very animals helping keep ecosystems clean could be exposed to a potentially lethal drug simply because someone failed to dispose of a pet's remains responsibly.

    Recent findings suggest that the scandals also raise questions about oversight of the pet aftercare industry. A business permit cannot demonstrate that every animal entrusted to a facility has been handled properly.

    Families should be able to expect accountability throughout the process, from collection and identification to transportation, cremation, and the return of ashes. Records should establish which animal was received, where it was taken, and what happened to its remains.

    The Philippine Animal Welfare Society (PAWS) says the case has also highlighted a potential legal gap. According to the organization, the alleged deception may not fall directly under the Animal Welfare Act because the animals were already deceased when entrusted to the crematorium. However, the alleged conduct may constitute âestafaâ, or fraud by deceit, under the Revised Penal Code.

    Affected families have been encouraged to preserve receipts, cremation certificates, photographs, messages, and other documentation that could support their complaints.

    The Casa XibalbÃ¡ case in Mexico revealed a similarly disturbing situation, with more than 180 animal carcasses reportedly discovered and families allegedly receiving urns filled with soil instead of their pets' ashes. Two countries, two scandals, and far too many grieving families betrayed by businesses they trusted.

    Recent findings suggest that the death of a beloved pet is already a difficult time. Families make end-of-life decisions, discuss euthanasia with their veterinarians, arrange transportation, and decide how they would like to remember their companions.

    For some, receiving an urn containing their pet's ashes brings comfort. It becomes something tangible to keep beside a favorite photograph or in a special place at home. And while emotional cost is the most painful aspect for the affected pet owners, itâs also worth noting that individual cremation usually comes at a premium price; a price paid for a service not performed. But regardless of whether these pets were to have undergone individual or commingled cremation, families deserve honesty about the service they purchase.

    They should never have to question whether the ashes they brought home belong to their furry family member.

    There is something particularly upsetting about the possibility that an animal cherished throughout life, treated as family, and surrounded by affection could have its remains handled so carelessly.

    In a recent development, people entrust pet aftercare providers with something deeply personal. They are saying goodbye to someone they loved. That deserves respect.
