    Hi GPOD! Today we’re heading to Griffin, Georgia, for an enhancement from Connie Raines. We first visited Connie’s garden shortly after she moved into her new home and transplanted many of her plants. Now, a little over a year later, she’s back with a few highlights from spring and late summer. Here’s Connie:.

    I have lived in this house and garden for a little over a year. When I moved here, I worked hard to transplant many of my plants, and the garden continues to be a work in progress.

    Delphinium (Delphinium cvs., Zones 3–7) with coleus (Coleus scutellarioides, annual).

    Native swamp rose mallow (Hibiscus moscheutos, Zones 5–9) and zinnias.

    Perennial begonia (Begonia grandis, Zones 6–9), a soft mahonia bush just planted this spring, and amaranth.

    A watermelon my husband grew in our garden area created by a latest stepped retaining wall.

    A work in progress… I transplanted this hearts-a-bustin’ (Euonymus americanus, Zones 6–9) from a different spot where I originally had it. It was crowded in and now will be able to spread out.

    In a recent development, this celosia (Spicata group) actually grew from seeds of plants that were in a pot last summer. The ground in this area is where a tree used to be, and the roots are rotting and creating wonderful soft soil.

    Thanks for sharing another update from your garden, Connie! And I have to know: What variety of watermelon did your husband grow? It’s huge and oblong! I hope it was delicious. Looking forward to the next update! 🙂.

    #147538. Backyard Birds Love This Forgotten Winter Food Recipe – Here's How to Make Marvel Meal

    Backyard Birds Love This Forgotten Winter Food Recipe – Here's How to Make Marvel Meal

    📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (967 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, go down the bird food aisle this time of year and the choices just keep going, from seed blends to suet cakes in a dozen flavors.
    • In a recent development, that recipe is Marvel Meal, and if you're feeding birds on a budget, it's hard to beat.
    • Industry observers note that chickadees, titmice, and wrens come for the soft dough – and so do bluebirds, which don't always bother with a seed feeder.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, go down the bird food aisle this time of year and the choices just keep going, from seed blends to suet cakes in a dozen flavors. Some people walk right past all of it. They make their own at home, and one old recipe reveals up in their kitchens again and again.

    In a recent development, that recipe is Marvel Meal, and if you're feeding birds on a budget, it's hard to beat. The whole batch is peanut butter, vegetable shortening, cornmeal, and flour. Odds are you've got all four in the cupboard right now.

    Industry observers note that chickadees, titmice, and wrens come for the soft dough – and so do bluebirds, which don't always bother with a seed feeder. It's cheap, it keeps in the freezer, and kids can help mix it. And if you love helping birds in your backyard, then enter our competition to win a Birdfy smart feeder.

    In a recent development, its exact origin is hard to pin down, but bluebird fans have been passing the recipe around for years, and Penn State Extension still shares it today. There's nothing to cook and no beef fat to render, which some suet recipes call for. You also won't find a ring of spilled seed under the feeder the way you do with a seed mix.

    Insect eaters get the most out of it. Bluebirds rarely eat seeds, and woodpeckers, nuthatches, and wrens lean on insects for much of the year. Come winter, bugs get hard to find. A rich, fatty food fills that gap with the calories birds need to stay warm through long nights, at a time when natural food can be scarce.

    Beat the peanut butter and shortening together in a substantial bowl until it's smooth. Then work in the cornmeal and flour a cup or so at a time, and stir the seeds in last. You're after a soft dough that holds its shape when you squeeze a lump of it. If kids are helping, check for peanut allergies before anyone digs in.

    Marvel Meal doesn't need to go in the fridge first. Soft is good, since that's what lets you press it into a feeder. If you'd rather have firm blocks for a suet feeder, spread the dough in a pan lined with wax paper, freeze it, and cut it into pieces.

    Log feeders, like this Pennington red cedar suet feeder from Walmart, are the old standby. Press the dough into the drilled holes. You can also just smear some on rough bark or a pinecone, or fill half a coconut shell.

    Place frozen blocks of Marvel Meal in a basic suet cage, like this Kingsyard all-metal double suet bird feeder with perch. The cage keeps squirrels and bigger birds from making off with the whole chunk. But never use a mesh onion bag – birds can get their feet tangled and stuck.

    For bluebirds, roll the dough into small balls and set them in an open dish with some cover over it. Audubon's Woodlink dome-top seed and bluebird feeder, available at Home Depot, has a roof right above the dish. Wet weather turns the dough to mush, and a clear plastic squirrel baffle hung over a hanging feeder helps keep the rain off. Don't put out more than the birds will clean up in a day or two.

    Penn State lists chickadees, titmice, wrens, and bluebirds as fans. Woodpeckers, nuthatches, blue jays, and even cardinals stop by too, though European starlings can turn into pests.

    It has been revealed that bluebirds are the hard ones. They don't go to feeders the way chickadees do, and a lot of them have to learn that a dish means food. Who shows up in your yard depends on what lives around you and how you set out the food. Try a couple of spots and give it a few days. Hang feeders near trees or shrubs so small birds have somewhere to dart, just not so close that a hawk can sit hidden in them.

    Industry observers note that marvel Meal is a winter treat, not a year-round meal. Start putting it out when the nights get cold in late fall and natural food is getting scarce. Birds don't need a steady diet of rich food, and heat brings its own problems. When highs climb to about 65°F to 70°F (18–21°C), the fat goes soft and can go rancid – and greasy food can mat feathers and even get onto eggs in a nest. Once spring stays warm, take it down.

    Recent findings suggest that leftover dough keeps in sealed bags in the fridge, and the extra can go in the freezer. Keep seed somewhere cool and dry as well. The Gamma2 Vittles Vault from Walmart holds up to 35 pounds (16kg). Toss anything that's moldy, wet, or smells rancid. About every two weeks, scrub feeders in a mix of 1 part bleach to 9 parts water, and do it more often when it's wet or the feeders are busy. Rinse them well and let them dry before you fill them again.

    Fill a log with Marvel Meal on a frosty morning, and a chickadee will probably find it before your coffee gets cold. Keep the batches small and the feeders clean, and they'll stick around all winter.

    • Sources indicate that turkey is safe and healthy for dogs, with a few conditions.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that dogster is reader-supported. When you buy via links on our site, we may earn a commission at no cost to you. Read about privacy.

    It has been revealed that letâs face it: despite its somewhat complicated and controversial history, these days,Thanksgiving is built around food, which makes it one of the trickiest holidays for dogs that want to join you around the table, since many common dishes contain ingredients that are toxic to them. Some foods are fine to share in small amounts, while others can cause anything from an upset stomach to life-threatening illness. Knowing which is which makes it easy to include a dog in the day without risking an emergency.

    Sources indicate that turkey is safe and healthy for dogs, with a few conditions. The skin is fatty and usually coated in bastings and spices, and too much fat can lead to obesity and pancreatitis. Turkey bones can splinter and damage a dogâs mouth and digestive tract, so they should be avoided. Seasonings, including salt, can cause toxicity, so processed turkey should be skipped too. Plain meat is the safe choice, with no sauces or gravy.

    It has been revealed that plain pumpkin is considered healthy, which is why so many dog foods contain it. Canned or fresh both work, provided the canned kind isnât pre-seasoned and nothing has been added. Pumpkin pie, with its spices and sugar, is a definite no.

    Recent findings suggest that sweet potatoes are full of nutrients and vitamins, but they should be cooked and served in small amounts, without marshmallows, seasoning, or butter. Green beans offer vitamins, fiber, and manganese. They can be steamed, raw, canned, or cooked, as long as they are plain and not part of a casserole.

    According to recent reports, corn is healthy without butter or salt, but only if it's been taken off the cob. Corn cobs are a relatively common source of intestinal blockage in dogs. Carrots, celery, and peas are fine cooked or raw and unseasoned, and carrots and celery should be cut into bite-sized pieces to prevent choking.

    It has been revealed that plain cranberries are safe in moderation, though cranberry sauce and juice contain too much sugar. If they come from a dried fruit pack, only the cranberries should go to the dog. Apple slices are healthy and tasty, but the core and seeds should go in the trash. The seeds contain small amounts of cyanide that wonât harm a dog unless it eats too many, but itâs best to be cautious. The pie is for the people.

    Recent findings suggest that cheese makes a tasty treat unless a dog is lactose intolerant, and low-fat versions suit dogs watching their weight. A small piece of plain bread is safe unless the dog has a grain allergy. It should have no raisins, seeds, or nuts, and since bread offers few nutritional benefits, it should only be an occasional snack.

    Onions are highly toxic to dogs, along with everything in the onion family, including shallots, chives, and leeks, as they can cause anemia and liver damage. Garlic should also be avoided, and garlic powder is especially potent. It can also cause anemia, among other problems, so it shouldnât be anywhere near your pet.

    Stuffing is also off limits. It usually contains onion, and it often carries a large amount of butter, which makes it too fatty for a dogâs diet. Mashed potatoes are fine if completely plain, but most are made with plenty of salt, butter, and other ingredients that arenât good for dogs, so itâs best to skip them. Gravy is a problem because of its high sodium, and it usually contains onions or garlic.

    Chocolate is toxic because of two chemicals, theobromine and caffeine. It can lead to death if left untreated, and the signs can appear relatively swiftly. Caffeinated drinks are risky for the same reason. Dogs are smaller and lighter than people, so it doesnât take much caffeine to cause trouble, and that rules out coffee, tea, and soft drinks.

    Yeast-based bread dough is dangerous even though small amounts of baked bread are fine. The yeast expands in a dogâs stomach and can lead to bloat, which can progress to a life-threatening condition called gastric dilatation-volvulus. Alcohol of any kind causes poisoning in dogs, whether itâs a drink, rubbing alcohol, or hand sanitizer.

    A final but deadly ingredient to be aware of is the artificial sweetener, xylitol. Sometimes listed as birch sugar, even in small amounts, this seemingly minor ingredient causes severe hypoglycemia, and even if dogs survive this, irreversible liver damage can finish them off. Always keep an eye out for this one, commonly included in sugar-free mints, gums, candy, and peanut butter, to name a few.

    A dog caught eating something toxic needs to go straight to a vet or the nearest emergency animal clinic. Bringing the packaging, along with a sample of whatever the dog ingested, helps the vet treat that particular substance. When itâs unclear whether something was toxic, the ASPCA Animal Poison Control at (888) 426-4435 and the Pet Poison Helpline at (855) 764-7661 can help. Both charge a fee, but they can guide the next steps and get a pet immediate help.

    When it comes to ingested toxic ingredients, timing is everything. If you know your dog has eaten something potentially dangerous, or even if you just suspect it, donât wait for clinical signs to appear. By then, it may already be too late. Far better to pay for an overcautious detox than risk the life of a four-legged family member.

    Thanksgiving can be enjoyable for the whole family, dogs included, as long as ingredients and leftovers arenât left out for a dog to gobble down. Be familiar with ingredients that are harmful to pets, particularly anything toxic. A little care with what gets shared keeps the day safe and lets everyone relax.

    #147536. How to Winterize Your Lawn Mower – 6 Easy Steps to Keep It Running Smoothly Next Spring

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1433 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    How to Winterize Your Lawn Mower – 6 Easy Steps to Keep It Running Smoothly Next Spring

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1433 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Ah, the last lawn-cutting Saturday comes and goes, so it’s the happy end of mowing for the entire calendar year.
    • Sources indicate that you can’t just put that mower to bed for a long winter’s nap without first doing some lawn mower maintenance.
    • I'm here to walk you through the steps to prepare your lawn mower for its winter rest.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Ah, the last lawn-cutting Saturday comes and goes, so it’s the happy end of mowing for the entire calendar year. All you want to do is push that lawn mower into the shed and close and lock the door. But you can’t, and you’ll regret it if you do. Come the following spring, you’ll pull out a mower that is sluggish, with stale fuel, clogged carburetors, and broken parts. It’s entirely possible that that lawn mower won’t start in spring at all.

    Sources indicate that you can’t just put that mower to bed for a long winter’s nap without first doing some lawn mower maintenance. It’s not as nice as tucking that mower away and drinking a cool beer, but it’s not all that difficult either. Once you learn how to winterize a lawn mower, you’ll find that it’s easier to jump in and do the work before you move your machine into winter storage.

    I'm here to walk you through the steps to prepare your lawn mower for its winter rest. Just follow this practical step-by-step approach. It won't take long if you tackle it alongside your other garden winterizing chores.

    It has been revealed that it only takes a month for the gasoline in a gas-powered motor to start to break down. When it does, it leaves gummy deposits in the carburetor. This doesn’t do anything good for the mower. You can tackle this in either of two ways.

    Industry observers note that first, and some would argue best, is to add a lawn mower fuel stabilizer to the remaining fresh gasoline in the tank. Sta-Bil, available on Amazon, is a good choice, but Sea Foam and Ethanol Shield are other popular options. But check your mower manufacturer's recommendations, as some don't advise this step.

    To use a fuel stabilizer, first check the product instructions for the correct amount to add based on the gasoline volume. Add the stabilizer to the tank, then top up with fresh gasoline, leaving a little room for expansion. Run the engine for around 5-10 minutes, or as directed on the product label, to allow the treated fuel to circulate through the fuel system. This helps prevent gasoline from deteriorating during winter storage, reducing the risk of deposits forming in the carburetor and causing starting problems in spring.

    Recent findings suggest that the second option to winterize a gas mower is to empty the tank so that there is no gasoline to break down. You can do this easily by running the mower until it is totally out of gas. You can also empty the tank by draining the tank and carburetor bowl manually.

    It has been revealed that before you start, switch off the engine, let it cool completely, and disconnect the spark plug wire for safety. If you need to tip the mower to access the underside, tilt it with the air filter and carburetor facing upward, as tipping it the wrong way can allow oil or fuel to leak into the air filter or engine intake.

    Next, clean the underside of the mower, scraping away grass clippings and dirt with a plastic scraper or stiff nylon brush. Leaving damp debris in place over winter can cause corrosion on steel mower decks.

    Once the underside is clean and completely dry, apply a protective coating. Mo-Deck Non-Stick Mower Deck Spray helps prevent grass clippings and debris from sticking to the deck, making cleanup easier when mowing season returns. Follow the product instructions and allow it to dry before storing the mower.

    In a recent development, draining the oil is not fun, but it’s not that difficult either. First, check your mower's manual, as some newer engines only require oil top-ups rather than regular changes. If yours needs an oil change, run the mower for a few minutes to warm the oil, then switch off the engine, let it cool enough to work safely, and disconnect the spark plug wire before proceeding.

    Drain the old, dirty oil into a suitable container, following your mower's instructions. A Briggs & Stratton oil extractor kit makes the job much less messy, allowing you to remove oil through the fill tube without tipping the mower.

    Recent findings suggest that does your mower have an oil filter? If so, change it now, using a replacement designed for your engine. Then refill with the correct amount of fresh motor oil. This will depend on your model, but common options include SAE 30 and synthetic 5W-30. Check the oil level with the dipstick to avoid overfilling, and take the used oil to a recycling facility.

    In a recent development, your lawn mower blade needs to be sharp and free of cracks. With the engine off and the spark plug wire disconnected, follow your mower's instructions to safely access and remove the blade. Wear thick gloves and check carefully for nicks, cracks, bends, or dull edges.

    According to recent reports, you can sharpen a dull blade with a hand file, but it's easier to use a proper lawn mower blade sharpener, like this Sporgain lawn mower blade sharpener and balancer from Amazon. However, if your lawn mower blade is cracked or badly damaged, it's better to replace it.

    Recent findings suggest that if you sharpen the blade yourself, follow the manufacturer's recommended angle and make sure it's properly balanced before reinstalling it. An unbalanced blade can cause excessive vibration and damage the mower.

    At the same time, inspect the spark plug for wear, corrosion, or heavy carbon buildup. Remove it using a spark plug socket (this Milwaukee set from Home Depot has three sizes), and if the plug is damaged, badly worn, or heavily coated, it's best to replace it with a newly introduced one recommended for your mower. Otherwise, gently clean away any light buildup with a soft brush before putting it back. Check your mower's manual for any specific instructions.

    The great thing about winterizing a battery-operated mower is that you don’t have to worry about gasoline issues. On the other hand, you do have to worry about looking after the battery. This is also key if your gasoline-powered mower has an electric starter.

    In a recent development, proper winter storage is essential. If the battery is removable, take it out of the mower and store it in a cool, dry place indoors, away from freezing temperatures and extreme heat. Check your manufacturer's recommendations for the ideal storage temperature, as requirements vary between batteries.

    For lithium-ion batteries, most manufacturers recommend storing them partially charged, rather than fully charged or empty. Check the charge periodically throughout winter and top it up if needed.

    In a recent development, however, if your mower uses a lead-acid battery, you generally need to keep it fully charged during storage. A compatible battery maintainer can help prevent them from going flat. The Noco Genius1 Smart Battery Charger and Maintainer maintains the battery's charge throughout winter so it's ready to go when mowing season returns. Do make sure any charger or maintainer you use is suitable for your battery type.

    In a recent development, move your mower into a dry shed, garage, or other sheltered space where it will be protected from rain, snow, and ice. Ideally, keep it on a clean, dry surface, as sitting on damp ground over winter can cause rust and corrosion.

    A breathable, water-resistant lawn mower cover, like this Himal Outdoors Push Lawn Mower Cover from Amazon, is a good idea because it helps keep dust, dirt, and moisture off the mower when it's not in use. Make sure the mower is completely cool and dry before covering it.

    It has been revealed that avoid storing your mower near corrosive household chemicals, fertilizers, or pool chlorine, as their fumes or spills can damage metal components over time. If you're storing it in a garage or shed, leave enough space around the machine for ventilation and easy access.

    Teo Spengler is a master gardener and a docent at the San Francisco Botanical Garden, where she hosts public tours. She has studied horticulture and written about nature, trees, plants and gardening for more than two decades. Before turning her focus to gardening, she worked as an attorney and legal writer, experience she also brings to her role as our Gardening Lawyer. Her extended family includes some 30 houseplants and hundreds of outdoor plants, including 250 trees, which are her main passion. Spengler at the moment splits her life between San Francisco and the French Basque Country, though she was raised in Alaska, giving her experience of gardening in a range of climates.

    Hi GPOD! Longtime contributor Kielian is back today with another beautiful look at her garden in Hamilton, Montana. We’ve followed this garden through the seasons for years, and GPOD readers may even remember Kielian’s first autumn tour from more than a decade ago. Today she’s sharing what fall looks like on the ranch nearly 17 years into the garden’s evolution.

    In the Bitterroot Valley of Montana, fall imparts her special light and changing colors to the ranch. The gardens are closing in on 17 years of beauty and, interestingly, have decided which design they like the most… on their own.

    In a recent development, my detailed blueprints and drawings of plantings have been changed by Mother Nature, who knows so much more than I do about proper placement. Birds deposit valuable seeds in areas I would never have approved of, and the failure of certain plants to survive makes room for those that forge ahead with gusto. Ahh, autumn, how delightful are your colors and resilience.

    Late October in Montana: The ‘Pee Wee’ oakleaf hydrangeas (Hydrangea quercifolia ‘Pee Wee’, Zones 5–9) are showing off, and the ornamental pear tree was not going to be outdone.

    The front garden early in the morning: Shadows enhance the color changes.

    Sources indicate that the back deck was sprinkled with maple-tree graffiti. The linden tree boasted brilliant yellow, and a gorgeous crabapple by the pump house screamed for attention with bright red leaves.

    A smokebush (Cotinus coggygria, Zones 4–8) and aspen tree drip with early morning rain.

    A golden sunset scattered early October rays on quaking aspens (Populus tremuloides, Zones 1–6), enhanced by the Bitterroot Mountains as a backdrop.

    Tessa came running along the path through early November changing leaves.

    An ornamental pear tree with fading black-eyed Susans in front. Winter is on her way.

    In a recent development, thanks for sharing another season in your garden with us, Kielian! After seeing this garden in spring, summer, fall, and even covered in snow over the years, it’s hard to pick a favorite season. But that golden sunset over the pond with the Bitterroot Mountains in the distance certainly makes a strong case for fall!

    #147534. Miley Cyrus' Wedding Flowers Are a Rose Lover's Dream – Now's the Time to Recreate the Look in Your Garden

    Miley Cyrus' Wedding Flowers Are a Rose Lover's Dream – Now's the Time to Recreate the Look in Your Garden

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, if there's one thing Miley Cyrus knows how to do, it's make a statement.
    • The couple's romantic ceremony featured masses of beautiful white roses, with a breathtaking floral arch creating a dreamy backdrop for the celebrations.
    • Industry observers note that so, while Miley might have had a team of florists to bring her wedding vision to life, you can take a slightly more long-term approach.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, if there's one thing Miley Cyrus knows how to do, it's make a statement. And her recent wedding to musician Maxx Morando has given us plenty of inspiration – particularly when it comes to the flowers.

    The couple's romantic ceremony featured masses of beautiful white roses, with a breathtaking floral arch creating a dreamy backdrop for the celebrations. It's classic, understated and wonderfully romantic. And, honestly? We're already dreaming about recreating the look in our own backyards. The good news is that November is one of the best times to get started. Bare-root roses are coming into season, making this the perfect opportunity to plant your own romantic rose display – often for considerably less than you'd spend on established container-grown plants.

    Industry observers note that so, while Miley might have had a team of florists to bring her wedding vision to life, you can take a slightly more long-term approach. Plant now, give your roses time to establish over winter, and you could be enjoying your own beautiful floral display come spring and summer. After all, as Miley herself once reminded us, we can absolutely buy ourselves flowers. But growing them ourselves? Even better.

    There's something wonderfully timeless about an all-white flower display. While colorful planting schemes certainly have their place, sticking to one color can create a much more elegant look – and white roses, as Miley Cyrus' wedding photos have proven, are particularly lovely for this.

    A post shared by MILEY (@miley).

    Sources indicate that the beauty of this look is that you don't need hundreds of individual plants to make an impact. A well-positioned rose bush, a climbing variety trained over an arch or trellis, or even a small collection of white roses along a garden path can create a n atmosphere that's just as romantic.

    Better still? Well, there's no need to wait until spring to start planning your own rose garden, because November is actually the ideal time to get planting. Bare-root roses become available from late fall and are generally much more affordable than their container-grown counterparts, making them a brilliant option if you're hoping to plant several together.

    If you're looking for something that combines good looks with wildlife appeal, this shrub rose produces fragrant white blooms, followed by ornamental rose hips that provide additional seasonal interest.

    For something a little closer to the full-bodied blooms seen at Miley's wedding, this floribunda variety produces gorgeous double white blooms, sometimes with the faintest blush of pink.

    According to recent reports, of course, if it's the dramatic floral arch you're hoping to recreate, you'll want to consider a climbing rose. This pretty variety is ideal for training over arches, pergolas and trellises.

    In a recent development, the good news? You don't need an elaborate wedding installation to achieve that same Miley Cyrus-inspired look; you just need a sturdy garden arch like this pergola from Outsunny, and pop it somewhere that gets plenty of sunlight. (Most roses need at least six hours of direct sunlight each day).

    Next, plant a climbing rose on either side of your structure, allowing the canes to grow and training them horizontally and upwards as they develop. Be patient, though, as your rose arch won't become an overnight sensation, and it may take a couple of growing seasons to achieve the look you're craving.

    It has been revealed that and there you have it: a little celebrity-inspired garden magic without the celebrity price tag. Miley Cyrus' wedding might have lasted just one day, but with the right roses and a little patience, you can enjoy your own romantic floral display year after year. Talk about a love story worth growing, eh?

    Recent findings suggest that the owners of this 1940s house wanted to add more space for a growing family, but site restrictions would only allow them to build upward, meaning the small home would tower over surrounding houses. To preserve the house’s place in the neighborhood and keep costs down, the solution was to remodel the existing space with a more functional layout, transforming the second floor from two bedrooms and one bath into three bedrooms and two baths while making the home feel more spacious, flexible, and connected.

    Outside, the remodeled house maintains the same proportions of the original but incorporates modern updates such as the ACRE composite-wood entry accents and the single entry-door sidelight. To improve flow inside, the main staircase was relocated to create a more functional, open interior. Upcoming sliding glass doors offer more light inside and a seamless connection to the outdoors, maximizing the feeling of space. The basement stairs are now accessed via a hidden floor hatch, preserving the open main living area.

    Creating a more functional home within the same footprint means making the most of every inch of usable space. The area under the main staircase now houses deep storage drawers, and a upcoming window seat offers extra space next to the picture window.

    On the exterior, the window-seat bump-out lets the house live larger without increasing its footprint. Clad in the same wood as the front entry, the bump-out creates a cohesive and striking connection between the front and back of the house.

    #147532. Tech Report: Why Evergreen Shrubs Have Black or Brown Leaves in December – and When You Should Act Fast if You Spot This Leaf Damage

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1593 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Tech Report: Why Evergreen Shrubs Have Black or Brown Leaves in December – and When You Should Act Fast if You Spot This Leaf Damage

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1593 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that evergreen shrubs are workhorses in the garden, providing year-round green foliage, privacy hedging, and focal points in beds.
    • Sources indicate that the mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth.
    • Sources indicate that blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that evergreen shrubs are workhorses in the garden, providing year-round green foliage, privacy hedging, and focal points in beds. They're the backbone of a winter garden, which is why it's so disappointing to find brown or black leaf tips on a hebe, photinia, choisya, arborvitae or other evergreens after the first cold snap. And this year, evergreen shrubs with dead leaf tips are a problem many gardeners are facing as temperatures drop.

    Sources indicate that the mild fall in many areas this year allowed many shrubs to delay dormancy and even put out fresh growth. Without the time to build cold resistance before winter weather arrives, evergreen foliage is left vulnerable to leaf damage.

    Sources indicate that blackened or brown evergreen leaf tips don't necessarily mean your shrubs are dying, but they are cause for concern and a clear sign you need to prepare your garden for winter. Understanding what's caused the damage is notable so you know what to do next to save your beloved evergreen shrubs. So, great work getting here to Garden ER where you'll find straightforward solutions to treat this season’s biggest planty problems. Come on in and let’s diagnose and treat your evergreen shrubs with black or brown leaf tips in late fall or early winter.

    If your shrubs are experiencing damage related to our mild fall this year, you're likely to spot these symptoms:.

    In a recent development, if the damage is confined to a few leaf and needle tips, there's no need to worry: your shrub will recover, and it's a good idea to take steps to prevent further damage. If the damage is more significant, there's still a high chance of recovery but you should better protect plants from frost and have plenty of patience.

    Recent findings suggest that there are two primary and most likely causes of dark, dry tips on your evergreen shrubs. The distinction matters because the underlying cause determines how you help your shrub recover.

    Your shrubs naturally harden off for winter, a process triggered by less daylight and gradually dropping temperatures. They slow their growth and undergo some internal processes that allow them to better withstand freezing winter temperatures. To get more specific, soluble sugars begin to accumulate in the cells of leaves and needles. These sugars make it harder for water in the cells to freeze and allow the plant to better regulate water movement. As the youngest leaves go through this process, they become woodier, more mature, and more resistant to freezing injuries.

    During a mild fall, as many of us have experienced this year, some evergreens might continue producing fresh, soft growth instead of entering the dormancy period. This disrupts the vital process of winter hardening-off, leaving cells with high water content and underdeveloped protection. So, when temperatures finally drop, the water in cells freezes more readily. These frozen cells then rupture. Affected leaves, needles, and tips die as a result of the damage and turn brown or black.

    Industry observers note that some of the evergreens most susceptible to this type of damage include hebe, choisya, camellia, and photinia. Even plants that normally tolerate cold winters can be affected after an unusually warm fall.

    Industry observers note that desiccation or wind scorch, also known as winter burn, is another potential cause of black or brown evergreen foliage, and this can occur regardless of an unseasonable fall. Evergreen shrubs lose moisture through their leaves, even as growth slows, and cold air, winter winds and bright sun increase this moisture loss. Once the ground – and the moisture held in the soil – freezes, the shrubs’ roots can't take up water to replace what's being lost. This moisture imbalance can cause leaf and needle tissue to dry out and turn brown or black, and damage often begins at foliage tips and margins.

    Distinguishing leaf damage caused by winter desiccation from new foliage that's died in the first cold snap is easy: if wind scorch is the glitch, damage will be on the windy side of the shrub. You’ll also see that the outer leaves and needles are most affected, with the inner foliage protected. The damage from wind scorch is typically gradual rather than suddenly appearing after a frost or freeze, too.

    Sources indicate that evergreens with shallow roots like arborvitae, boxwood, rhododendron, yew, juniper and holly are particularly susceptible to winter desiccation. Any evergreen can be damaged this way, however, depending on moisture in the soil, wind levels and how protected the shrub is.

    First – and most importantly – of all, don’t rush to snip off those black tips. You can’t recover that dead tissue, and cutting it off now can cause more damage. If your shrubs are victims of the poor hardening-off that resulted from a mild fall, trimming could trigger more vulnerable growth, and also expose currently sheltered foliage to further harm. Similarly, the damage on a wind-scorched shrub will protect the foliage beneath.

    The next step depends on the cause of the leaf damage.

    It has been revealed that now you know your shrub isn’t ready for the cold, protect it from the rest of the winter weather to come. A zip-up plant jacket is an easy way to winterize shrubs that only need protecting ahead of a predicted cold snap rather than being wrapped up all winter. Another option is to wrap plants up in burlap – rolls of hessian are available from Walmart – or horticultural fleece such as this from Amazon, unwrapping plants after the cold weather has passed.

    When covering shrubs, be sure to do so loosely and use stakes inserted in the soil to hold fabric away from leaves. If your shrub is growing in a container, then wrapping the pot in bubble wrap and burlap protects roots during a prolonged freeze, too. Choose the level of protection based on your zone and how badly damaged your evergreen shrub is.

    Recent findings suggest that if those dead leaf tips are caused by a wind and moisture imbalance, first check the moisture in the soil around the plants. If you're using a moisture meter, make sure it's one with a long probe like this moisture meter on Amazon so you get a reading where it matters. If the soil is dry and the ground isn’t frozen, give the root zone a good soak.

    Next, apply a layer of mulch made from natural materials like Back to the Roots Organic Mulch, available from Amazon, around the base of each shrub. This will help conserve moisture and insulate the soil. Just be sure to keep the mulch a few inches away from the stems to prevent moisture accumulating there and causing rot or fungal disease.

    Now you need to protect your shrub from further damage from wind scorch. You could pop a frost jacket on your shrub whenever high winds are forecast, or use burlap to create a windbreak. You don’t necessarily need to cover the whole shrub; just provide a barrier from the prevailing winds. Keep checking shrubs throughout the winter, adding windbreaks and watering when the soil thaws as needed.

    Sources indicate that these steps will help prevent more damage, but they won’t reverse the damage that has already occurred. Now, you’re probably wondering when you can remove those unsightly dead leaf tips – and you're going to have to be patient. It’s important not to prune off dead leaves or branches now as this can trigger fresh growth, introduce damage or disease at the cut areas, and leave interior foliage vulnerable.

    Wait to prune until spring when there is no more risk of a severe frost, then use clean, sharp shears to remove dead tips. If larger areas have browned or blackened, cut these stems back to the first healthy, live bud. You can check if a branch might regrow by scraping back the outer layer with your fingernail. If it’s brown underneath, it’s dead and should be removed. If you see green, it could still sprout new growth.

    Keep your pruning light in spring. Trim back the damaged parts and then let healthy branches and leaves grow back in before you do any heavier pruning or shaping.

    The damage for this year is done and gone, but you can learn from the incident to save your evergreen shrubs from harm next year:.

    It has been revealed that dead leaf tips on evergreen shrubs are usually a cosmetic problem, not a death sentence for your favorite plants. Follow these guidelines and your shrubs should recover, ready to shine again next year.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Hey, garden gang! Longtime contributor Susan Warde is back today with a closer look at her garden in St. Paul, Minnesota. We’ve seen what the end of the season looks like in Susan’s garden before, but today she’s focusing on the smaller details that are easy to overlook this time of year.

    I understand the reasons for not cutting down perennials and for letting leaves lie untouched over the winter, but it takes me about 10 weeks to clean up. I have a large garden, family commitments, unpredictable weather, and a limited number of yard-waste bags that our pickup service will take at one time. Ten weeks in the spring would put me into mid-June before I could get the weeds and overwintered mess under control.

    So I’ve been cleaning up, and the garden has been looking pretty bare recently, positively grim on overcast days. But during the process I was struck by small vignettes of beauty that stood out in an otherwise desolate landscape.

    The underside of some Korean maple leaves (Acer pseudosieboldianum, Zones 4–8).

    A ‘Northern Hi-Lights’ azalea (Rhododendron ‘Northern Hi-Lights’, Zones 4–7) with bright fall color… and buds that promise spring.

    The seed head of ‘Guernsey Flute’ clematis (Clematis ‘Guernsey Flute’, Zones 4–9) that had a second late flowering.

    One last blossom on a ‘Max Frei’ bloody cranesbill (Geranium sanguineum ‘Max Frei’, Zones 3–8).

    Raindrops on columbine (Aquilegia cvs., Zones 3–8) leaves.

    The yellowed leaves of a bulblet fern (Cystopteris bulbifera, Zones 3–8) that I’d overlooked during the cutting-down process.

    A bee enjoys the very last plant in bloom, black cohosh (Actaea racemosa, Zones 3–8).

    Evergreen Christmas fern (Polystichum acrostichoides, Zones 3–8) and moss.

    I had never before looked closely at the bark of a blue beech (Carpinus caroliniana, Zones 3–9), which from a distance just looks taupe.

    Industry observers note that five minutes before taking the photo, I’d cleaned out this birdbath—the one I leave available in winter, and then only on above-freezing days. The leaves are from a ‘North Wind’ maple (Acer × pseudosieboldianum ‘IslNW’, Zones 4–7).

    Sources indicate that thanks for sharing these small moments from your garden, Susan! There are so many things to love about a garden, but I often find that the small details people tend to gloss over are even more reason to celebrate. There’s so much happening at once! You just have to look closely to see it. (:.

    #147529. Mini Greenhouse or Cold Frame? Discover Which is Better to Protect Your Plants From Winter Weather

    📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1567 w)
    📖 Baca
    General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Gardeningknowhow ↗ Open Full Page

    Mini Greenhouse or Cold Frame? Discover Which is Better to Protect Your Plants From Winter Weather

    📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1567 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Gardeningknowhow

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that when the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is.
    • A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover.
    • Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that when the forecast drops below freezing for the first time in late fall, half the neighborhood rushes out to tuck bedsheets over their mums – unless they have a greenhouse, that is. But while most folk don't have the space or the budget for a full-size glasshouse, a mini greenhouse or cold frame is the affordable option to get plants through winter unscathed. But which is best when it comes to protecting plants from winter weather?

    A mini greenhouse is a tall but narrow enclosure with wire-mesh shelves zipped inside a clear plastic cover. A cold frame is a low, bottomless box with a see-through lid that sits right on the dirt. Both catch sun all day, but they handle the night very differently, making the best one for you dependant on what you grow. And a Georgia winter is a very different beast from a Minnesota one, which affects how you winterize your garden in late fall.

    Here's everything you need to know to make the right decision to protect your plants from frost and snow this winter.

    Recent findings suggest that most mini greenhouses are made from a light steel frame with two to four tiers of wire-mesh shelves. This is covered with a PVC or polyethylene cover that zips up the front, or some designs have rigid polycarbonate panels, which is why they're often referred to as 'plastic greenhouses'. To vent, you unzip and roll up the door.

    Mini greenhouses are cheap and give you a lot of growing space for a small footprint, but the plastic cover can wear out and be hard to replace, and not all products stand up to winter winds unless they're positioned in a sheltered spot. If you only use a mini greenhouse in winter, it's easy to pack up and store away for summer, or if you can remove the shelves then they're useful for growing tomatoes.

    Cold frames are typically made from wood, aluminum or brick with a hinged glass or polycarbonate lid that can be propped open on warm days. Only holding one layer of pots, a cold frame and will only fit fairly low-growing plants. They generally cost more, unless you put your DIY skills to the test and build your own cold frame, but a sturdy design with a rigid lid lasts for years. A cold frame doesn't buy you any extra growing room, however.

    Plants will usually come through a harsh 20°F (-7°C) night better in a cold frame than a mini greenhouse. Because the frame has an open base and sits directly on the ground, it benefits more from the heat of the sun. Soil soaks up the solar heat all day, which is why it's a good idea to prop the lid open a few inches on sunny days if temperatures rise above 40°F (4°C). But close the lid by late afternoon and the interior stays warm as the soil gives the heat back overnight, and the frame's solid sides slow the loss. For extra warmth, it's an easy task to bank straw or soil against the walls. too.

    So, vegetables such as lettuce, spinach, kale and other winter greens will keep growing slowly under a cold frame lid into early winter. Low perennials and young transplants often do well too, and so do plants that rot when winter rain sits on their crowns.

    Space is where a mini greenhouse wins over a cold frame. With several tiers of shelves, you can stack seedling trays, rooted cuttings and pots of hardy herbs in a space about the size of a doormat. However, a mini greenhouse sitting on paving has no soil to draw from, so it doesn't stay as warm overnight. While the interior still heats up in the day (so needs venting), thin plastic sides allow the warmth to quickly escape, so it doesn't take long for the air inside to drop to the same temperature as the air outside. A tall mini greenhouse catches every gust of wind, too, and cold air finds any gaps around zippers and seams.

    If you have a sheltered sunny wall to stand a mini greenhouse against, however, that structure will absorb the sun's heat during the day and give it back through the night, helping to stabilize temperatures. Still, don't trust thin plastic in a hard freeze – but a mini greenhouse does a great job at keeping wind and rain off hardy container plants.

    A mini greenhouse gives you extra growing space on a balcony or in a small urban garden, too.

    When buying a cold frame, it's good to know that wood insulates better than metal if you live in a harsh climate. It's heavier, though, so if you want to be able to move your cold frame, then an aluminum frame also has the advantage it won't rot. Either way, look for a sturdy frame that doesn't wobble and a lid that props open at more than one height. Automatic venting is a useful upgrade if you're not at home during the day, as a temperature-activated hinge lifts the lid as the inside warms up.

    Cedar wood frame, 3.5mm polycarbonate insulation and fully opening lid with venting positions.

    Aluminum frame, 4mm polycarbonate panels and a collapsible design for easy summer storage.

    Cedar and powder-coated steel, double-wall polycarbonate lid and temperature-activated automatic lid opening.

    Sources indicate that when buying a mini greenhouse, there's a balance to be had between budget and cover quality. A mini greenhouse with polycarbonate panels is more expensive but holds heat far better than a floppy plastic cover. If you opt for a cheaper flexible cover then look for one made of PE (polyethylene), preferably reinforced PE, rather than PVC.

    PE stays flexible in freezing temperature and copes with long-term UV exposure well. PE that's reinforced with mesh also means any rips are easily fixed, and still lets in around 85% of sunlight. PVC (polyvinyl chloride) is usually clearer so lets more light through, but tends to split and yellow over time.

    According to recent reports, look for a stiff, robust frame because a wobbly one means the cover flaps until the seams gape. It's vital that you can anchor the mini greenhouse down, too, and that the method used is suitable for the ground you plant to stand it on. Most designs will have base flaps that you can weigh down with bricks or stones, while some offer additional anchoring with ground stakes – useful if your garden is at all exposed.

    In a recent development, double-layer roof design for ventilation, UV-resistant PE cover and zip-up door. Measures 50" H x 27.6" W x 19.7" D.

    In a recent development, reinforced PE cover, mesh racks and 4 ropes and ground stakes. Measures 76.8" H x 57.9" W x 30.3" D.

    4mm polycarbonate panels, roof vent, sliding door and rain gutter. Measures 71.65" H x 75.98" W x 27.16" D.

    Industry observers note that it's a simple task to upgrade a cold frame or mini greenhouse when winterizing your garden, and the cheap fixes go a long way. You could save bubble wrap to repurpose in the garden, clipping a layer inside the cover for an extra layer of trapped air. Always pick major bubbles since they generally insulate better, like this 24-inch-wide roll of large-bubble clear wrap from Amazon. Bubble wrap does cut some light, however, and packing-grade wrap breaks down in the sun faster than horticultural film.

    On a bitter night, spreading frost cloth like this from Amazon over the plants inside also helps to insulate them, and it's easily pulled off in the morning.

    Recent findings suggest that A tall mini greenhouse can tip in strong wind, and even if anchoring stakes are included, they're usually flimsy. A shed anchor kit like this from Amazon with 18-inch ground screws and steel cable will do a much better job of holding your mini greenhouse down through winter weather.

    If you mostly grow winter greens and low perennials, buy the cold frame since the open soil base and solid sides will give plants steadier nights. If you need plenty of space for seedlings, cuttings or taller pots, go with a mini greenhouse and expect bigger temperature swings.

    Whichever you pick, park it in a sunny spot out of the wind, and hang a cheap digital max/min thermometer like this from Amazon in there so you know just what degree of winter protection your plants are getting. Neither a cold frame nor a mini greenhouse will protect frost-tender plants in severe cold weather without extra insulation or a safe heat source, so bring them inside before a hard freeze. And if you do add heat, do it carefully – a soil-heating cable on a GFCI outlet turns a cold frame into a hotbed, but keep heaters away from plastic and never run a fuel-burning heater in a small closed structure.

With a microbiology background focused on fungi, he’s spent over a decade solving tough and intricate gardening problems. After spinal injuries and brain surgery, Tyler’s approach to gardening changed. It became less about the hobby and more about recovery and adapting to physical limits. His growing success shows that disability doesn’t have to stop you from your goals.

    How to Make Homemade Window Cleaner

    📅 28 Feb 2021 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1657 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • It has been revealed that dirty windows or a streaky glass door are easy to notice and are easy to clean.
    • Save some dollars and keep things simple by mixing up your own DIY window cleaner with nothing more than a few pantry staples you likely have on hand.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    It has been revealed that dirty windows or a streaky glass door are easy to notice and are easy to clean. Yet, cleaning windows and doors always seems like a chore we put off—even though it requires minimal work. No more excuses! You don’t need any fancy cleaners or tools when you can make this DIY glass cleaner recipe for free from supplies in your house.

    Save some dollars and keep things simple by mixing up your own DIY window cleaner with nothing more than a few pantry staples you likely have on hand. The following homemade window cleaner is a solution of ingredients that you can actually pronounce, like vinegar and water, and can whip up quickly and leave under your sink for the next time it’s needed. Here’s the recipe for success:.

    Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

    According to recent reports, before learning how to clean windows with vinegar, you’ll first want to gather the materials for this DIY glass cleaner. You’ll need distilled white vinegar (or lemon juice) and dish soap—a fragrant essential oil is nice to add, but not necessary.

    In a recent development, in this recipe, as with so many other nontoxic homemade cleaners, white vinegar plays a key role. Its acidity cuts through dirt and grease, an attribute that well equips the window cleaner to remove stuck-on debris and streaks.

    If you’ve washed your windows for years with a commercial cleaner such as Formula 409 or even Windex, it’s likely that the glass sports a subtle, waxy film. That residue comes off easily with ordinary dish detergent, another ingredient contributing to the efficacy of homemade window cleaner.

    In a spray bottle, combine ¼ cup of white vinegar with ½ teaspoon of liquid dish soap. Dilute the solution with 2 cups of water, then shake the bottle vigorously to mix the components. If you don’t have white vinegar on hand, you can substitute lemon juice. Like distilled white vinegar, lemon juice has a mild acidity that cuts through grease and grime with equal panache.

    As a cleaning agent, there’s much to love about vinegar, but the strong odor isn’t everyone’s favorite thing. Fortunately, you can go a long way toward camouflaging the scent of your homemade glass cleaner by adding essential oil to the mixture in the spray bottle. Pick your favorite oil and add 10 to 15 drops.

    With your homemade window cleaner now ready, spray the window glass with it. Then, using a lint-free cloth such as a microfiber cloth or chamois, wipe the cleaner across the entire surface you’re cleaning. The cleaner will dry fairly promptly, leaving behind a streak-free shine. For best results, follow up with a window squeegee, like the highly rated Mr. Siga window cleaning squeegee and scrubber.

    This window-cleaning recipe works like a dream, but what do the individual components contribute to the mix? We’ll break it down for you.

    According to recent reports, the main reason distilled white vinegar makes such a good glass cleaner is because it contains acetic acid. The colorless organic compound gives white vinegar its pungent flavor and odor, and kills some bacteria. When you wash windows with vinegar, not only will you be able to break down and remove dirt, grease, and mineral deposits, you’ll also be able to kill germs on hard surfaces around the home.

    It is crucial to note, however, that vinegar-based cleaning solutions should not replace true sanitizing cleaners that remove 99.9 percent of disease-causing bacteria and viruses, the EPA standard for products labeled as sanitizers.

    Like white vinegar, the acid in lemon juice can effectively break down grime on windows and other glass surfaces. Citric acid in lemon juice is technically a bit stronger than vinegar’s acetic acid, though both are about equally effective when it comes to cleaning around the house.

    Industry observers note that several ingredients make up most liquid dish soaps on the market, but one ingredient in particular, sodium lauryl sulfate, gives dish soaps their impressive grease-busting abilities. The component bonds with oily particles and lifts them off of surfaces, which allows for easy removal when used with water.

    Recent findings suggest that the best homemade window cleaner leaves behind an appealing scent. Many essential oils contain natural chemical components that are both cleansing and pleasantly scented. Tea tree essential oil, for example, doesn’t just smell great—it has antibacterial, antiseptic, and antifungal properties. Mixing it into your homemade window cleaner can help prevent mold and mildew growth, too.

    This set of 6 Lagunamoon essential oils includes orange, lavender and other aromas perfect for scenting cleaning solutions.

    According to recent reports, as is the case when cleaning other parts of the home, water temperature makes a difference. Hot water has more kinetic energy than cold water, so it more easily agitates and lifts dirt particles off surfaces. While this may help with cleaning dishes and laundry to some extent, warm water isn’t essential for cleaning windows. Cold or tepid water will work, too.

    It has been revealed that A thorough window cleaning should be at the top of every homeowner’s seasonal cleaning to-do list. The start of spring when the weather warms is an opportune time to tackle this task both inside and outside your home. Before you start spritzing the glass, consider these useful window-cleaning tips:.

    Recent findings suggest that “Don’t forget to inspect your window hardware. If your finishes have dulled, you can apply a coat of beeswax to preserve and restore them. Also, it’s never a bad idea to take the time to put dry lubricant on the gears of your windows to keep all components functioning smoothly for seasons to come.”.

    —Michael Wandschneider, director of product management for Marvin.

    While you could use paper towels, a soft microfiber cloth works best for first removing dust and loose debris from windows. Use a separate clean microfiber cloth to work the homemade window cleaner along the glass surface and remove stubborn dirt and residue. Coffee filters are also handy for cleaning windows, as are squeegees. The latter are especially useful for deep-cleaning the outside of your windows, which you can DIY rather than paying for professional window cleaning.

    In a recent development, the stainless-steel Unger Pro squeegee doesn’t leave streaks when cleaning glass, and can be used with an extended-reach pole. See the review.

    Using natural ingredients is eco-friendly and safer for your skin and lungs compared to the chemicals found in many commercial cleaners, but there are still a few safety considerations to be aware of when making your own window cleaner. Natural ingredients such as white vinegar, lemon juice, and essential oils are effective in homemade glass cleaners, but they do not replace true sanitizers that are proven to kill 99.9 percent of disease-causing pathogens.

    Recent findings suggest that the most important thing to remember when making window cleaner (or any other homemade cleaning solutions) is never to mix vinegar with chlorine bleach. When sodium hypochlorite, the basic chemical compound in bleach, mixes with the acetic acid found in vinegar, it gives off toxic chlorine gas. Chlorine gas can burn skin, cause shortness of breath, and can even be fatal with long-term exposure.

    In a recent development, formulas for specialized commercial glass cleaners are often ammonia-based, and can leave streaks or foggy spots on some types glass. Car windows, for example, should not be cleaned with ammonia-based window cleaners because the residue poses a risk of obstructing the driver’s view. Natural glass cleaners that do not contain ammonia, such as the homemade window cleaner recipe above, don’t leave behind residue or streaks when wiped away using a clean microfiber cloth.

    Industry observers note that the best window cleaning solution is safe, natural, and effective. Following this recipe for a natural window cleaner can help you achieve all of these goals and leave you with clear, clean, and streak-free windows.     • Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.
    • Recent findings suggest that “This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” noted Assistant Attorney General A.
    • “Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” remarked U.S.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.

    Recent findings suggest that “This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” noted Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Cybercriminals who terrorize American businesses cannot evade justice by operating from abroad or hiding behind sophisticated technology. Artem Stryzhak’s sentence underscores the Justice Department’s resolve to dismantle ransomware groups, hold them accountable, and protect American businesses and people from cyber extortion.”.

    “Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” remarked U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”.

    “Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We are proud of our law enforcement partners for their skilled investigative work in bringing this criminal to justice.”.

    According to recent reports, “Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” said Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Branch. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners. Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”.

    Sources indicate that according to court documents, Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, Spain, conspired with others to perpetrate ransomware attacks on behalf of multiple ransomware groups against victim computer networks in the United States and other countries. The conspiracies caused significant damage to victim computer systems. Beginning in approximately June 2021, Stryzhak joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate. Stryzhak was given access to the Nefilim ransomware and agreed with one of the Nefilim ransomware group administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the Nefilim administrators, including Tymoshchuk, 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims in exchange for Stryzhak’s access to the Nefilim ransomware.

    According to recent reports, the ransomware attacks that Stryzhak conducted with Nefilim ransomware included a June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole data from a organization in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, Stryzhak created email addresses that were incorporated in a ransom note sent to the victim company. Stryzhak conspired with the Nefilim ransomware actors until at least October 2021. If a victim paid the ransom demand, the perpetrators provided the decryption key, enabling the victim to decrypt files locked by the ransomware.

    Sources indicate that also according to court documents, Stryzhak separately joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive conspirators attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals, and businesses. Hive ransomware attacks caused major disruptions in victim daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. In one case, a hospital attacked by the Hive ransomware group had to forgo digital technology to treat existing patients and was unable to accept upcoming patients immediately following the attack.

    In his role as a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators deployed Hive ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dentist office, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. Victims were unable to access their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long disruption campaign against the Hive ransomware group, provided a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, thereby allowing that victim to decrypt its encrypted data without having to pay a ransom.

    Sources indicate that stryzhak was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. Stryzhak pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

    The FBI Springfield Field Office investigated the Nefilim ransomware case and the FBI Tampa Field Office investigated the Hive ransomware case. The Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs, the FBI’s New York Field Office, and Spanish law enforcement authorities provided substantial assistance locating, arresting, and extraditing Stryzhak.

    Acting Assistant Deputy Chief James S. Yoon of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), former CCIPS Senior Trial Attorney Brian Z. Mund, and Assistant United States Attorneys Alexander F. Mindlin and Ellen H. Sise of the Eastern District of New York’s National Security and Cybercrime Section prosecuted the Nefilim ransomware case. CCIPS Trial Attorneys Alison M. Zitron and Christen M. Gallagher and Assistant United States Attorney Hannah Watson of the Middle District of Florida prosecuted the Hive ransomware case.

    Recent findings suggest that the U.S. Department of State’s Transnational Organized Crime (TOC) Rewards Program has offered a reward of up to $11 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction or location of Stryzhak’s charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. Anyone with information about Tymoshchuk should contact the FBI via phone at +1-917-242-1407, by email at TymoTips@fbi.gov, by contacting your local field office, if in the United States, or by contacting the nearest U.S. Embassy, if located overseas. More information about the Tymoshchuk TOC reward offer and one related to Hive ransomware is located on the State Department website.

    It has been revealed that CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 180 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $350 million in victim funds.

    Breaking: How to Wire an Outlet
