    • If the outlets in a room aren’t where you need them and you’ve got extension cords running amok, adding an outlet can eliminate those trip hazards and make everyday living a bit easier.
    • It has been revealed that however, if an outlet’s cover has melted, if the outlet has been smoking, or if there’s a burning smell, there’s likely a bigger issue than just the outlet.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    If the outlets in a room aren’t where you need them and you’ve got extension cords running amok, adding an outlet can eliminate those trip hazards and make everyday living a bit easier. Or maybe you need a latest outlet in a bathroom, laundry room, or doggy wash station in your mudroom, which means you’ll need to install a ground fault circuit interrupter (GFCI) outlet, required for any outlet within 6 feet of a water source. The good news is, wiring an outlet, whether standard or GFCI, is a project that you can do yourself, but you must take proper safety precautions.

    It has been revealed that however, if an outlet’s cover has melted, if the outlet has been smoking, or if there’s a burning smell, there’s likely a bigger issue than just the outlet. In these instances, it’s best to consult with a licensed electrician before you attempt to rewire it.

    Read through these steps for how to wire an outlet before you get started.

    Industry observers note that while a capable homeowner can wire an outlet, it’s not a job for a reluctant or unsure DIYer. Start by assessing your comfort level, and call in a pro if you have doubts.

    In many instances, you can wire an outlet from another outlet. In fact, if there’s an existing outlet in a room on the opposite side of the wall from where you’d like to add an outlet, the job can be pretty simple. In this situation, you can usually cut a latest opening, install an electrical box, and add a new outlet without having to snake wires through studs. Use a stud finder to locate the studs on either side of the existing outlet and make sure to situate the new outlet within the same stud bay.

    If you simply want more outlets in one location, it’s possible to replace an existing duplex outlet, which takes just two plugs, with a quad receptacle, which takes four. This can be helpful in a workshop or even in kitchens and bathrooms where two outlets just won’t cut it.

    In either case, it’s vital that there’s enough capacity on the circuit to accommodate the additional draw. For 15-amp circuits, the maximum is usually eight outlets or lights. Any more receptacles than that might draw too much current for the breaker.

    Old-fashioned two-prong outlet connections aren’t grounded, which makes them dangerous in the event of an electrical fault. Without an electrician, it’s safe to convert a two-prong to a three-prong outlet only if the electrical box housing the outlet is metal and the cable feeding the box is armored. If these conditions are met, the box provides ground-fault protection (even though the outlet does not).

    According to recent reports, how can you tell, without opening the wall, if the electrical box meets the criteria? Simple: Use a voltage tester. Insert one prong into the outlet’s shorter slot (the “hot slot”), then touch the other prong to the screw securing the faceplate. If the tester lights up, the electrical box is grounded, and you can go ahead and convert the two-prong to a three-prong. If your electrical box isn’t grounded, you can still convert to a three-prong, but the replacement must be a GFCI (the type of outlet with a red button on its front).

    Industry observers note that over time, electrical outlets can start to look dingy or dirty, or the plastic can crack and make the outlet dangerous to use. To keep power flowing where you need it, it’s important to learn how to replace an electrical outlet safely and efficiently.

    4-in-1 screwdriverVoltage testerOutlet.

    Before you go any further, it’s imperative that you cut power to the outlet you are replacing. At your home’s electrical panel, toggle off the switch associated with the circuit that sends electricity to the outlet in question.

    According to recent reports, after you shut off the power to the outlet, use a voltage tester to double-check that it’s really off. Insert the tester’s probes into the top two slots on the outlet. If the tester lights up, you toggled the wrong switch on the electrical panel and you’ll have to try again. Continue by trial and error until you are certain the outlet is no longer receiving electricity. (When you’re done, relabel the circuits in the panel so you know which is which.).

    Don’t have a voltage tester? You can use a lamp instead, so long as you know the lamp works. Plug the lamp into the outlet, and if it doesn’t turn on, it’s safe to proceed. This method is inherently riskier, so use it only as a last resort.

    After you confirm that the power is off to the outlet, stick a piece of black electrical tape across the breaker so no one can flip it back on while you are working.

    Sources indicate that the Fluke 1AC II has a flashing red  indicator to show that it’s working. A loud, audible beep sounds when it detects power. Read the review.

    Sources indicate that most faceplates have a single screw in the middle. Remove that screw, and the plate should come off easily. Next, unscrew the mounting screws that secure the outlet to the electrical box. Finally, gently pull the outlet away from the receptacle.

    You can now see three wires extending from the wall to the outlet. If the wires are attached to screws on the outlet, loosen those screws to free the wires. If the wires are snaked into holes in the back of the outlet, press the release slot and pull the wires out, assuming they don’t come out on their own. Put aside the old outlet.

    You’re now ready to wire in the replacement. First, connect the neutral wire (white) to the silver screw on the side of the outlet. Make sure to orient the hooked end of the wire so that its curve goes clockwise, the same direction in which you will tighten the screw.

    Connect the ground wire to the green screw, using the technique described above.

    Connect the hot wire (black) to the gold screw, the last one remaining on the outlet casing.

    Carefully maneuver the wires back into the electrical box, then screw the outlet to the box using the mounting screws at the top and bottom. Finally, position the faceplate over the outlet and screw it back on.

    Recent findings suggest that go back to the electrical panel and restore power to the outlet that you’ve finished replacing. Check the outlet installation by testing the device with a voltage tester or a lamp.

    Industry observers note that sometimes a simple replacement isn’t enough—you absolutely need another outlet. Maybe you want to accommodate a fresh appliance or entertainment device, or you’re setting up a workshop. You can frequently solve this problem by wiring a new outlet from an existing outlet on the other side of the wall from the desired location of the new outlet. This project is a bit more involved, but a safety-minded DIYer can take it on.

    Note: Be sure you’re using an “old work,” “rework,” or “remodeling” electrical box for the fresh outlet. These boxes have tabs that squeeze the box against the back of the drywall to hold it in place.

    4-in-1 screwdriverVoltage testerNeedle-nose pliersLineman pliersWire strippersDrywall sawElectrical cableOutletRemodeling box (also known as an old work box)Wire connectorsWire running kit (optional).

    According to recent reports, be sure to shut off the power to the existing outlet before doing anything else. Check the outlet for power with the voltage tester, and then go to the electrical panel to shut off the corresponding breaker.

    Head back to the outlet and use a voltage tester to ensure that the power is off. Once you confirm that the power is off, it’s a good idea to place a piece of black electrical tape across the breaker to prevent anyone from carelessly flipping it back on.

    Place the electrical box face-first against the drywall where you blueprint to install it. Trace along the box’s edges with a pencil, and then cut along the marks with a drywall saw. Sometimes it’s easier if you score the drywall with a utility knife first.

    Head back to the existing outlet. If it’s been some time since you shut the breaker, test the outlet again to make sure it’s still off. Next, remove the faceplate and remove the screws holding the outlet in the box. Carefully pull the outlet out and let it hang to one side, providing access to the back of the box.

    It has been revealed that push the fresh wire through an opening in the back of the box, feeding enough wire into the wall to reach the new outlet opening plus 1 foot. This can be challenging, so be patient and use pliers to pull the tab open if necessary. On this same side, cut the new wire approximately 10 inches from the box. Carefully strip back the plastic sheathing, leaving approximately 1 inch of sheathing in the box.

    Industry observers note that use the screwdriver to loosen the screws holding the existing wires onto the outlet and straighten the hooks with needle-nose pliers. Use wire strippers to remove approximately ⅝ inch of sheathing from the hot (black) wire and neutral (white) wire.

    It has been revealed that still working with the existing outlet, cut a 6- to 7-inch length from the spool of electrical cable. Remove the white, black, and ground wires from within the sheathing, and strip the ends back approximately ⅝ inch. This wire is called a pigtail.

    Use the lineman pliers to twist the ends of the existing wire, the new wire, and one end of the pigtail into a clockwise twist. Do this in three sets: all black wires, all white wires, and all ground wires. Cap each twist with a wire connector.

    Recent findings suggest that use the needle-nose pliers to bend the wires at the other end of the pigtail into a J-shape and hook them onto the outlet. White (neutral) goes to silver, black (hot) goes to gold, and ground goes to green. Be sure that the hooks are running clockwise before tightening the screws.

    It has been revealed that head to the other side of the wall to the space you’ve cut out for the new outlet. If the new wire isn’t easy to find, use a fishhook or tape from a wire running kit to fish it out from the wall. Pull the electric outlet wiring through the new opening, and feed the end into the new remodeling box.

    Fit the box into the opening and turn the screws attached to the tabs clockwise until the box is secure. You should have about 10 inches of new wire coming through the box. Strip the plastic sheathing back to expose the hot, neutral, and ground wires, leaving approximately 1 inch of sheathed cable inside the box.

    Industry observers note that use the wire stripper to strip the sheathing from the ends of the hot, neutral, and ground wires, exposing approximately ⅝ inch of bare wire. Use the needle-nose pliers to bend the ends of the wires into hooks, and slip them over the screws on the new outlet. Remember to follow typical receptacle wiring techniques: Connect the white wire to the silver screw, the black wire to the gold screw, and the bare copper wire to the ground screw. Finally, bend the wires so they will fold nicely as you attach the outlet to the box.

    In a recent development, tighten the screws at the top and bottom of the outlet until it is snug in the box. Put the faceplate on the outlet and tighten the screw. Flip the breaker back on and test the outlet.

    Recent findings suggest that learning how to wire an electrical outlet isn’t overwhelmingly difficult, and it’s a skill that some DIYers will use time and time again. With a little bit of background and proper safety techniques, adding an outlet for a TV or a newly introduced tool or appliance can be a breeze. Just remember to work safely, test and retest electrical outlets before you start, and follow the instructions above for a reliable and safe electrical outlet installation.

    According to recent reports, there are many types of electrical wires, and to explain them all would require an electrical engineering textbook. The most common residential wiring, including standard electrical outlet wiring colors, involves three types.

    Recent findings suggest that you absolutely can wire a light switch to an outlet, and there are several ways to do so. The switch can either be installed between the source of the power (typically the panel) and the outlet, or on a loop after the outlet.

    To install it in-line, simply run the wire through an electrical box, connect the hot wire to the switch so it can interrupt the flow of power, and then continue the hot wire out to the outlet and wire as normal.

    To install the light switch after the device, connect the neutral wire in the box as usual, then run a length of wire from the outlet to the switch. Connect one end of the wire to the existing hot wire in the box using wire connectors. Next, connect the black wire from this length to one side of the switch, and connect the white wire to the other side. Finally, head back to the outlet and connect the white wire to the gold screw and wrap black electrical tape around the wire to indicate that it is now the hot lead coming from a switch.

    The easiest way to fix an outlet that does not have a proper ground wire is to replace it with a GFCI outlet. These devices detect ground faults and interrupt the circuit right away. Install a GFCI in place of the first power outlet in the run to offer grounding protection.

    Of course, contact a local electrical inspector to ensure this meets local codes.

    #147523. National Security Division Unveils First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

    📅 27 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (777 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Fbi ↗ Open Full Page

    National Security Division Unveils First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

    📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fbi

    ⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • The Department of Justice declared today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.
    • The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.
    • According to recent reports, this agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    The Department of Justice declared today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc. The tech giant agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

    The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

    According to recent reports, this agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution. While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

    In a recent development, “This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” noted Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”.

    “HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”.

    The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

    Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

    Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

    Sources indicate that although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

    The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

    This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

    Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

    Now that working from home has become commonplace, many of us are trying to create quiet environments in which we can complete our work without being distracted by noises from the next room or an overhead apartment.

    Whether you’re part of the growing gig economy and looking to soundproof your home office, your teen has rock star dreams, or your 8-year-old has started tap-dancing, you’ll find that a little soundproofing can go a long way toward keeping the peace and quiet at home.

    According to recent reports, first, set reasonable expectations. Don’t expect an utterly silent room because you won’t get it. Room soundproofing techniques will reduce sound transfer from one room to another, but they won’t eliminate the loudest noises. Still, by employing the following methods, you can reduce distracting noise to a bearable level. These techniques can be used for any type of room—a home office, a nursery, or a family room, or to create a soundproof bedroom.

    Where possible, use the techniques in the adjacent rooms as well as the one you’re looking to soundproof. For example, if an attached garage that’s used as a workshop shares a common wall with the master bedroom, use soundproofing techniques on both the garage wall and the inside of the master bedroom wall for the best results. Learn how to soundproof a bedroom or other room to create a space where noises aren’t distracting.

    In a recent development, creating soundproof walls is most effective when done during construction, but there are several ways to put a damper on ambient and active noise after the fact to make a soundproof room. To minimize noise, consider the two strategies outlined here for how to soundproof a wall.

    Sources indicate that mass-loaded vinyl (MLV) is a sound-dampening product used everywhere from nightclubs and recording studios to hockey rinks, and it’s among the best soundproofing materials available. It comes on a roll and costs around $2 per square foot, depending on weight, length, and width. The thicker it is, the better it will be for blocking noise and ending echoes, but thickness, which can range from 1/16 inch to 1/4 inch, may not be listed in product specifications. It may instead be labeled by weight. Half-pound MLV weighs 1/2 pound per square foot of coverage and is 1/16 inch thick; 1-pound MLV is 1 pound per square foot of coverage and is 1/8 inch thick; 2-pound MLV is 1/4 inch thick.

    While MLV can be hung directly on a wall, it performs best when sandwiched between drywall sheets. Doing so also allows you aesthetic options since the usually black, shiny MLV isn’t the most decoratively appealing surface. Keep in mind that MLV, such as Soundsulate, is heavy and awkward to work with. Hanging it is a two-person job, so be sure to enlist a helper.

    Tape measureMass-loaded vinylHeavy-duty scissors or utility knifeStep ladderDrywall nailsHammerType X drywall (optional).

    Sources indicate that prior to ordering MLV, carefully measure the walls you want to soundproof. Leaving gaps in MLV will drastically compromise its effectiveness, so you’ll want to buy enough for complete coverage from wall to wall and floor to ceiling. When calculating your needs, note that MLV tends to be sold on rolls of 2-foot or 4-foot widths.

    According to recent reports, measure a length of MLV that will reach floor to ceiling and then cut out a sheet with the scissors or utility knife. Cutting on top of scrap wood would be wise to protect your floor or work surface.

    In a recent development, position the step ladder and put the MLV against the wall starting at either end, working to the other corner. To install it, snug it up against the ceiling, with your helper holding it in place. Using drywall nails and a hammer, attach the MLV to the upper portion of the wall at 12-inch intervals. Then attach the bottom portion at 12-inch intervals, and finally at 12- to 24-inch intervals down the sides of the sheet.

    Sources indicate that repeat Steps 2 and 3 as required until the entire wall is covered. For the best soundproof wall, butt the MLV right up against the preceding sheet so there are no gaps. You can overlap it for a potentially greater sound barrier, but you’ll have bumps and ridges if you do so. Overlapping is not recommended if you plan to paint, install wallpaper, or install additional drywall panels.

    Hang drywall on top of the MLV to make the soundproofing twice as effective and give you a surface for paint or other wall covering decor. Or read on for a quick solution to hiding the glossy black vinyl with curtains—a no-commitment decor project that will also enhance soundproofing. Sometimes called “soundproof drywall,” Type X drywall is 5/8 inch thick and fire rated, making it among the best options for noise dampening.

    Recent findings suggest that not for windows only, curtains can create drama on the walls of any room while offering considerable soundproofing benefits. They’re relatively inexpensive and as easy to remove as they are to install. While there are curtains specifically marketed as sound dampening or “acoustic,” blackout and thermal curtains, which are primarily sold to keep light out and warmth in, also provide noise reduction. Don’t let the term “blackout” fool you, though. These curtains come in many colors and styles—it’s the inner liner that provides the blackout/thermal effect. Even heavy fabrics like velvet provide some soundproofing.

    Keep in mind that when you double the weight of the fabric, its sound-reduction ability nearly triples. Yet more key than weight is curtain construction; pleated curtains can be three times as effective against noise as those that hang straight. The pleats double the fabric’s thickness in many areas and act as baffles, absorbing sound waves and stopping them in the fabric folds.

    It has been revealed that remember, sound dampening is the goal, so floor-to-ceiling curtains covering the entire wall will have the most impact. For the best results, hang multiple panels of soundproof curtains to fill the wall. Good options include the BGment Blackout Curtains and Nicetown’s 100% Blackout Curtains. If you’re feeling adventurous, mix colors and patterns for a funky feature wall!

    The Pony Dance Blackout Insulated Soundproof Curtains reduced sound by 10 decibels during our hands-on testing. See our full review.

    Tape measureSound-absorbing curtains (preferably floor-to-ceiling length)Bathroom scaleHanging system for curtains (rods, wires, or other systems rated for your curtain weight)ScrewdriverScrewsStud finder (optional)Weight-rated drywall anchors (optional)Iron or Steamer.

    Measure the walls before purchasing the curtains. When shopping, check package info for the curtains’ weight; you’ll need this to choose rods or another hanging system sturdy enough to hold them. If you’re set on curtains that don’t include the weight on the packaging, weigh them on your bathroom scale at home. Tip: Keep them in the package so they’ll sit easily on the scale.

    Purchase a hanging system weight-rated for the curtains (packaging or website marketing should tell you the weight load they can handle). If they weigh 40 pounds and the wall to be covered is 12 feet long, you’ll need a rod or hanging system that can handle roughly 3.5 pounds per foot, so keep that weight rating in mind when making your choice. Heavy-duty, ceiling-mount brackets, such as the KXLIFE brackets, will hold the heaviest curtains.

    Recent findings suggest that before mounting the hanging system, ensure enough space above it for the top of the curtains to move freely without bunching against the ceiling—a half-inch or inch should do. Locate wall studs with a stud finder, or use proper weight-rated wall anchors before boring into the wall with screws. Affix the rod or hanging system to the walls as recommended by the manufacturer.

    Sources indicate that iron or steam curtains to remove creases and wrinkles from the packaging. Check the label to see what temperature the manufacturer suggests and iron accordingly.

    Recent findings suggest that hang the curtains on the rod or wire system and then “bunch” them together in equal amounts across the entire wall for a consistent look. When soundproofing a room, keep in mind that pleated, bunched fabric will absorb more sound than flat fabric, so ample curtains are a plus.

    Recent findings suggest that soundproofing a room’s walls will go a long way toward reducing unwanted noise, but for an even quieter room, consider soundproofing other areas. Depending on the type of noise and where it’s coming from, you may also want to add noise-dampening materials to windows, doors, and other areas in the room.

    Recent findings suggest that windows let in fresh air and light, but if the window faces a busy urban street, the hustle and bustle of commuters, barking dogs, and emergency vehicles can make it seem as though they’re right in the room. To soundproof a room and mute noise transfer through windows, consider hanging one or more layers of thick curtains over windows, installing storm windows, or using a soundproof weather strip product, such as a draft stopper, to block noise. Soundproofing windows is a vital step in reducing unwanted noise.

    According to recent reports, interior doors often have a gap at the bottom that allows air (and noise) to enter a room. Soundproofing a door typically involves using a product that will seal the gap. To soundproof a bedroom door or home office door, try installing a door sweep, such as Suptikes’ Huge Gap door draft stopper.

    For renters who aren’t allowed to attach anything to a door, roll up a towel and use it to block the under-door gap to reduce noise transfer. Commercial products are also available, such as the Sunolga draft stopper, and they often come with loops on the ends to hang the item on a door knob when not in use.

    Trying to focus on work when the kids are playing in the room overhead is challenging at best, virtually impossible at worst. Reducing noise transfer through a ceiling can be accomplished by soundproofing the floor of the room that lies overhead. For those who live in an apartment and don’t have access to the room above, noise-dampening methods are limited.

    Homeowners can sandwich a layer of MLV between the existing ceiling drywall and then hang a second layer of drywall. Unlike the MLV method mentioned above to soundproof walls, the simplest way to install MLV overhead is to cut and attach it first to the latest drywall panels and then install the panels. Since MLV is heavy, a drywall lift will be necessary for raising the panels.

    It has been revealed that in a rented apartment, fewer good options are available. Still, renters can reduce ceiling sound transfer using ultra-lightweight foam boards, such as UCreate foamboard. Attach the boards to the ceiling with removable mounting putty, such as Gorilla Mounting Putty, that won’t harm the ceiling.

    In a recent development, soundproofing floors by reducing noise transfer from a room below is relatively easy by carpeting the floor or covering hard flooring with one or more large area rugs. When used in combination with the other soundproofing techniques, this may be enough to dampen most noises to a tolerable level.

    Homeowners may want to soundproof the ceiling of the room below (described previously) for additional noise reduction.

    Sources indicate that renters typically cannot structurally modify floors or ceilings, so if adding rugs isn’t sufficient, consider covering hard flooring with a layer of cork, such as Corksidol’s ½-inch-thick cork tiles, to help absorb sound. A large area rug can be added over the cork to protect it and offer a finished look.

    Water hammer is the product of hydraulic shock, and it can be loud enough to startle anyone who isn’t expecting it. Water hammer occurs when the water is shut off abruptly, and the water supply pipe reacts by jerking and bumping into other pipes or framing members in walls or floors.

    Sources indicate that if you have access to the offending pipes, slipping some foam pipe insulation around them, such as Foam King Brand foam pipe insulation, will usually stop the problem. Alternatively, a plumber can install a water hammer arrester, such as the Sioux Chief water hammer arrester, to keep the pipe from jerking when the water is turned off.

    In a recent development, hard objects, such as metal and solid wood tables and chairs, do not absorb sound so that noise can bounce around a room. Swapping hard chairs for upholstered chairs and overstuffed sofas will help dampen sound waves and keep them from echoing in the room.

    Industry observers note that additionally, following beneficial feng shui practices can also help block noise. Feng shui is a Chinese system of orienting rooms and adding features in a harmonious and pleasing manner. By adding a water feature, the trickling sound of the water will help distract from background noises, and placing live plants throughout the room will help absorb sound while freshening the air.

    It has been revealed that effective soundproofing involves using a combination of techniques to block sound transfer from outside a room while absorbing sounds inside the room. The best time to soundproof a home (or room) is during construction, when the walls and floors can be framed in a manner to reduce sound transfer, but unwanted noises can be significantly stifled in existing homes too.

    In general, products and materials that are dense and soft will absorb the most noise, including MLV, carpeting, cork, and curtains. Whether you own or rent your home, you don’t have to live with distracting sounds. Learning how to make a room soundproof goes a long way toward maintaining a comfortable living space.

    Recent findings suggest that real egg cartons are not used to block sound. Rather, egg carton-shaped foam, such as Jdejiela‘s egg crate panels, are used to line walls to dampen noise.

    The best sound-blocking materials are dense and soft, such as foam and carpeting.

    The most effective way is during fresh construction by utilizing staggered wall studs and joists to create a dead-air space that reduces sound transfer.

    Yes, but making a room completely soundproof involves specialized construction practices that create dead-air spaces in floors and walls. Sound reduction is what most are going for.

    Breaking: What to Do When Your Toilet Is Bubbling

    📅 22 Jan 2018 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1206 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bobvila

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • According to recent reports, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs.
    • While bubbling or gurgling is a relatively common toilet problem, it’s not an glitch you want to ignore.
    • Sources indicate that depending on the severity of the clog, you may be able to clear it yourself with a plunger or an eco-friendly Drano alternative.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    According to recent reports, we may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    While bubbling or gurgling is a relatively common toilet problem, it’s not an glitch you want to ignore. When a toilet bubbles, it indicates that negative air pressure (suction) is building up in the drain line, creating an airlock of sorts. Most likely this buildup of air is due to a clog.

    Sources indicate that depending on the severity of the clog, you may be able to clear it yourself with a plunger or an eco-friendly Drano alternative. Otherwise, you might have to call a plumber. Is a gurgling toilet dangerous? Not typically, but if the culprit is a broken or collapsed sewer line, it will have to be fixed, and the sooner the better. If the job is put off, waste could back up into toilets, showers, or tubs. The following guide will help you get to the root of toilet bubbling, and offer solutions to the problem.

    Clogs typically occur in one of two areas: somewhere in the drain system, which could be close to the toilet or farther down the main sewer line that connects to your community’s sewer system, or in your home’s vent stack (the pipe that allows sewer gasses to escape through the roof). To fix the gurgling toilet once and for all, you’ll need to identify the location of the clog and take steps to remove it.

    Sources indicate that ridgid’s Power Spin+ has an easy-to-use pull trigger and handle; can be attached to a power drill to dislodge serious blockages. Read the review.

    Addressing clogs is key to fixing air bubbles in your toilet—but not all clogs are created equal. A few troubleshooting steps can help you identify whether the solution is DIY-friendly, or if it’s time to call a plumber.

    Recent findings suggest that if the cause of the gurgling is in the drainpipe, simply plunging the toilet might create enough pressure to dislodge a light-to-moderate clog. Bathroom fixtures (tub, sink, shower) often connect to the same drain line that runs from the toilet, so you’ll want to seal off these drains with duct tape before plunging. If you plunge without sealing the drains, the pressure plunging creates can escape through other drain fixtures instead of dislodging the clog.

    According to recent reports, start by selecting the right plunger, such as the JS Jackson accordion-style plunger, which was a top pick in our researched guide to the best plungers. With the toilet bowl full of water, fit the head of the plunger tightly to the drain hole in the bottom of the bowl. Try to dislodge the clog with 10 to 15 firm pumping motions, then wait to see if the toilet gurgles again. If you don’t have a plunger handy, other ways of unclogging a toilet without one may be just as effective. However, if the gurgling continues, move on to the following steps.

    According to recent reports, A sewer snake (also known as a plumber’s snake or plumber’s auger) can often remove tough clogs in a drainpipe that plunging can’t manage. Featuring a long cable and a head with cutting blades for chopping through stubborn clogs, the best drain snakes may even have a manual or motorized crank.

    It has been revealed that if you’re not sure how to snake a toilet, a manual toilet auger ($25 to $100 at home-improvement stores) is inserted into the toilet bowl. As you turn the crank, the head works its way down the drainpipe, cutting through clogs. This type of auger is limited to the distance of its cable reach, generally 5 to 15 feet.

    Sources indicate that if a clog is so deep in the drainpipe that a small sewer snake cannot reach it, you can upgrade to a motorized auger that will reach 50+ feet, or rent a medium-sized drain cleaner from a home improvement store. Renting the equipment for an afternoon might run you $40 to $50, whereas calling a plumber to snake the drain could run you $150 to $300. Additional repairs, such as removing tree roots from a sewer line or fixing a broken sewer line, may be even costlier.

    Sources indicate that since the auger head on a motorized sewer snake is often too large to wind its way through the toilet bowl, the toilet should be removed from its base and the auger inserted into the drainpipe at floor level. When the machine is turned on, the auger will work its way down the line, its razor-sharp blades cutting through tough clogs.

    For clogs even deeper in the sewer line—as far out as the middle of your yard—you’ll want to auger the lines from the sewer cleanout, which is just outside of your home, directly over the sewer pipe. To locate the cleanout, check your basement or crawlspace to see where the main sewer line exits your house. Many cleanout pipes extend a few inches above the ground and feature a large PVC cap, but others may terminate just below ground level. You may need to do a little digging to uncover it. Once you’ve removed the cap from the cleanout pipe with an adjustable wrench, auger the sewer line from there. If the toilet gurgling stops, you’ve successfully removed the sewer clog that caused it; if the sounds continue, try troubleshooting the vent stack.

    Sources indicate that checking and clearing the vent stack requires getting on the roof, so if you’re not completely comfortable with that, be safe and call the pros. Here’s how to check the vent stack yourself:.

    Vent clogs are often caused by leaves and debris, or even the carcass of a small animal that got stuck in the pipe. If the clog is within a few feet of the top of the pipe, you may be able to remove it with a straightened-out wire coat hanger or a toilet brush. Deeper clogs can often be removed by running water from a garden hose in the pipe, which can dislodge the clog, washing it down the pipe and out through the sewer.

    It has been revealed that can a gurgling toilet fix itself? Unfortunately, the answer is no. If the troubleshooting methods above failed to silence your gurgling toilet bowl, it’s time to call the plumber. Plumbers have specialized emergency plumbing tools and equipment, such as powerful sewer augers that can chop through anything blocking the main sewer line.

    Industry observers note that according to Roto-Rooter, gurgling toilets can also indicate that tree roots have grown into the sewer line. If this is the case, repairs are best left to a professional plumber. Professionals can use mini cameras that drop into vent stacks to locate the source of the problem. There’s also a slim chance that the main sewer line in your yard has broken or collapsed, in which case excavation and professional repairs might be necessary.

    The two most essential factors in a heated vest are how well it fits and how well it keeps the wearer warm. The first step in the testing process was to fully charge the batteries (for those that came with batteries), so we charged each overnight to ensure it was fully charged.

    We connected the batteries (be aware that some battery connections take a while to find) and cycled the vests through their heat levels. We then set the vests to the High setting and noted how long the batteries lasted. We wore each vest outdoors and made a note of how comfortable it was when reaching, bending, and twisting, and we also observed how well it blocked the cold wind.

    After wearing each vest outdoors for about an hour, we removed it but left the heat zones turned to High. We then checked every 30 minutes to see if the vest was still producing heat and made a note of the time when it stopped heating.

    In a recent development, we also examined the quality of the vest’s materials and the seam quality. We scored each vest using a rubric and then tallied the final scores to choose the best ones for this lineup.

    Heated vests will help raise the body temperature when it’s chilly outdoors, but because they don’t have sleeves, they’re not a substitute for a full coat if the temperatures are bitterly cold. Wear a heated vest over a flannel shirt or sweater when just a bit of warmth is needed or under a heavier coat to provide a temperature boost. Heated jackets are often better for severe cold or long exposure and are worth considering if shoppers often need to be outside during frigid weather.

    In a recent development, when the vests started arriving, we noticed that virtually all of them were either black or dark gray. When it comes to heated vests, function takes precedence over fashion.

    Industry observers note that the outer shell of a heated vest can be made of several materials, including fleece or a moisture-resistant polyester blend. Inside, there is usually a fleece lining for softness and comfort. Some heated vests feature an outer shell that is moisture-resistant but not completely waterproof, which can trap sweat against the body and create a clammy feeling. The most comfortable heated vests are often made from breathable fabrics that wick sweat away from the body.

    Sources indicate that many of the heated vests we tested feature an outer nylon shell, which is a good option for moisture resistance when worn as an outer layer. Others were thinner and less water-resistant but designed to be paired with an overcoat, so they would be protected from getting wet.

    In a recent development, the heating elements in a heated vest include a series of panels with wires that warm different sections of the body. These strategic panels are most commonly placed along the upper back and the chest area of the vest.

    In a recent development, some heated vests offer even more panels, often located in the lower front, lower back, and sometimes along the back of the neck if the vest has a high collar. Depending on the outdoor temperature and the level of added warmth needed, some people may be happy with just a few panels, while others may want as many as possible.

    Recent findings suggest that two or three temperature settings are the norm, allowing users to select just the right temperature for the environment, though some heated vests have only one: on or off. The temperature-selection button is commonly found on the vest’s front, either above a chest pocket or on a lower front pocket for convenience.

    Industry observers note that some temperature-control buttons feature different-colored lights that make it easy to identify which heating mode is right now in use, such as a red light for the highest temperature, a yellow light for a medium temperature, and a green light for the lowest temperature. By simply pushing the temperature button, wearers can adjust the warmth level to the most comfortable heat setting.

    In a recent development, heated vests require rechargeable batteries or a chargeable power bank. The low-voltage lithium-ion batteries (5 volts and 7.4 volts) used in heated vests will usually hold a charge for 4 to 10 hours, depending on the heat level. The battery will drain more swiftly at a higher temperature than it will at a Medium or Low setting.

    According to recent reports, most rechargeable batteries have a similar lifespan, but after 3 to 5 years, a lithium-ion battery typically loses some capacity and won’t hold a charge as long as it once did. Extreme cold will also shorten battery life. If the vest doesn’t stay warm as long as it did when it was first purchased, replacing the battery might be all that’s needed to get it back into top working order.

    Although heated vests run on electricity, the voltage is so low that there is no risk of being electrocuted. Many heated vests are even safe in the washing machine—once the battery has been removed, of course.

    The rechargeable lithium-ion battery contains ingredients that can irritate skin, eyes, and mucus membranes, causing itching, burning, and redness. If a lithium-ion battery becomes damaged and its contents leak, discard the battery and replace it with a new one.

    Many of the vests we tested were advertised as “moisture-resistant” or “water-resistant,” but the owner’s manual that comes with each warns the user not to wear it if the interior lining is wet, due to a risk of shock.

    Industry observers note that any water-resistant properties relate solely to the outer shell of the vests, which is usually made from nylon to block both wind and light rain or snow. The vests are typically washable on the delicate cycle (with the batteries removed) and then hung up to dry.

    Many heated vests feature two front pockets at the waist that can come in handy for storing items like a wallet or keys. Some vests offer additional chest pockets and provide a special zippered pocket to keep a mobile phone safe.

    While most vests have a zipper front, several button-front models are available as well as hooded models to keep wearers’ heads warm and dry in cold or inclement weather. Some heated vests feature a built-in timer that will automatically turn off the heat after a few hours; if more heat is desired, just turn the vest back on.

    Wearing a heated vest during outdoor activities can make the difference between feeling cold and miserable or being warm and comfortable. If this is your first time shopping for a heated vest, you likely have some questions. Below are answers to some popular queries about heated vests.

    According to recent reports, yes, the lithium-ion batteries used to generate heat are low voltage and will not cause an electrical shock. But while the outer nylon shell may be water-resistant, the inner lining is not, so don’t wear a heated vest if the inside is wet. If moisture gets into the battery connections, it increases the risk of shock.

    You can wear a heated vest under a larger coat for maximum heat, or over a thick shirt or sweater for just a bit of added warmth.

    A heated vest can add some welcome warmth, whatever the temperature might be when you get chilly. For many individuals, that’s around 40 to 50 degrees Fahrenheit. They’re also suitable for pairing with an overcoat if you need to stay warm and toasty in even colder temperatures.

    Recent findings suggest that initiative to charge the lithium-ion battery for at least 3 hours to reach full capacity before wearing your heated vest. Or better yet, overnight, if possible.

    In a recent development, most heated vests are machine washable, but be sure to remove the battery first. Check the apparel’s label for additional instructions about suitable water temperature and whether you can place the vest in the dryer or should hang it up to dry.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In this video, Andrew LeGrand of LeGrand Tiling Company walks through a full backsplash installation, sharing his product recommendations and pro tips along the way. From prepping the work area, laying out the tile, and mixing and applying thinset, to cutting and installing the tile, grouting the tile, cleaning the tile surface, and sealing the tile, you’ll learn how to get quality results every time. Whether you’re tackling your first tile project or want to tighten up your technique, this video shows exactly how a pro gets it done.

    Hey guys, this is Andrew LeGrand with LeGrand Tiling. We’re in Upstate Upcoming York and we’re working on a backsplash here. In preparation we took off all the switch plates and all the outlet plates.

    In a recent development, although drywall is a good substrate to install tile to, behind wet areas I do like to add waterproof board, and between the countertop and the waterproof board I’ll do a bead of silicone just to ensure some waterproofing back there. So we’re using a 3×6 tile. We’re going to do very minimal spacing, and we’re going to do a subway pattern throughout this backsplash.

    With these ceramic tiles what I’ll do is I’ll soak them for a couple minutes. What that does is introduces water to the ceramic, and it gives me a better bond with my thinset. Now these tiles have been soaking for a couple minutes. We’re going to pull them out and let them dry for a little bit before we install them.

    Recent findings suggest that on my backsplashes, I like to use MULTIMAX™ Lite. It’s a premium thinset. When I’m mixing, I like to add water to my bucket and then add the thinset that is desired, and I start mixing.

    I’m looking for kind of a frosty peanut butter, toothpaste-type consistency. After I mix it for one minute and have the consistency that I like, then I let it slake for five minutes, and then I whip it back up before using it to install.

    Industry observers note that I’m going to use a drywall knife to first add the mud to the drywall, and then I’ll be able to come through with my notch trowel and add the notches. I’ll take my drywall knife here or my margin trowel and I’ll just back-butter the tile. I’ll adhere it to the wall, and I’ll give it a little bit of a wiggle just to collapse those ridges.

    And that is the kind of the coverage we want. Overall that’s pretty good coverage. As you can see, I am installing the tile directly to the countertop. There is a slight natural edge to this tile, and that’ll give it some space so sealant can grab in there.

    In a recent development, now that we have our first row installed, we’re doing a brick pattern, so I’m going to measure my tile. It’s about 5-1/16. So what I’ll do is go 2-1/2 and just a hair over 2-1/2 right there, and then I’ll put this tile on my score and snap, lining it up with the centerline, snap it, and then take this piece, put this on the inside there.

    When it comes to doing outlets, I typically like to set my tile tight up against the one to the right and line up so the outlet is where it needs to be.

    I will make a mark over here at the end of this outlet box and a mark over here, and then I’ll take my tile, set it on top of there, and I will make a mark just about here, trying not to cover up where the screw mounts to the box.

    Now that we’ve finished this section of the backsplash, we’re going to add a metal trim piece along the wall here to bridge the tile and the drywall. I’m going to take some thinset on my drywall knife, and I’m just going to push thinset into those voids to adhere it to the wall. We’re going to add a little bit more thinset to the wall. We’ll come through with our notch trowel and add our notches to the wall.

    Industry observers note that now that I’ve finished up this backsplash here, we’re going to roll on to installing this wall into our lower section and our wet wall and start installing tile there. So we’ve finished installing our tile. We’re now going to mix up a little bit of grout, just about half the bag.

    We’re going to add a little bit of water. And then I prefer to mix by hand. We want to mix our grout for a couple minutes until we have a smooth consistency, and then we’ll let it sit for five minutes and come back and stir it back up. To grout, I’m going to take my grout float, get it in the bucket, just get a little bit on it, and just push that grout right into the grout joints.

    Now that we’ve given our grout about 30 minutes to set up, we’re going to take a clean sponge and a clean bucket of water and we’re going to wipe down our grout.

    Now that we’re done wiping with our sponge and getting the majority of the grout off the surface of our tile, we’re going to give it about 10 minutes. We’ll come back through with a damp microfiber and wipe off any excess and smooth out the grout joints.

    Now that our grout is cured, we’re going to seal our grout. First, we’re going to wipe down with a dry microfiber to remove any excess dust or debris, and then we’ll come through, put the sealer on this microfiber, and apply it to our grout surface.

    Now that we’ve applied the sealer, we’re going to let it sit for about 10 or 15 minutes. We’ll come through with a dry rag and wipe off all the excess sealer.

    In a recent development, now that we’ve sealed our tile, we’re going to move on to the final step. We’re going to use 100% silicone in between where our tile meets our countertop, where our tile meets in the inside corner, and where our tile meets the bottom of the cabinets.

    According to recent reports, one thing I like while installing silicone is wearing a pair of gloves, so that as you run your finger and tool that silicone, it doesn’t get on your skin and contaminate the silicone. Another thing I like is doing my best to keep the tip of my silicone as clean as possible while I’m running my bead.

    According to recent reports, the backsplash is done. We’ve got our outlet and switch covers on. We’re going to remove our site protection and clean up.

    Breaking: How to Clean a Furnace

    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    • Recent findings suggest that don’t wait until temperatures plummet to perform basic electric and gas furnace maintenance and cleaning.
    • The following steps can help you learn how to clean a furnace and keep the unit in tip-top shape throughout the winter.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›.

    Recent findings suggest that don’t wait until temperatures plummet to perform basic electric and gas furnace maintenance and cleaning. By performing basic furnace cleaning and maintenance tasks now, you can avoid the expensive inconvenience (and danger) of leaving your family without heat during the coldest part of the year. You can also actually prolong the life of your furnace and coax it into operating at maximum energy efficiency.

    The following steps can help you learn how to clean a furnace and keep the unit in tip-top shape throughout the winter.

    There are several reasons why it’s necessary for a homeowner to either know how to clean a gas furnace or know when to schedule a professional cleaning with an HVAC expert. However, the most crucial reason is that regular cleaning and maintenance help to extend the life of a furnace and HVAC system, while reducing the number of costly repairs and breakdowns.

    In a recent development, most system failures stem from dirt and dust choking out vital parts like the burners and flame sensors. Learning simple cleaning tasks, like how to clean a flame sensor on a furnace or how to clean the burners, prevents small problems from turning into expensive emergency repairs. Routine removal of soot, dirt, and dander as part of a furnace tune-up reduces wear and tear on internal components, helping the unit last its full 10- to 15-year expected lifespan.

    If you still aren’t sure this is a necessary part of HVAC maintenance, check out this list of additional reasons for why it’s best to clean your furnace.

    Bobvila.com may earn a commission from purchases made through these links.

    It has been revealed that most common furnace maintenance is not complicated—you just have to have a good vacuum cleaner and some basic tools and supplies. However, you do need to take a few precautions, so make sure to read and follow these steps in order to avoid skipping any important safety measures.

    Sources indicate that always turn off the electrical power and fuel supply before you start any furnace project. You can turn off the electricity by either toggling the on-off switch on the unit or turning off the breaker in your breaker panel.

    According to recent reports, in order to turn off the gas, locate the fuel shutoff valve. The location of the valve varies depending on whether you have an oil or a gas furnace. The valve should either be near the oil tank for an oil furnace or on the incoming gas pipe for a gas furnace. After you locate it, turn the valve off.

    Industry observers note that wait several minutes to allow hot components to cool down before opening any panels. While you wait, use a microfiber cleaning cloth to wipe down the exterior of the furnace.

    With a screwdriver, unscrew and remove the upper and lower service panels to gain access to the interior cavity of the furnace.

    The Ridgid vac has a 7-foot heavy-duty locking hose and a 15-foot cord and made quick work of both wet and dry messes in our tests. Read the review.

    Locate the small metal flame sensor rod near the burner assembly (often marked with a red or white connector). Unscrew and carefully pull the sensor out. Then gently scrub away soot or white-gray oxidation using fine-grit sandpaper or a wire brush until the metal shines. When you are done, wipe it clean and screw it back in.

    In a recent development, basic furnace filters are designed to trap dust, dirt, and airborne particulates before they can enter the furnace and potentially damage its components. As filters become full, they become unable to filter the air. While some filters can be cleaned, while others need to be replaced. During the heating season, clean or replace the furnace filter every 1 to 3 months.

    Sources indicate that detach the burner cover and carefully slide or lift the burners out if they appear dirty or rusty. Brush any surface debris away with a soft-bristle brush or wash them in warm soapy water. After washing, rinse the burners thoroughly and dry them completely with compressed air before reinstalling.

    Industry observers note that inspect the blower wheel fins for heavy dust buildup with a flashlight or your phone camera. If you see dust, use your vacuum to clean loose dust from the fins using a brush attachment. However, when the blower wheel is heavily caked in grime, it’s best to call a technician for a deep wash. It isn’t recommended for an inexperienced DIYer to remove the blower, so it’s best to stick to light vacuuming and dusting for this part of the process.

    Put all access panels and doors back into place, ensuring any safety door switches are properly depressed, then turn the gas valve back on (parallel to the pipe) and restore power at the breaker or switch. Set your thermostat to Heat and watch to make sure the igniter glows, the gas catches smoothly into clean blue flames, and the blower kicks on.

    Sources indicate that ideally, you should clean the furnace once a year to keep it in top condition before the fall heating season begins. It also is a good idea to perform a quick clean in the spring, vacuuming up any dust or soot. Proper care and maintenance will help prolong the life of your furnace, and keep it running at peak efficiency.

    According to recent reports, strategy to replace or clean your furnace air filters every 1 to 3 months, clean the furnace about once a year in the spring, and hire a pro to inspect and deep clean it every fall. Also, consider having your home’s air ductwork cleaned every 3 to 5 years.

    Although basic furnace maintenance can be handled by most homeowners, it makes sense to hire a professional for some tasks. For example, if you’ve noticed the furnace rumbling and can’t figure out why, then it’s best to call a pro for some on-site troubleshooting.

    Additionally, there are some cleaning jobs that should be left to the experts, so instead of trying to figure out how to clean a furnace heat exchanger, remove a blower, or clean the coils, it’s better to book a deep furnace cleaning with a trained furnace technician. Save yourself some time and potential problems by calling an HVAC pro for any of the following complications.

    Your furnace is a major investment in your home and your family’s comfort and safety. Regular cleaning and maintenance can save you money in the long run, because it will maximize the effective lifespan of your unit. Whether you are looking to maximize the efficiency and performance of a fresh or existing unit, just a couple of hours of cleaning and maintenance every year will help keep your investment in tip-top shape and make sure your family stays comfy and cozy during the colder winter months.

    Cleaning, changing filters, and lubricating your furnace are fairly simple steps in a process that really doesn’t take long. For a first-timer, it might take a few hours, since you might be dealing with unfamiliar equipment. After you have done it a few times, however, a full furnace clean should only take 1 to 2 hours. Changing the filters is even faster, and it only takes a few minutes to ensure that your air is clean and filtered.

    It has been revealed that you should clean or service your furnace when you notice weak airflow, strange smells, or a spike in your energy bills. Here are other common signs that you should clean your furnace: • The furnace turns on and off rapidly when there are dirty flame sensors, clogged filters, or blocked burners that cause the unit to overheat.• Banging, screeching, or rattling sounds can mean the blower wheel is caked in debris or motor bearings need attention.• If dust settles promptly around your furniture or return grilles soon after cleaning, your filter or blower compartment is likely overloaded.• The burner flame should burn steady and blue. A yellow flame means poor combustion and possible soot or carbon monoxide buildup.• An increase in sneezing, congestion, or dust-related irritation when the heat runs means the system is circulating allergens instead of trapping them.

    Failing to clean your furnace can lead to carbon monoxide leaks, higher energy bills, and system breakdowns. Dirt and soot can cause incomplete combustion or crack the heat exchanger, releasing invisible, odorless, and deadly carbon monoxide gas into your home.Thick accumulations of dust, lint, and debris near the burners, wiring, or moving components can overheat and spark an electrical or mechanical fire. Also, a dirty filter or blocked flame sensor can cause the furnace to repeatedly turn on and off in short bursts, failing to heat your home evenly. Additionally, clogged air filters and dirty internal parts block airflow, forcing the system to work harder and consume more fuel or electricity to heat your space. Neglected filters stop trapping dust, pollen, pet hair, and allergens, which then circulate through your vents and trigger asthma or allergy symptoms. All of this added strain wears out the blower motor, flame sensor, and other mechanical parts much faster, significantly cutting down the typical 15- to 20-year lifespan of a furnace.

    Recent findings suggest that the average cost to clean a furnace ranges from about $70 to $400, depending on the type and location of your furnace. Typically, oil furnaces will cost more since they require deeper cleaning, and any units located in the attic or crawlspace will naturally cost more due to the difficulty accessing these areas.

    We tested six air purifier and humidifier combinations for two months throughout a home, placing them in bedrooms, an office, a kitchen, and larger shared living areas. One model, the Blueair 2-in-1 Pro, had already been in long-term use for more than a year and was retested alongside the newer machines.

    We evaluated setup, controls and apps, humidification, purification response, noise, cleaning and refilling, and overall day-to-day usability. We also paid particular attention to automatic operation, noting how promptly each purifier responded when activities such as cooking or burning a candle changed surrounding air conditions. Since these are appliances many people leave visible and running continuously, design, reservoir access, maintenance, and how intrusive each unit felt during ordinary use also factored heavily into our scores and final awards.

    Living with dry and unclean air can negatively affect comfort and health. Dry indoor air can cause an uncomfortable feeling at best and cracked skin at worst. Even “clean” indoor air can benefit from an air purifier, which can remove common pollutants such as pollen, pet hair, and smoke. Air purifying is even more crucial for allergy and asthma sufferers, who may notice a reduction in symptoms with a good air purifier.

    There is a difference between air purifier and humidifier units: Purifiers remove pollutants from air, whereas humidifiers add moisture to the air. Combination units do both. Consider the following factors when shopping for the best air humidifier and purifier: room size, filtration system, reservoir capacity, and additional user-friendly features.

    Air humidifier and purifier combo units are intended for use in one room. (Whole-house humidifier and air purifier options are separate products and are usually professionally installed into the home’s climate control system.) For optimal performance, a unit should most often be used in a room that is the size of the manufacturer’s recommendation.

    Recent findings suggest that it’s possible to use a unit rated for a larger room in a smaller room, however, as long as a unit has a humidistat and auto-shutoff. The humidistat measures the ideal humidity, usually between 30 and 50 percent, and triggers the unit to shut off when ideal humidity is reached. Just know that if there’s no auto shut-off feature, a large humidifier can make a small room too humid.

    While it’s important to take room size into account, the recommended room size can sometimes be misleading, so consider the CADR rating as well, explained ahead.

    Sources indicate that air humidifiers and purifiers can have a few filter types, and many have a multistage filtration system. These systems can include activated carbon filters to remove odors, large particle filters, dust and pet hair filters, and the “gold standard,” HEPA (high-efficiency particulate air) filters. HEPA filters remove over 99.97 percent of dust mites, mold, pollen, bacteria, and other airborne particles measuring 0.3 microns (and actually trap smaller and larger particles even more effectively).

    Recent findings suggest that these extremely effective humidifiers with filters are shown to improve air quality. Shoppers who are interested in an air purifier and humidifier for allergies will want to look for a unit with a HEPA filter.

    Industry observers note that air humidifiers and purifiers have a CADR (clean air delivery rate) score. This rating is used to measure an air purifier’s efficiency. It indicates the amount of filtered air a unit can deliver per minute and is often broken down into separate ratings for tobacco smoke, dust, and pollen. Products certified by the AHAM (Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers) are proven to live up to their CADR rating.

    Recent findings suggest that the higher the CADR score, the faster the filtration system. CADR is often used to calculate the appropriate square footage for a unit. The AHAM recommends that the CADR score of a unit should be a minimum of two-thirds of the room’s square footage.

    According to recent reports, some units don’t display a CADR score and only display the room size the unit is suitable for. Knowing the CADR score is more reliable, as some manufacturers will recommend a room size that does not align with the AHAM’s recommendations. According to the AHAM, the recommended room size should be based on 4.8 air changes per hour (how many times the purifier cleans and circulates the air in a room). Many manufacturers will share a recommended room size based on only one or two air changes per hour to boost their square footage recommendation.

    Air humidifier purifier units have a reservoir to hold water, which the machine turns into moisture to release into the air. The unit’s overall size (and therefore reservoir size) often corresponds to its suited room size. Small units are usually ideal for small or medium-size rooms, but they may need more frequent refilling if they also have a small reservoir tank. Larger units will need less frequent topping up, but they’ll also take up more space.

    Sources indicate that keep in mind that usage habits will also affect how often the water tank needs refilling. Many air humidifiers and purifiers have a water tank between a half gallon and 1 gallon, but extra-large options are also available—we’ve included one with a 3-gallon-plus capacity on this list.

    In our testing, reservoir design mattered almost as much as capacity. A slightly smaller tank that’s easy to remove, carry, and clean can be less frustrating than a larger reservoir with awkward access.

    Daily cleaning and maintenance can ensure that your air cleaner humidifier operates correctly and does not emit any harmful particles into a space. Owners are encouraged to use distilled water in their humidifiers and purifiers to reduce general maintenance and germ buildup. Wash and dry the humidifier after each use to remove any potential bacteria, mold, minerals, and chemicals.

    The Environmental Protection Agency advises using a 3 percent hydrogen peroxide solution to clean these machines every few days, clearing out any potential toxins. Finally, filters should be replaced as recommended by the manufacturer to ensure all contaminants are being removed.

    Recent findings suggest that A good air humidifier and purifier should have a built-in humidistat that measures room humidity and adjusts operation accordingly. At minimum, the humidifier should shut off once the set humidity is reached to prevent the room from becoming overly damp.

    Industry observers note that digital onboard controls are also useful, especially when they make it easy to adjust fan speed, humidity targets, and operating modes. Some models include a remote control for making changes from across the room.

    It has been revealed that smart models can connect to Wi-Fi and a smartphone app for monitoring air quality, setting schedules, and changing settings remotely. In our testing, however, we often found the physical controls faster for everyday adjustments. Apps were most useful for checking air-quality data and receiving maintenance alerts.

    Filter-change and refill reminders are particularly helpful, whether they appear in an app or through indicator lights on the unit itself.

    It has been revealed that choosing the best air humidifier and purifier for your home really comes down to choosing a user-friendly option that’s suitable for the intended room size. Still wondering if a combined purifier and humidifier is the right choice? Read on for some frequently asked questions and answers on room air purifiers and humidifiers to narrow down the best option for your needs.

    Recent findings suggest that no, air purifiers do not dry out a space’s air supply, especially when the machine includes a humidifier. These machines are designed to improve indoor air quality by removing particles, microorganisms, and gases.

    It has been revealed that no—air purifiers trap mold and common allergen particles in the air, but not the mold spores that may be present somewhere in the home. To completely get rid of a mold problem, consider an effective mold remover.

    In a recent development, yes. Air purifiers and humidifiers perform different functions, so they can be used at the same time without interfering with each other. An air purifier filters airborne pollutants, while a humidifier adds moisture to dry air. In fact, combination units like the ones we tested are specifically designed to perform both jobs from the same location. Just avoid over-humidifying the room; aim to keep indoor humidity between about 30 and 50 percent.

    Recent findings suggest that yes. Air purifiers are designed to be left on at all times. In fact, running an air purifier as often as possible is the most effective way to improve air quality. After all, indoor air quality is always changing depending on the air quality outside and what you do inside, like cooking, cleaning, or smoking. Leaving the air purifier on will help improve air quality, regardless of exterior factors.

    Industry observers note that in a way, yes. Stand-alone humidifiers don’t remove pollutants, but they do improve overall air quality by making the air feel more comfortable. Humidifiers can help keep indoor air humidity at an ideal level between 30 and 50 percent. Keeping indoor humidity in this sweet spot reduces the chance of mold growth and dust mites, which in turn can help maintain better air quality. To further improve air quality, look for a combined air purifier humidifier unit.

    It has been revealed that no, not necessarily. A humidifier is useful if you struggle with dry indoor air. It’s not necessary (and can even be detrimental) to run a humidifier in humid homes. If the air in your home often dips beneath 30 percent, consider using a humidifier.

    According to recent reports, the unit needs to run for a certain length of time for you to take full advantage of the air purifier and humidifier benefits. Effectiveness depends on a wide range of factors, including the room size, the air purifier’s filtration system, the unit’s settings, and the surrounding humidity level. Consider the CADR rating and recommended room size to find a suitable unit. When these metrics are all taken into account, a good air purifier should create cleaner air in around just 15 minutes.

    Sources indicate that paul Rankin is a product tester and editor with years of experience reviewing home appliances and everyday gear. He takes a hands-on, real-world approach to testing, focusing on performance, usability, maintenance, and value to help readers understand what products are actually like to live with.
